chunks.text: Durante el período se realizaron **99 consultas** en César Nieves y las jornadas móviles en el Polideportivo José María Vargas alcanzaron un acumulado de **2.678 consultas**. Asimismo, la OIM impartió capacitaciones dirigidas a **29 trabajadores humanitarios**, incluyendo personal de HIAS y de los equipos de salud mental, apoyo psicológico y CCCM de la OIM, abordando Primeros Auxilios Psicológicos (PAP), abordaje comunitario y metodologías institucionales para la prestación de servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicológico. A la fecha, las intervenciones apoyadas por la OIM han permitido realizar **7.641 consultas médicas a 6.753 personas afectadas**. La OIM continuó las actividades de registro y gestión de información mediante el Sistema Unificado de Gestión de Información (IMS) en los campamentos transitorios. Durante el período, equipos de la Matriz de Seguimiento de Desplazamiento (DTM, por sus siglas en inglés) continuaron el levantamiento de información en comunidades afectadas por los terremotos en **La Guaira y Morón (Carabobo).** Asimismo, se realizaron evaluaciones de necesidades de alojamiento en **Guatire (Miranda)**.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #20 (4 al 6 de agosto 2026)
chunks.text: La OIM continuó las actividades de registro y gestión de información mediante el Sistema Unificado de Gestión de Información (IMS) en los campamentos transitorios. Durante el período, equipos de la Matriz de Seguimiento de Desplazamiento (DTM, por sus siglas en inglés) continuaron el levantamiento de información en comunidades afectadas por los terremotos en **La Guaira y Morón (Carabobo).** Asimismo, se realizaron evaluaciones de necesidades de alojamiento en **Guatire (Miranda)**. A la fecha, la OIM ha caracterizado **51 alojamientos afectados por los terremotos**. En protección, la OIM continuó brindando asistencia legal, gestión de casos, actividades de protección infantil, prevención de la trata de personas, prevención de la violencia contra mujeres y niñas y mecanismos de información comunitaria. chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 32** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **07 August 2026** **Time: 2:00 pm** **Highlights** **Nearly 212,000 people affected by the earthquakes have accessed humanitarian assistance and essential services** through a coordinated multi-sector response involving humanitarian organizations, United Nations agencies, communities, and national and local authorities. As of 03 August, authorities reported **6,125 deaths and 60,992 people that received care at hospitals**, **and 16,740 injuries** as a result of the earthquakes. The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency to address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months**. **Situation overview** Venezuela continues to face the consequences of the two major earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck the north-central region of the country on 24 June at 18:00 local time, causing significant humanitarian impacts and damage to infrastructure. The first earthquake, measuring 7.2, was centered along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo).

chunks.text: To date, 5,804 children under five, pregnant and lactating women, and caregivers have been reached through health facilities, community outreach and transitional camps across the seven earthquake-affected states.  They has reached 3,275 children aged 6–59 months with nutritional screening, 1,724 caregivers with infant and young child feeding counselling, and 805 pregnant women with micronutrient supplementation.  Essential nutrition supplies distributed to prioritized health facilities have strengthened their capacity to serve up to 77,000 children and pregnant and lactating women in the coming months.  During World Breastfeeding Week (1–7 August), UNICEF and partners are conducting daily activities in the three existing breastfeeding corners and establishing five additional corners in transitional camps. Protection (including Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence)  The Protection Cluster, the Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence Areas of Responsibility, together with 36 partner organizations, reached 13,476 people in 50 transitional camps located in La Guaira (19), Distrito Capital (16), and Miranda (15).  Since the onset of the earthquake response, 69 per cent of the people assisted are women, of which 63 per cent are adult women, 29.7 per cent are girls and adolescents, and 7.2 per cent are older women. Men account for 31 per cent of those reached, of which 43.8 per cent are adult men, 50.4 per cent are boys and adolescents, and 5.8 per cent are older men. United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) OCHA | 5  Among those reached, 65 per cent accessed psychosocial and socio-emotional support activities, helping restore daily routines and strengthen emotional coping and grief management; 21 per cent received specialized protection services, including case management support, legal counseling, and legal assistance. Additionally, 12 per cent participated in information sessions and received targeted guidance on protection risks.  Activities led by UNFPA and its implementing partners AVESA, PLAFAM, and Tinta Violeta reached 1,152 people through awareness-raising sessions.

chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 32** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **07 de agosto de 2026** **Hora: 2:00 pm** **Destacados** **Cerca de 212.000 personas afectadas por los terremotos (54% mujeres y niñas) han accedido a asistencia humanitaria y servicios esenciales** mediante una respuesta multisectorial coordinada entre organizaciones humanitarias, entidades de las Naciones Unidas, comunidades y autoridades nacionales y locales. Hasta el 03 de agosto, las autoridades reportaron **6.125 personas fallecidas, 60.992 personas atendidas en hospitales y 16.740 heridas a causa de los terremotos**. El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los** **próximos seis meses.** **Situación general** Venezuela continúa enfrentando las consecuencias de los dos sismos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio a las 18:00 hora local en la región centro-norte del país, los cuales provocaron importantes impactos humanitarios y daños en infraestructura.

chunks.text: Alcance de la Respuesta Humanitaria  Al 06 de agosto, 211.700 personas afectadas por los terremotos (54% mujeres y niñas) accedieron a servicios esenciales y asistencia humanitaria a través de la respuesta coordinada entre comunidades, entidades de Naciones Unidas, organizaciones humanitarias, autoridades y donantes. La respuesta, implementada por al menos 75 organizaciones, comprendió más de 4.000 actividades. Más del 90% de las personas alcanzadas se concentra en los siete estados directamente afectados, particularmente en La Guaira, Miranda, Distrito Capital y Aragua. Las intervenciones incluyeron actividades de seguridad alimentaria; agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH); salud; alojamiento; nutrición; protección, incluida la protección de niñas, niños y adolescentes y la respuesta a la violencia basada en género (VBG); y educación.  Para más información sobre el alcance de la respuesta humanitaria, consulte la infografía 5W: Respuesta Humanitaria por Sector Seguridad Alimentaria1  Desde finales de junio, 29 socios del Clúster de Seguridad Alimentaria y Medios de Vida han alcanzado a más de 240.000 personas en 56 parroquias de los municipios afectados. Esta cobertura representa el 20% de la meta sectorial establecida para 1,2 millones de personas.  Hasta la fecha, la respuesta incluye la distribución de 98.000 canastas alimentarias familiares, 91.000 canastas listas para consumir, más de 1,5 millones de comidas calientes y más de 12.000 transferencias monetarias destinadas a cubrir las necesidades alimentarias más urgentes.  Diez parroquias del Distrito Capital y La Guaira, junto con 14 municipios de los estados Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, Miranda y Yaracuy, registran una cobertura inferior al 10% de sus metas territoriales, y la mayoría de ellas no ha recibido asistencia hasta la fecha.

En total, durante el período de reporte, se distribuyeron 544,996 toneladas métricas de asistencia alimentaria.  Aunque La Guaira continúa siendo la zona más afectada, se prevé ampliar la respuesta a Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón y Yaracuy, de acuerdo con las evaluaciones en curso y las necesidades identificadas, fortaleciendo además los mecanismos de retroalimentación comunitaria y monitoreo para garantizar una respuesta transparente y centrada en las personas. Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene  Desde el inicio de la emergencia, 25 organizaciones han alcanzado a 129.048 personas en 14 municipios de siete estados, con un enfoque prioritario en La Guaira, Miranda, Distrito Capital y Aragua. Las actividades se han centrado principalmente en garantizar el acceso a agua potable segura, la distribución de artículos de higiene y el fortalecimiento de los servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH, por sus siglas en inglés) en comunidades, campamentos transitorios y establecimientos de salud.  UNICEF y sus socios implementadores Acción contra el Hambre y CISP, en coordinación con el Ministerio del Poder Popular de Atención de las Aguas (MINAGUAS), continúan realizando evaluaciones técnicas para apoyar la recuperación de la infraestructura y los servicios de agua en los estados afectados.

chunks.text: Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene  Desde el inicio de la emergencia, 25 organizaciones han alcanzado a 129.048 personas en 14 municipios de siete estados, con un enfoque prioritario en La Guaira, Miranda, Distrito Capital y Aragua. Las actividades se han centrado principalmente en garantizar el acceso a agua potable segura, la distribución de artículos de higiene y el fortalecimiento de los servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH, por sus siglas en inglés) en comunidades, campamentos transitorios y establecimientos de salud.  UNICEF y sus socios implementadores Acción contra el Hambre y CISP, en coordinación con el Ministerio del Poder Popular de Atención de las Aguas (MINAGUAS), continúan realizando evaluaciones técnicas para apoyar la recuperación de la infraestructura y los servicios de agua en los estados afectados. Asimismo, se distribuyeron 1.700 kits de higiene familiar entre la población afectada.  Las actividades de WASH de la OIM se enfocaron en garantizar el acceso a agua segura y promover prácticas esenciales de higiene entre las familias afectadas en La Guaira, Guatire (estado Miranda) y Carabobo, para reducir los riesgos para la salud pública y fortalecer las condiciones sanitarias y de higiene en los campamentos transitorios. Para ello, se distribuyeron 3.867 contenedores plegables para agua, 289 contenedores semiplegables de 10 litros y 2.836 kits de higiene.  Para mejorar el acceso a agua segura en el campamento transitorio del Campo de Golf, apoyado por las Naciones Unidas, la OIM instaló una planta de tratamiento de agua con una capacidad de producción de 20.000 litros diarios que permite cubrir las necesidades de aproximadamente 189 familias residentes en el campamento, así como de una población pendular estimada en 600 personas que acceden diariamente a los servicios disponibles.  Project HOPE distribuyó artículos individuales de higiene en campamentos transitorios en La Guaira, Miranda y Distrito Capital para apoyar las operaciones de sus clínicas móviles. Además, realiza evaluaciones de necesidades en materia de ASH en 14 establecimientos de salud de Distrito Capital, Miranda y La Guaira para identificar requerimientos de reparaciones menores e intervenciones específicas.  ADRA brindó asistencia a 1.048 familias afectadas mediante la distribución de kits de higiene, recipientes de 20 litros y tabletas purificadoras.  International Medical Corps (IMC) lleva a cabo pruebas rutinarias de calidad del agua en los campamentos transitorios y suministró 132.000 litros de agua segura mediante camiones cisterna a los campamentos transitorios de Playa Verde y Campo de Golf.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
chunks.text: **FAST FACTS** On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela consecutively, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira. Official figures have confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 17,907 people who have lost their homes. The earthquakes have compounded pre-existing humanitarian vulnerabilities, leaving millions of people with limited access to healthcare services, clean water, food and other basic services. **Our Response** International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,336 consultations since beginning operations on July 1. On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an [Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility]( to provide free medical services to affected communities.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
chunks.text: The earthquakes have compounded pre-existing humanitarian vulnerabilities, leaving millions of people with limited access to healthcare services, clean water, food and other basic services. **Our Response** International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,336 consultations since beginning operations on July 1. On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an [Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility]( to provide free medical services to affected communities. To date, we have provided 3,109 consultations through the EMT. Our teams have delivered 290,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting some 3,820 people. Our teams have so far provided 463 mental health consultations.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
chunks.text: Our teams have delivered 290,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting some 3,820 people. Our teams have so far provided 463 mental health consultations. Our team is continuing to provide services to about 130 patients per day at the EMT. As patient loads have grown, we have been able to keep up with the demand by training and hiring locally recruited staff who are now managing EMT operations as we rotate out international personnel. The integration of local staff has helped to ensure we have the human resources necessary to scale up our response in La Guaira as needs evolve, and to transition our response programming responsibly and sustainably.

The integration of local staff has helped to ensure we have the human resources necessary to scale up our response in La Guaira as needs evolve, and to transition our response programming responsibly and sustainably. International Medical Corps is also delivering medical and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services through three mobile medical units (MMUs) in La Guaira that have provided 3,336 patient consultations to date. As needs within affected communities evolve, International Medical Corps will continue to coordinate closely with national and international partners to ensure that services are targeted to areas where they will have the greatest impact.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
chunks.text: International Medical Corps is also delivering medical and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services through three mobile medical units (MMUs) in La Guaira that have provided 3,336 patient consultations to date. Our mobile teams have recently reported an increase in patients presenting with noncommunicable diseases, many of whom have likely never received treatment for their condition. As a result, many patients present at the MMUs experiencing severe complications of chronic illnesses, including diabetic ketoacidosis and advanced kidney disease, both of which can be life-threatening if left untreated. As needs within affected communities evolve, International Medical Corps will continue to coordinate closely with national and international International Medical Corps’ nurses manage a triage tent at the EMT. partners to ensure that services are targeted to areas where they will have the greatest impact. As earthquake survivors grieve their losses, they are living with fear, anxiety, sadness, sleeplessness and other stress reactions, with many requiring focused or specialized mental health care. This need has been further exacerbated by the destruction of health facilities and the limited number of MHPSS providers in the region, leading to significant increases in the number of people seeking support for post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and situational depression at our facilities. Our MHPSS team has also reported that the situation is particularly dire for vulnerable individuals such as the elderly, those with pre-existing mental illnesses and those with neurological and cognitive disorders.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
chunks.text: This need has been further exacerbated by the destruction of health facilities and the limited number of MHPSS providers in the region, leading to significant increases in the number of people seeking support for post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and situational depression at our facilities. Our MHPSS team has also reported that the situation is particularly dire for vulnerable individuals such as the elderly, those with pre-existing mental illnesses and those with neurological and cognitive disorders. In response to these urgent needs, International Medical Corps is delivering MHPSS services across our MMU and EMT operations, providing 463 MHPSS consultations since July 3. We are continuing to provide psychological first aid, basic psychosocial support, psychoeducation to promote healthy coping mechanisms, a safe space for those coming in search of support, and safe referrals for those in need of higher levels of care. We are also integrating MHPSS assistance into our medical operations—referring patients to our MHPSS staff for further support as needed to ensure that they receive comprehensive care.

chunks.text: We are continuing to provide psychological first aid, basic psychosocial support, psychoeducation to promote healthy coping mechanisms, a safe space for those coming in search of support, and safe referrals for those in need of higher levels of care. We are also integrating MHPSS assistance into our medical operations—referring patients to our MHPSS staff for further support as needed to ensure that they receive comprehensive care. Water availability, sanitation coverage and hygiene conditions across transitional camps in earthquake-affected communities remain below minimum humanitarian standards, heightening the risk of communicable diseases. In response, International Medical Corps is continuing to provide WASH services through our EMT and at transitional camps. We have delivered 30 portable toilets and eight 2,000-liter water tanks for safe water storage across settlement sites, and are continuing to provide safe water through water trucking, so far delivering 290,000 liters of clean water, benefitting an estimated 3,817 people in seven camps.

chunks.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.7 (Earthquake Response), 25 July - 3 August 2026
chunks.text: **Highlights** UNICEF continued to scale up its humanitarian response across earthquake-affected areas, supporting the continuity of essential health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, and education services for children and families in temporary camps and affected communities. To date, UNICEF has reached 25,483 people with primary health care, 22,424 children, adults, and pregnant women with routine and catch-up vaccinations, 9,412 people with critical WASH supplies, 5,804 children and caregivers with nutrition services, and 6,134 children, adolescents, and caregivers with child protection services, including MHPSS. UNICEF is supporting the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), leading the WASH and education sectors. The PDNA will inform recovery priorities and help accelerate the restoration of essential services.

chunks.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.7 (Earthquake Response), 25 July - 3 August 2026
chunks.text: UNICEF is supporting the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), leading the WASH and education sectors. The PDNA will inform recovery priorities and help accelerate the restoration of essential services. In addition to its US$137.6 million 2026 HAC appeal, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to sustain critical interventions and support the implementation of the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
chunks.text: Context Five weeks after the June 24 earthquakes in Venezuela, the death toll and affected population continue increasing. OCHA has formalized the national response into a six-month Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July–Dec. 2026). Toll: 5,546 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Rescuers describe no longer searching for survivors, and international search and rescue missions are scaling back.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
chunks.text: Toll: 5,546 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Rescuers describe no longer searching for survivors, and international search and rescue missions are scaling back. There are critical information gaps related to missing persons. Children: CECODAP estimates that over 1,400 children and adolescents remain at significant risk of harm due to the earthquake. Displacement: As of July 26, 107 transitional camps for affected populations are housing 24,477 people (87% capacity).

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
chunks.text: Children: CECODAP estimates that over 1,400 children and adolescents remain at significant risk of harm due to the earthquake. Displacement: As of July 26, 107 transitional camps for affected populations are housing 24,477 people (87% capacity). Most displaced people remain concentrated in Caracas and La Guaira. Education: According to civil society organizations, over 900 schools have been affected, including 18 school facilities that have totally collapsed and 40 that have severe structural damage. 120 teachers have been reported dead. Economic effects and reconstruction costs: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
chunks.text: Education: According to civil society organizations, over 900 schools have been affected, including 18 school facilities that have totally collapsed and 40 that have severe structural damage. 120 teachers have been reported dead. Economic effects and reconstruction costs: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate. National reconstruction cost estimates now range from USD 12–15 billion. Government and private sector banking institutions are exploring credit programs for housing repair and replacement. Humanitarian funding request: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026).

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
chunks.text: Government and private sector banking institutions are exploring credit programs for housing repair and replacement. Humanitarian funding request: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026). This is in addition to the USD 930 million humanitarian funding required for 6.2 million people in Venezuela prior to the earthquake. Priority needs as per the OCHA Rapid Needs Assessment: health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%), shelter (17%).

chunks.title: Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response appeal raises more than $7.5 million for life-saving aid
chunks.text: *With support from generous Canadians and the Government of Canada, our members are reaching more than 40,000 people with critical assistance* After back-to-back earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, Canadians rallied to support people affected through the Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response. With the Government of Canada’s matching fund, the appeal raised more than **$7.5 million** from June 25 to July 14, 2026. "We’re very moved by the generosity of Canadians," said Tiffany Baggetta, Executive Director of the Humanitarian Coalition. “Every dollar given and every dollar matched will help our members deliver life-saving relief to families affected by the Venezuela earthquakes.

chunks.title: Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response appeal raises more than $7.5 million for life-saving aid
chunks.text: "We’re very moved by the generosity of Canadians," said Tiffany Baggetta, Executive Director of the Humanitarian Coalition. “Every dollar given and every dollar matched will help our members deliver life-saving relief to families affected by the Venezuela earthquakes. We’re extremely grateful to our donors, our community and media partners, and the Government of Canada for standing with communities as they continue to face the devastating impacts of displacement and destruction.” In temporary camps and affected communities, the Humanitarian Coalition’s 12 member organizations are working tirelessly to provide essential support, such as: **Emergency food assistance** for families living in temporary shelters and other affected communities. **Safe water, sanitation and hygiene services**, including water trucking, handwashing stations, water treatment supplies and hygiene promotion activities. **Shelter and essential household items**, such as shelter kits, mattresses and kitchen supplies for families who have lost their homes and belongings. **Health services**, including mental health and psychosocial support, community health activities and rehabilitation services for people injured by the earthquakes. **Protection services** for families, including child-friendly spaces and psychosocial support. **Nutrition programs**, such as malnutrition screening for children, treatment and referral for acute malnutrition cases, and nutrition counselling. **Support for people with disabilities** and those recovering from serious injuries. As humanitarian needs in Venezuela remain high, the Humanitarian Coalition is continuing to accept donations for the[ **Venezuela Emergency Response**]( **Notes:** The Humanitarian Coalition is immensely grateful to the following supporters and charitable partners for their contributions to the Venezuela Emergency Response: Bell Media, CanadaHelps, Canadaland, Canadian Affairs, CanadianSME, CHOQFM, Cogeco Média, Corus, Fairchild Radio, Golden West Media, Jazz 91.1 FM, Métro, Rabble, Rogers tv, SJC, The Free Press, The Globe and Mail, The Walrus, TLN Media Group and Venezuelan Canadian Society of British Columbia.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #19 (31 de julio al 3 de agosto 2026)
chunks.text: El Reporte de Situación No. 19 presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, cubriendo el período comprendido entre el 31 de julio y el 3 de agosto de 2026. ## Aspectos destacados Entre el 31 de julio y el 3 de agosto, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación y gestión de campamentos, salud, protección, Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene (WASH), gestión de información y Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS). Durante el período, la OIM distribuyó **245 lonas plásticas, 234 lámparas solares, 234 bidones plegables, 235 sets de cocina, 227 kits de higiene y 74 mosquiteros** para atender necesidades prioritarias de alojamiento y enseres domésticos de familias afectadas por los terremotos. A la fecha, los equipos apoyados por la OIM han realizado **7.615 consultas médicas a 6.733 personas afectadas** mediante servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas. La OIM inició la caracterización de asentamientos comunitarios afectados por los terremotos, alcanzando **20 asentamientos en La Guaira, uno en Miranda y uno en Carabobo**, ampliando el monitoreo de necesidades y desplazamiento fuera de los campamentos transitorios. ## Actividades de la OIM La OIM continuó la cogestión de cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Polideportivo José María Vargas, Playa Grande y César Nieves, apoyando la prestación de servicios, el registro de población, los mecanismos de información comunitaria y la coordinación operativa.

En Campo de Golf continuó la asignación de nuevas carpas familiares, la ampliación de iluminación solar y la adecuación de espacios comunitarios y de atención. En Mare Abajo II inició el abordaje comunitario para promover los servicios disponibles, identificar necesidades y fortalecer los canales de comunicación con la población alojada, mientras continuaron las actividades de registro y verificación de grupos familiares. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para **796 personas pertenecientes a 221 grupos familiares**, incluyendo registro, orientación comunitaria, conectividad y restablecimiento de contacto familiar.

En protección, la OIM continuó brindando asistencia legal, gestión de casos, actividades de protección infantil, prevención de la trata de personas, prevención de la violencia contra mujeres y niñas y mecanismos de información comunitaria. Asimismo, inició actividades de abordaje comunitario en Mare Abajo II y apoyó la coordinación de una jornada de documentación que permitió a **182 personas** acceder a servicios de cedulación. Como colíder del Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales junto con ACNUR, la OIM continuó apoyando la coordinación operativa, el mapeo de servicios, la gestión de información y la planificación conjunta en los campamentos transitorios.

Como colíder del Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales junto con ACNUR, la OIM continuó apoyando la coordinación operativa, el mapeo de servicios, la gestión de información y la planificación conjunta en los campamentos transitorios. En PEAS, la OIM realizó sesiones de refrescamiento con **24 trabajadores humanitarios**, distribuyó **1.000 volantes informativos y mensajes clave** al equipo de NFI y llevó a cabo actividades de sensibilización con **15 lideresas comunitarias** y **17 trabajadores humanitarios** en Playa Grande. ## Respuesta Prevista de la OIM La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la infraestructura, la prestación de servicios, las intervenciones WASH, el apoyo en alojamiento y las actividades de Coordinación y Gestión de Campamentos (CCCM) en los campamentos transitorios. La OIM también continuará prestando servicios de salud, salud mental, apoyo psicológico y protección, al tiempo que fortalecerá los mecanismos de derivación para asistencia especializada. Asimismo, mantendrá el monitoreo de movilidad, las actividades de registro, la gestión de información, las evaluaciones en asentamientos comunitarios y la coordinación con autoridades y organizaciones implementadoras para apoyar la planificación de una respuesta basada en evidencia.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #19 (31 July to 3 August 2026)
chunks.text: The nineteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 31 July to 3 August 2026. ## Highlights Between 31 July and 3 August, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and camp coordination and management, health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). During the reporting period, IOM distributed **245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets** to address priority shelter and household needs of earthquake-affected families. To date, IOM-supported teams have delivered **7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people** through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities. IOM initiated the characterization of earthquake-affected community settlements, reaching **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, expanding needs and displacement monitoring beyond temporary accommodation sites. ## IOM Activities IOM continued co-managing five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, supporting service delivery, population registration, community information services and operational coordination.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #19 (31 July to 3 August 2026)
chunks.text: To date, IOM-supported teams have delivered **7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people** through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities. IOM initiated the characterization of earthquake-affected community settlements, reaching **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, expanding needs and displacement monitoring beyond temporary accommodation sites. ## IOM Activities IOM continued co-managing five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, supporting service delivery, population registration, community information services and operational coordination. At Campo de Golf, the allocation of new family tents, expansion of solar lighting and improvement of community and service spaces continued. At Mare Abajo II, community outreach activities began to promote available services, identify needs and strengthen communication channels with site residents, while household registration and verification activities continued. At Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for **796 people from 221 households**, including registration, community orientation, connectivity and restoring family links.

During the reporting period, IOM initiated data collection in earthquake-affected community settlements, characterizing **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, while Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) teams conducted additional assessments in Carabobo. In protection, IOM continued providing legal assistance, case management, child protection activities, trafficking in persons prevention, violence against women and girls prevention and community information services. Community outreach activities were launched in Mare Abajo II, and IOM supported the coordination of a documentation campaign that enabled **182 people** to access national identification services. As co-lead of the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group together with UNHCR, IOM continued supporting operational coordination, service mapping, information management and joint planning across temporary accommodation sites.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05 (Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026)
chunks.text: *This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.* **Summary Points** Since 05 July, an inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination and lead efforts to identify connectivity gaps and operational requirements for targeted humanitarian response support. A new inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator will assume the role on 03 August and continue supporting the response.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05 (Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026)
chunks.text: The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.* **Summary Points** Since 05 July, an inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination and lead efforts to identify connectivity gaps and operational requirements for targeted humanitarian response support. A new inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator will assume the role on 03 August and continue supporting the response. The inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator is working with UN OCHA, Comisión Nacional de Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL), Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, Digitel, G-Network, emergency.lu, Grupo Telefónica, and other partners to deploy connectivity solutions in the most affected areas. Through the Internet for Communities solution, GNetwork’s fibre internet connection will remain free for all users at Polideportivo, César Nieves, and a third site until the end of the year or until the emergency ends. This helps address immediate concerns related to service contracts and recurring connectivity costs.

Situation Overview The humanitarian situation in Venezuela remained severe during 24 – 31 July, driven primarily by the aftermath of the devastating 24 June earthquakes, which compounded pre-existing vulnerabilities linked to food insecurity, weakened public services, and chronic humanitarian needs. One month after the disaster, humanitarian actors continued to scale up life-saving assistance while recovery and reconstruction efforts of civil infrastructure advanced in heavily affected areas, particularly La Guaira, Caracas Metropolitan Area, Petare, and Catia. 1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025. Bringing logistics and emergency telecommunications under one coordination structure, the WFP-led LTC is the backbone of the entire humanitarian response, enabling humanitarian action to move, communicate, coordinate, and deliver lifesaving assistance. Many households reported reducing meal portions and skipping meals, while disrupted livelihoods and constrained market access continued to affect recovery. In response, WFP had provided food assistance to more than 120,000 people through hot meals, food baskets, ready-to-eat rations, and electronic vouchers, while planning to reach up to 500,000 people during the initial response phase Despite extensive relief efforts, humanitarian organizations warned that substantial funding gaps and growing recovery needs could hamper the response. International partners continued to appeal for additional resources to support emergency assistance, early recovery, livelihood restoration, and reconstruction efforts.

Telecommunications Overview Telecommunications and electricity remained among the most severely impacted sectors following the earthquakes. Although targeted emergency interventions and repair works have restored partial telecommunications services in key population centres, damaged network infrastructure, power instability, and intermittent connectivity disruptions persist across La Guaira, Petare, Catia, and other affected communities.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05 (Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026)
chunks.text: Telecommunications Overview Telecommunications and electricity remained among the most severely impacted sectors following the earthquakes. Although targeted emergency interventions and repair works have restored partial telecommunications services in key population centres, damaged network infrastructure, power instability, and intermittent connectivity disruptions persist across La Guaira, Petare, Catia, and other affected communities. Reliable communications remain essential for humanitarian coordination, information management, and access to assistance. While mobile network operators (MNOs), including CANTV, Movistar, and Digitel, maintained operations across most of the country, localized outages and reduced network performance continued in earthquake-affected areas. Service providers and authorities are actively restoring damaged infrastructure; however, sustained operational support is required to stabilize connectivity and close remaining coverage gaps.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05 (Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026)
chunks.text: While mobile network operators (MNOs), including CANTV, Movistar, and Digitel, maintained operations across most of the country, localized outages and reduced network performance continued in earthquake-affected areas. Service providers and authorities are actively restoring damaged infrastructure; however, sustained operational support is required to stabilize connectivity and close remaining coverage gaps. At the same time, damage to electricity transmission and distribution networks continues to disrupt households, health facilities, water systems, telecommunications equipment, and temporary displacement sites. These power constraints are slowing the restoration of essential services and complicating broader recovery efforts. Accelerated investment in telecommunications and energy infrastructure repairs, complemented by emergency connectivity solutions, remains critical to restoring reliable communications, strengthening humanitarian response capabilities, and supporting the longterm recovery of affected communities.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Country Appeal (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck on 24 June 2026. The states most affected include La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and neighbouring areas. The loss of livelihoods, disruption of health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of gender-based violence and harmful coping mechanisms, especially among women, girls and adolescents. The health system is under severe strain.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Country Appeal (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: The loss of livelihoods, disruption of health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of gender-based violence and harmful coping mechanisms, especially among women, girls and adolescents. The health system is under severe strain. Many health facilities have sustained structural damage and are facing critical shortages of medicines, medical equipment and personnel, while disruptions to electricity, water supply and supply chains continue to hamper service delivery. To respond to the crisis, UNFPA is seeking US$10 million to scale up life-saving sexual and reproductive health services and strengthen gender-based violence prevention and response across the affected areas. UNFPA is targeting 64,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric care, antenatal and postnatal care, neonatal care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, family planning services, clinical management of rape, and essential reproductive health information.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Country Appeal (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: To respond to the crisis, UNFPA is seeking US$10 million to scale up life-saving sexual and reproductive health services and strengthen gender-based violence prevention and response across the affected areas. UNFPA is targeting 64,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric care, antenatal and postnatal care, neonatal care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, family planning services, clinical management of rape, and essential reproductive health information. In addition, UNFPA is aiming to reach 57,780 people through gender-based violence prevention and response programmes, providing case management, psychosocial support, psychological first aid, the distribution of dignity kits, and awareness sessions on risk mitigation and available support services for survivors. As humanitarian needs continue to grow, these interventions are critical to protecting the health, rights and dignity of those most at risk, preventing further loss of life, and ensuring continued access to essential care as affected communities recover and rebuild.

chunks.text: Venezuela Earthquakes Country Appeal July - December 2026 Snapshot On 24 June, two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 on the Richter scale struck the northern area of Venezuela, causing widespread devastation. The most urgent needs for affected populations are healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health (SRH); safe water; food; shelter; mental health and psychosocial support; sanitation and hygiene; and specialized protection services, particularly for gender-based violence (GBV). The loss of livelihoods, disruptions to health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—especially for those residing in temporary shelters—is increasing the risk of GBV and harmful coping strategies, particularly for women, girls and adolescents. Older persons and people with disabilities also face heightened vulnerabilities and additional barriers to accessing information and protection services.

To date, 5,398 people are reported to have died and 16,740 injured.1 Authorities indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes. UNFPA United Nations Population Fund UNFPA Venezuela Earthquakes Appeal / Venezuela / July - December 2026 Sexual and reproductive health priorities UNFPA is supporting national and provincial authorities to ensure the continuity of life-saving maternal, newborn and obstetric care. In maternity wards of hospitals across La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda, UNFPA is: ● Delivering critical medical equipment and reproductive health supplies. ● Providing on-the-job training for health personnel. At displacement shelters, UNFPA and implementing partners are delivering critical sexual and reproductive health services, including: ● Antenatal care for pregnant women. ● Referrals for emergency obstetric care. ● Family planning services, including providing contraceptives and distributing condoms. ● Testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). ● Clinical management of rape. ● Conducting SRH awareness and information sessions on prenatal care, family planning services and STI prevention. Gender-based violence priorities UNFPA is delivering GBV services for women and adolescent girls through both mobile and static facilities in transitional shelters in La Guaira, providing safe spaces to deliver: ● Psychosocial support and psychological first aid. ● GBV case management. ● Legal counselling. ● Dignity kits containing essential items for health and menstrual hygiene management, along with key messages on the prevention of GBV and information on available services. ● GBV awareness-raising and information sessions on GBV risk mitigation and available support services. ● Conducting safety audits and risk and needs assessments in displacement shelters and providing technical recommendations on improvements to site planning and strengthening risk mitigation interventions. ● Training frontline responders in temporary shelters on protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), covering safeguarding, safe camp management, psychological first aid, and referral pathways.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Following the June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela, Project HOPE and its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a needs assessment across 12 health facilities and 160 households in Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira to evaluate health service capacity, WASH conditions, and community protection needs. The assessment found significant gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health and psychosocial support services, water quality monitoring, handwashing infrastructure, and protection mechanisms, despite generally strong community knowledge of disease prevention and existing health system capacity. Findings indicate that humanitarian response efforts should prioritize restoring essential health supplies and infrastructure, strengthening WASH systems, expanding mental health and protection services, and addressing barriers that prevent communities and health facilities from translating existing knowledge into effective practices.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: On June 24, 2026, Venezuela was struck by a series of major earthquakes, triggering a humanitarian emergency in the north-central region of the country. The earthquakes caused significant damage to homes, health facilities, water systems, and transportation infrastructure, affecting the response capacity of communities and institutions. The emergency occurred against a backdrop of preexisting vulnerabilities: limited access to health services, deteriorated infrastructure, and shortages of medicines and medical supplies. These conditions exacerbated the impact of the disaster. To understand the initial impact on health services, Project HOPE, through its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a Rapid Needs Assessment at 16 health facilities in the states of La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital within 48 hours of the first earthquake.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: These conditions exacerbated the impact of the disaster. To understand the initial impact on health services, Project HOPE, through its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a Rapid Needs Assessment at 16 health facilities in the states of La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital within 48 hours of the first earthquake. The findings revealed severe impacts: 43% of facilities sustained structural damage, 69% partially or completely suspended their outpatient services, and 81% reported difficulties in getting staff to their workplaces. All facilities reported an increase in demand for care, primarily due to traumatic injuries, hypertensive crises, and psychological stress. Water and electricity supplies were also affected: 63% of facilities reported interruptions in their water supply and 56% in electricity services.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: All facilities reported an increase in demand for care, primarily due to traumatic injuries, hypertensive crises, and psychological stress. Water and electricity supplies were also affected: 63% of facilities reported interruptions in their water supply and 56% in electricity services. Availability of medications was another critical challenge, with 47% of priority supplies depleted. Only 13% of facilities had disaster preparedness protocols in place. The assessment also identified an increase in the need for psychosocial support and protection, with signs of stress and anxiety among the population, as well as concerns about displacement and the loss of livelihoods.

chunks.text: Only 13% of facilities had disaster preparedness protocols in place. The assessment also identified an increase in the need for psychosocial support and protection, with signs of stress and anxiety among the population, as well as concerns about displacement and the loss of livelihoods. In response, Project HOPE and Proyecto Esperanza launched a multisectoral intervention to strengthen access to health services, improve water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) conditions, and expand support for protection and mental health Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela – July 2026 Page 2 of 15 assistance. Based on these areas of intervention, Project HOPE recently conducted another Needs Assessment to guide its response. The remainder of this report details the methods, findings, and conclusions of that assessment.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Based on these areas of intervention, Project HOPE recently conducted another Needs Assessment to guide its response. The remainder of this report details the methods, findings, and conclusions of that assessment. Methodology and Context Given the operational need for systematic and up-to-date information on access to essential services, the operational status of health facilities, and community conditions in the intervention areas, Project HOPE and Proyecto Esperanza recently conducted a Needs Assessment to generate sufficient evidence on baseline conditions. These results will guide humanitarian interventions in a timely and effective manner. This assessment covered Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira states, prioritizing the usability of the information over absolute statistical representativeness.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: These results will guide humanitarian interventions in a timely and effective manner. This assessment covered Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira states, prioritizing the usability of the information over absolute statistical representativeness. The results are intended for various audiences — including health authorities, national and international humanitarian actors, and donors — with the common goal of informing Project HOPE’s operational planning and response decisions. Objectives The purpose of this needs assessment in Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira states is to generate timely and useful information on the operational status of health services, the availability of critical supplies, the condition of WASH infrastructure, the level of access to clean water and WASH supplies, and protection conditions at the community level. The specific objectives of this assessment are: Assess the operational capacity of health facilities in relation to the population’s needs Analyze the availability of critical medicines and supplies Assess the availability of key personnel in health facilities Examine the status of health facility staff and the barriers to their ability to report to work Analyze the status of water, sanitation, and hygiene systems in health facilities Identify protection risks, especially for children Assess the psychosocial impact of the crisis on households and children Generate evidence to identify gaps and response priorities Methodology This needs assessment was conducted using a mixed-methods design, combining census-style assessments at health facilities with a sample survey at the community level.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Objectives The purpose of this needs assessment in Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira states is to generate timely and useful information on the operational status of health services, the availability of critical supplies, the condition of WASH infrastructure, the level of access to clean water and WASH supplies, and protection conditions at the community level. The specific objectives of this assessment are: Assess the operational capacity of health facilities in relation to the population’s needs Analyze the availability of critical medicines and supplies Assess the availability of key personnel in health facilities Examine the status of health facility staff and the barriers to their ability to report to work Analyze the status of water, sanitation, and hygiene systems in health facilities Identify protection risks, especially for children Assess the psychosocial impact of the crisis on households and children Generate evidence to identify gaps and response priorities Methodology This needs assessment was conducted using a mixed-methods design, combining census-style assessments at health facilities with a sample survey at the community level. Since a census-based assessment was conducted at health facilities, no sampling procedures were applied for this component as all selected facilities were included. Data collection combined direct observation, structured interviews with healthcare personnel, and a review of available institutional records. The assessment covered the availability and capacity of health services, human resources, the availability of medications and medical supplies, mental health and psychosocial support services, care and referral mechanisms for cases of gender-based violence, epidemiological surveillance systems, and community outreach activities carried out by health facilities.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Data collection combined direct observation, structured interviews with healthcare personnel, and a review of available institutional records. The assessment covered the availability and capacity of health services, human resources, the availability of medications and medical supplies, mental health and psychosocial support services, care and referral mechanisms for cases of gender-based violence, epidemiological surveillance systems, and community outreach activities carried out by health facilities. In addition, a comprehensive assessment of WASH conditions was conducted at the same facilities, including direct observation of the infrastructure and interviews with key staff members. This made it possible to gather information on water supply systems, storage capacities, water treatment mechanisms, the availability and functionality of handwashing stations, the availability and condition of sanitation facilities, waste management practices, cleaning and disinfection protocols, and infection prevention and control (IPC) mechanisms. Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela – July 2026 Page 3 of 15 At the community level, a survey was conducted among households located within the catchment areas of the health facilities supported by the project, with the aim of identifying knowledge, practices, and perceptions regarding health, WASH, protection, gender-based violence, mental health, and child protection.

chunks.text: This made it possible to gather information on water supply systems, storage capacities, water treatment mechanisms, the availability and functionality of handwashing stations, the availability and condition of sanitation facilities, waste management practices, cleaning and disinfection protocols, and infection prevention and control (IPC) mechanisms. Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela – July 2026 Page 3 of 15 At the community level, a survey was conducted among households located within the catchment areas of the health facilities supported by the project, with the aim of identifying knowledge, practices, and perceptions regarding health, WASH, protection, gender-based violence, mental health, and child protection. The sample was calculated using a cluster design, with the catchment areas of the health facilities serving as primary sampling units, based on a 95% confidence level, an expected proportion (p) of 0.50, a margin of error of ±10%, a design effect of 1.5, and a nonresponse rate of 10%. The sample was distributed proportionally among the three states, and households within each cluster were selected through community visits and defined accessibility criteria. Based on these criteria, a final sample of 160 households was established.

chunks.text: The sample was distributed proportionally among the three states, and households within each cluster were selected through community visits and defined accessibility criteria. Based on these criteria, a final sample of 160 households was established. The data was collected and reviewed by Proyecto Esperanza’s Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability, and Learning (MEAL) team, which verified the consistency, integrity, and quality of the information before cleaning, validating, and consolidating the datasets. Results were analyzed using descriptive statistics to identify the main needs and existing gaps, triangulating information from different sources to strengthen the interpretation of the findings. Locations This study was conducted within 12 health facilities and across communities in the municipalities of Libertador, Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, and Vargas, within Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira states.

Findings Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela – July 2026 Page 5 of 15 Health Findings Operational Capacity and Human Resources This assessment identified a total of 844 healthcare workers at the facilities, 79.1% of whom are women. Nursing staff constitute the largest group with 195 workers, followed by general practitioners with 114. It should be noted that two facilities (Dr. Domingo Luciani Hospital and Jesús Reguetti Outpatient Clinic) did not report staffing information at the time of the survey; therefore, the aggregate figures reflect the situation at 10 of the 12 centers assessed. The most critical gaps in human resources are among specialized roles.

chunks.text: It should be noted that two facilities (Dr. Domingo Luciani Hospital and Jesús Reguetti Outpatient Clinic) did not report staffing information at the time of the survey; therefore, the aggregate figures reflect the situation at 10 of the 12 centers assessed. The most critical gaps in human resources are among specialized roles. Across the entire network of facilities evaluated, only one psychiatrist, six psychologists, and six social workers were identified. Emergency Services At time of data collection, 90.9% of the facilities offered wound prevention and management, the most widely available type of emergency service within the network. However, only 63.6% provided 24-hour care and an observation service, and only 54.5% had the capacity to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Emergency Services At time of data collection, 90.9% of the facilities offered wound prevention and management, the most widely available type of emergency service within the network. However, only 63.6% provided 24-hour care and an observation service, and only 54.5% had the capacity to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Noncommunicable and Communicable Diseases The management of noncommunicable diseases shows the strongest coverage in the assessment: 90.9% of the centers manage hypertension and diabetes mellitus, and 81.8% manage bronchial asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, this clinical capacity does not correspond to the availability of supplies, with salbutamol and ipratropium bromide — first-line medications for respiratory management — only available in 27.3% of facilities. For communicable diseases, the management of urinary tract infections and the availability of otolaryngological diagnostic equipment was documented at 90.9% of facilities, the strongest coverage area.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: However, this clinical capacity does not correspond to the availability of supplies, with salbutamol and ipratropium bromide — first-line medications for respiratory management — only available in 27.3% of facilities. For communicable diseases, the management of urinary tract infections and the availability of otolaryngological diagnostic equipment was documented at 90.9% of facilities, the strongest coverage area. The management of intestinal parasitic infections was documented as available at 81.8% of facilities. The gaps among communicable disease services were concentrated in diseases subject to epidemiological surveillance. No facility reports the capacity to manage malaria, only 9.1% have rapid malaria tests available, and only 9.1% have capacity to manage yellow fever.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: The gaps among communicable disease services were concentrated in diseases subject to epidemiological surveillance. No facility reports the capacity to manage malaria, only 9.1% have rapid malaria tests available, and only 9.1% have capacity to manage yellow fever. Although 63.6% of facilities have can manage dengue cases, only 18.2% have rapid diagnostic tests, and only 36.4% of staff have received technical training on the subject. Specialized HIV care is available at 9.1% of facilities, and care for sexually transmitted infections at 18.2%. Only 45.5% of the centers are part of the early warning sentinel system for diseases prone to epidemics.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Specialized HIV care is available at 9.1% of facilities, and care for sexually transmitted infections at 18.2%. Only 45.5% of the centers are part of the early warning sentinel system for diseases prone to epidemics. Maternal and Child Health Management of pregnancy complications and immunizations achieved 81.8% coverage, followed by prenatal care at 72.7% of facilities. Capacity is significantly reduced in childbirth care: only 36.4% of facilities provide childbirth care services, distribute childbirth kits, or have the capacity to manage obstetric complications. There is also a significant timebased gap in the availability of trained personnel to assist with deliveries, which drops from 81.8% on weekdays to 54.5% on weekends.

chunks.text: Capacity is significantly reduced in childbirth care: only 36.4% of facilities provide childbirth care services, distribute childbirth kits, or have the capacity to manage obstetric complications. There is also a significant timebased gap in the availability of trained personnel to assist with deliveries, which drops from 81.8% on weekdays to 54.5% on weekends. Support and education components show the lowest coverage figures in this category, with just 9.1% of facilities reporting the availability of training in Clinical Management of Childbirth and Newborn Emergencies (MCEPRN), mother-to-mother support groups, and parental education on early childhood development. Only 18.2% of facilities have a psychosocial support service or program and offer psychiatric care, psychopharmacological treatment, or psychotherapy.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Mental Health, Psychosocial Support, and Gender-Based Violence This service area had the most severe gap across the categories surveyed. Only 18.2% of facilities have a psychosocial support service or program and offer psychiatric care, psychopharmacological treatment, or psychotherapy. The World Health Organization’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) is implemented in just 9.1% of the surveyed facilities. 54.5% have some form of referral system for patients who cannot be treated locally. Only one facility — CLINP II Pastor Oropeza — offers the full range of mental health services evaluated. Only 9.1% of facilities have a specific service or program for addressing violence and abuse, and 27.3% report maintaining an active service for addressing sexual violence. 81.8% of the centers surveyed do not have a dedicated office for the clinical management of sexual violence, which limits the privacy and confidentiality required for this type of care.

chunks.text: Only one facility — CLINP II Pastor Oropeza — offers the full range of mental health services evaluated. Only 9.1% of facilities have a specific service or program for addressing violence and abuse, and 27.3% report maintaining an active service for addressing sexual violence. 81.8% of the centers surveyed do not have a dedicated office for the clinical management of sexual violence, which limits the privacy and confidentiality required for this type of care. Specialized care for adolescents is available at 18.2% of facilities. Availability of Medications and Supplies The average availability of essential indicator drugs is 69.5%, with extreme variations among facilities: one center (CPT III Aura Pinto) reported that all fourteen indicator drugs were out of stock, while three centers achieved full availability. The supplies with the highest availability are Ringer’s lactate solution (81.8%) and iron salts with folic acid (72.7%).

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Availability of Medications and Supplies The average availability of essential indicator drugs is 69.5%, with extreme variations among facilities: one center (CPT III Aura Pinto) reported that all fourteen indicator drugs were out of stock, while three centers achieved full availability. The supplies with the highest availability are Ringer’s lactate solution (81.8%) and iron salts with folic acid (72.7%). Medications for obstetric emergencies were at critically low levels, with an average availability of 12.7%. Hydralazine and methyldopa tablets are not available at any facility in the network, while misoprostol and injectable methyldopa are available at only one facility (9.1%). Only magnesium sulfate reaches 45.5% availability.

chunks.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
chunks.text: Hydralazine and methyldopa tablets are not available at any facility in the network, while misoprostol and injectable methyldopa are available at only one facility (9.1%). Only magnesium sulfate reaches 45.5% availability. This situation directly compromises the ability to respond to preeclampsia, eclampsia, and postpartum hemorrhage, in a context where 81.8% of facilities report managing pregnancy complications. Mental health medications are virtually nonexistent in the evaluated network. Anticholinergics show 0% availability across all facilities; antidepressants average 7.3%; antipsychotics, 10.9%; mood stabilizers, 12.7%; and anxiolytics, 25%.

chunks.text: Mental health medications are virtually nonexistent in the evaluated network. Anticholinergics show 0% availability across all facilities; antidepressants average 7.3%; antipsychotics, 10.9%; mood stabilizers, 12.7%; and anxiolytics, 25%. Nutrition Among surveyed facilities, 54.5% conduct nutritional assessments to screen for malnutrition risks, but their capacity to manage cases decreases progressively as the severity of the condition increases: 36.4% have capacity to manage moderate acute malnutrition, and only 18.2% have capacity to manage severe acute malnutrition or extreme thinness, meaning that most detected cases require referral outside of the facility where the case is identified. Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela – July 2026 Page 7 of 15 Physical Infrastructure and Care Conditions Areas with higher levels of complexity in the care they provide exhibit the widest gaps in availability: 72.7% of facilities do not have an operating room, a labor preparation room, or a recovery room, and 63.6% lack a neonatal unit, an observation room, and inpatient rooms. Spaces dedicated to psychosocial care and the clinical management of sexual violence are absent in 81.8% of the centers.

Regarding the physical condition of existing spaces, evident damage to walls was identified in 62.5% of immunization areas, 57.1% of gynecology clinics, 54.5% of pharmacies, and 42.9% of multipurpose emergency areas. Physical accessibility for people with limited mobility remains a significant gap: 54.5% of the centers have access ramps. In waiting rooms, 54.5% have sufficient chairs, but only 18.2% have seats properly designated for people requiring priority care, and 45.5% have visible signage identifying the spaces and services.

No facility relies on cisterns, rivers, or springs, nor do any extract water manually, indicating that the water distribution infrastructure remains operational even when the supply is intermittent. 11.1% report leaks in their internal piping systems. Of the 24 tanks surveyed, only 54.2% were functional according to the established criteria — lid, float, absence of visible damage, and connection to the water supply system — while 37.5% were not. 83.3% have a lid and 75% have a float, but only 58.3% have a valve or set of shut-off valves for cleaning, which hinders regular maintenance. Cleaning records indicate that less than half of the tanks have been maintained in the last twelve months, and several facilities reported that their tanks are not cleaned regularly. Additionally, only 20.8% of the tanks are equipped with water pumps, which limits internal distribution capacity in multi-level facilities.

chunks.text: Community Findings Disease Prevention Knowledge The community survey assessed the population’s knowledge on preventing diarrheal diseases, hypertension, dengue, and diabetes, finding, in general, a good level of knowledge regarding the main preventive measures. Regarding diarrheal diseases, 93% of respondents identified handwashing when preparing food as a preventive measure, 87% mentioned washing fruits and vegetables, and 80% cited the consumption of safe water (boiled, chlorinated, or bottled). Some minor misunderstandings persist, such as considering antibacterial soap or antibiotics as preventive measures (6% and 4%, respectively). Regarding hypertension, or high blood pressure, 87% recognized reducing salt and fat intake as preventive measures, and 76% mentioned physical activity. Incorrect responses were minimal (less than 4%).

chunks.text: From a programmatic perspective, this represents one of the clearest needs identified in the evaluation, as it has direct implications for the prevention of diarrheal diseases and other communicable infections. Community-Level Water Storage Household water storage is a widespread practice in the evaluated communities. Among assessed households, 69.9% had water storage containers inside or under their homes and 44.2% kept containers outdoors (jugs, buckets, drums, or tanks). This reliance on storage is partly explained by the fact that the public water system is not the primary source of water for most households: only 31.3% use it as their primary source, while 60.1% rely on other sources and 6.1% rely on water trucks. This forces households to store water to ensure its availability, making it especially important to maintain safe water handling practices.

chunks.text: This reliance on storage is partly explained by the fact that the public water system is not the primary source of water for most households: only 31.3% use it as their primary source, while 60.1% rely on other sources and 6.1% rely on water trucks. This forces households to store water to ensure its availability, making it especially important to maintain safe water handling practices. Although most households had adequate storage conditions, risks were identified in a smaller but significant proportion of the population: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela – July 2026 Page 11 of 15 11.7% stored water that was visually unfit for consumption or showed signs of contamination. 4.3% used containers without a tight-fitting lid. 3.7% kept dirty containers. 27.6% had potential vector breeding sites in their water storage containers. Taken together, these results show that water storage is a common strategy for coping with limited and intermittent access to water. Although communities possess basic knowledge of safe water strategies, gaps remain — particularly the presence of vector breeding sites — indicating that the need is not only for access to water but also for strengthening practices that reduce the health risks associated with storage.

Therefore, it is recommended to establish spaces that guarantee privacy and confidentiality, starting with hospitals and the most complex CPT III centers.
