chunks.text: Women have told Save the Children staff that some obstetricians and paediatricians were among the over 5,000 people killed in the disaster, leaving families uncertain where to seek care for themselves and their children. In La Guaira, which was hardest hit, the main maternity hospital remains closed and, while basic care is available, complicated cases must be referred to Caracas. Many pregnant women, caregivers, and their children who lost their homes are now living in temporary shelters where access to antenatal care, nutritious food, and clean water and sanitation is limited. At the same time, many are coping with the traumatic loss of loved ones. Research shows that high levels of stress and anxiety during pregnancy may affect a baby's brain development and immune system, increasing the risk of preterm birth or even miscarriage.

At the same time, women are grieving loved ones, coping with trauma and worrying about where they can access healthcare after losing trusted obstetricians and paediatricians.* *"Pregnancy and caring for a newborn can be challenging under any circumstances. No mother should have to navigate those challenges while living in a tent, mourning losses and worrying about whether her child can access the healthcare they need.”* Save the Children said it is imperative that pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding women, and their children, are prioritised in the humanitarian response and recovery in Venezuela through urgent coordination, adequate funding, and targeted actions. Save the Children is calling on international governments, donors and humanitarian partners to ensure that pregnant and breastfeeding women affected by the earthquake have continuous access to quality antenatal, delivery and postnatal care, skilled infant and young child feeding support, nutritious food, safe shelter, clean water and sanitation, and essential newborn supplies, both now and in the months ahead. Save the Children is on the ground in Venezuela, working with authorities and local partners providing primary healthcare through mobile clinics, distributing hygiene kits, clean water and essential supplies.

Save the Children is on the ground in Venezuela, working with authorities and local partners providing primary healthcare through mobile clinics, distributing hygiene kits, clean water and essential supplies. Save the Children is also supporting parents and caregivers to access services for small and nutritionally at-risk babies under six months to help them survive and thrive, including nutrition assessments for babies, and breastfeeding counselling and mental health support for caregivers. The organisation is also exploring potential support to maternal and paediatric services in coordination with national health authorities. Save the Children has been working in Venezuela since 2019.

chunks.text: **A. SITUATION ANALYSIS** **Description of the crisis** On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 1,000 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas.

chunks.title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #1 (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: Authorities have reported more than 1,000 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira, a popular destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes. As of 15 July, 4,829 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing1.

It is expected for these figures to continue to rise in coming days as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors moves towards a focus on recovery, identification and return to family members of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG)2. International search and rescue deployments are progressively concluding, with several Movement teams having completed their missions.

International search and rescue deployments are progressively concluding, with several Movement teams having completed their missions. A response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, shelter provision and efforts to bridge emergency relief to recovery and reconstruction efforts continues under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery. According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.3 A comprehensive technical evaluation of structures is underway by respective authorities to identify homes that can be repaired and those that are too dangerous to return to. Evaluation of safe areas to build permanent housing for those affected is also taking place.

sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Evaluation of safe areas to build permanent housing for those affected is also taking place. Damage to residences, commercial buildings and critical infrastructure also disrupted the functioning of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems, as well as public transportation and airport operations. Damaged roads and bridges have also restricted access and affected movement to and within some affected areas. The healthcare capacity has been particularly affected, with limited supply of water systems.

This increases the number of people and logistical capacity affected. The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with thousands of injured, many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, and with families displaced after the destruction or severe damage of their homes. Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks.

chunks.text: Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, uncertainty regarding housing and recovery, and exposure to damaged environments and recovery operations has contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected populations. Notably, La Guaira’s geographical location is prone to various types of emergencies. In December 1999, torrential rainfall triggered catastrophic landslides, flash floods and debris flows across the then State of Vargas—now La Guaira—causing widespread destruction and displacement.

sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: Notably, the VRC received 20,000 applications for new volunteers immediately following the earthquakes. As of 17 July, a total of 1,176 families (4,704 people) has been reached with distributions of essential household items (kitchen sets, blankets, sleeping kits), and relief items for health and hygiene promotion (cleaning kits, hygiene kits, jerrycans, buckets, water treatment tablets, mosquito nets, and water filters). The VRC’s response is coordinated with the Government-led emergency structure and relevant public institutions. National response arrangements have included Civil Protection and national and international Search and Rescue teams, activation of the public and private health network, establishment of temporary accommodation sites, delivery of essential supplies, and mechanisms for reporting missing people and housing damage. Within these arrangements, the VRC has coordinated directly with authorities on field operations, health services, temporary accommodation, affected water systems and access to communities, while maintaining its distinct humanitarian role and operational responsibilities.

To respond to the needs of the population after the earthquakes, the National Society established a field clinic and first aid posts, strengthened referral pathways and epidemiological surveillance, and expanded water, sanitation and hygiene services through the deployment of water treatment systems and sanitation facilities at operational sites and shelters. The VRC has managed over 2,700 restoring family links (RFL) and tracing requests and is operating connectivity services for families searching for missing relatives, expanding mental health and psychosocial support activities. Additionally, they are monitoring 107 accommodation centres across five states to inform response planning and on 29 June.

sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: Analysis conducted by the Venezuelan Red Cross estimates that approximately 331,068 people in La Guaira are in need of assistance from at least one humanitarian sector4. Three parishes—Catia La Mar, Caraballeda and Carayaca—were classified as having catastrophic levels of severity, while five additional parishes were classified as extreme. The following analysis takes into account primary and secondary data collection. The Venezuelan Red Cross has conducted a sectoral analysis covering health and care, MHPSS, WASH, shelter, PGI, CEA and volunteering to further define needs, gaps and response priorities. The analysis was developed through a collaborative process involving technical specialists from the Venezuelan Red Cross, IFRC and German Red Cross.

chunks.title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #1 (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: The Venezuelan Red Cross has conducted a sectoral analysis covering health and care, MHPSS, WASH, shelter, PGI, CEA and volunteering to further define needs, gaps and response priorities. The analysis was developed through a collaborative process involving technical specialists from the Venezuelan Red Cross, IFRC and German Red Cross. Sector focal points consolidated information from operational activities, rapid and sector-specific assessments, field observations and programme monitoring data, using a common analysis template to identify key needs, vulnerabilities, response gaps and priority actions. The analysis was further complemented by secondary data review, including official information, humanitarian reports and other relevant assessments, to support a comprehensive understanding of the evolving humanitarian situation. On 14 July, four VRC and IFRC teams visited prioritized temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira and the Capital District to review response progress and site conditions and help identify locations where distributions could be considered.

The teams engaged with affected people, local authorities and other stakeholders and reviewed a broad range of areas relevant to operational planning, including shelter conditions, essential household items, hygiene, safe water access and storage, existing capacities and access to services. It also includes perception-based assessments, such as the GeoPoll rapid needs assessment5 conducted through WhatsApp with 846 affected households, which has provided additional insights into priority needs, access to information and perceptions of the evolving humanitarian situation. The sections below provide a sector-by-sector analysis of the main needs, vulnerabilities and identified gaps.

The VRC sectoral analysis reports three hospitals were evacuated, 24 temporarily were affected, 20 with minor damage and approximately 50 health centres operating partially. Identified needs include follow-up trauma care and rehabilitation, continuity of medicines and consultations for people with chronic conditions, maternal and emergency obstetric care, epidemiological surveillance, infection prevention, nutrition screening and support for people with disabilities, older people, families with small children and those with reduced mobility. Operational gaps include shortages of qualified personnel, medical supplies, medicines, vehicles, fuel and ambulances; restrictions in referral routes; limited specialized mental-health capacity; and weaknesses in epidemiological and pre-hospital information systems.

chunks.text: Identified needs include follow-up trauma care and rehabilitation, continuity of medicines and consultations for people with chronic conditions, maternal and emergency obstetric care, epidemiological surveillance, infection prevention, nutrition screening and support for people with disabilities, older people, families with small children and those with reduced mobility. Operational gaps include shortages of qualified personnel, medical supplies, medicines, vehicles, fuel and ambulances; restrictions in referral routes; limited specialized mental-health capacity; and weaknesses in epidemiological and pre-hospital information systems. Additional needs include community-based health promotion and disease-prevention activities, particularly in areas affected by displacement and disruptions to basic services. These include health education, vaccination support, disease-prevention messaging and community surveillance activities linked to evolving public health risks. Moreover, the VRC and IFRC temporary accommodation visits identified additional needs related to the continuity of treatment for people living with chronic diseases and potential barriers to regular access to medicines and health services in temporary accommodations.

MHPSS volunteers and staff of the Venezuelan Red Cross have reported significant psychosocial distress among people reached through field clinics, temporary accommodation sites, mobile outreach and rescue-related activities. Analysis of MHPSS service records have identified frequent presentations of acute stress, anxiety, fear, sleep disturbance, crying, irritability, avoidance, somatic complaints and grief. These reactions occur in the context of bereavement, injury, repeated aftershocks, displacement, uncertainty regarding missing relatives and the loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks.

This is linked to prolonged shifts, repeated contact with distressed families and exposure to highly distressing situations, including serious injuries, deaths and the recovery of human remains. chunks.text: Preliminary WASH analyses indicate that needs remain widespread across all nine affected parishes of La Guaira. VRC identified WASH as the sector with the highest level of need, affecting an estimated 331,068 people, reflecting the extensive disruption of water systems across the state. Damage has affected public water infrastructure, including aqueducts, water-intake systems, pumping systems and internal networks serving schools, health facilities and shelters. Water provision in some areas depends on bottled water and tanker trucks, while the quality of tanker-supplied water is not always known. Although this is not part of the Red Cross response at the moment, it was observed by the RCRC teams during field visits.

sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: B. OPERATIONAL STRATEGY Update on the strategy Since publication of the Operational Strategy, the overall objectives, target population and geographic focus remain unchanged. The strategy has, however, been refined to strengthen the recovery lens across the operation, including greater emphasis on restoring safe housing and essential services, supporting livelihoods and self-sufficiency, reducing future risks, and further reinforcing the VRC’s institutional, operational and preparedness capacities. The indicators included below have been reviewed and updated for each strategic sector of intervention to better reflect the key interventions and progress achieved. PGI: Indicators have been adjusted to better represent the services delivered by the protection team, measuring the number of Restoring Family Links services provided to people affected by the earthquake rather than the number of individual people reached.

chunks.text: The indicators included below have been reviewed and updated for each strategic sector of intervention to better reflect the key interventions and progress achieved. PGI: Indicators have been adjusted to better represent the services delivered by the protection team, measuring the number of Restoring Family Links services provided to people affected by the earthquake rather than the number of individual people reached. CEA: Indicators now provide a more comprehensive view of community engagement and accountability by including CEA training for staff as well as volunteers. Health and MHPSS: Training indicators have been broadened from “volunteers trained in MHPSS” to “volunteers and staff trained in MHPSS”, with the target revised from 150 to 300 to reinforce sustainable MHPSS capacity within the National Society. The indicator “Number of people receiving psychosocial care services” has also been revised to “Number of people receiving MHPSS services” to better reflect the full range of psychosocial support and psychological interventions delivered through the operation.

Framed within the Sevilla Agreement 2.0, a Joint Statement between the Venezuelan Red Cross—as convener—the IFRC —as co-convener—and the ICRC was subscribed on 10 July reassuring the coordinated and aligned response that is being provided as one Movement. The roles among the parties were clearly stated and defined, the VRC is the convener of the emergency response at national level, defining the operational priorities and coordinating with the Government and public authorities. The IFRC’s Secretariat co-convenes the overall coordination of the emergency response, mobilises the international support from the Membership and activates the international response framework and tools needed by the operational priorities.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #15 (20 to 21 July 2026)
chunks.text: The fifteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 20 to 21 July. ## Highlights Between 20 and 21 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH and information management. To date, IOM has reached **8,542 unique individuals through 15,460 instances of assistance and services**, mainly in shelter and transitory camp coordination, protection, health and WASH. IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed **3,055 kitchen sets, 2,590 tarpaulins, 2,039 buckets, 1,676 solar lamps and 819 shelter kits** to affected households. ## IOM activities IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the operational transition of three of them to the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM maintained essential services for 316 families and supported registration activities.

chunks.text: VENEZUELA (BOLIVARIAN REPUBLIC OF) EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE SITUATION REPORT #15 FROM 20 TO 21 JULY 2026 STORYTELLER REBUILDING WHERE HE CALLS HOME Ramón, 59, has lived in his community all his life, raising 7 children and watching his family grow to include 15 grandchildren. When the earthquakes struck, his family took shelter under a wooden table before escaping outside. Although they survived, their home was left unsafe, his children lost their homes, and the nearby market where Ramón earned a living was completely destroyed. Now staying at the César Nieves transitory camp alongside neighbours who lost loved ones, he has seen how deeply the disaster has affected families, particularly children and young people.

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, mantuvo servicios esenciales para 316 familias y apoyó actividades de registro.

chunks.text: VENEZUELA (REPÚBLICA BOLIVARIANA DE) RESPUESTA A TERREMOTO REPORTE DE SITUACIÓN #15 20 AL 21 DE JULIO 2026 HISTORIA DE VIDA RECONSTRUYENDO SU HOGAR Ramón, de 59 años, ha vivido siempre en su comunidad, donde crió a sus 7 hijos y vio crecer a su familia, incluidos sus15 nietos. Cuando ocurrieron los terremotos, su familia se refugió debajo de una mesa de madera antes de salir de la vivienda. Aunque todos sobrevivieron, su casa quedó inhabitable, sus hijos perdieron sus hogares y el mercado cercano donde Ramón se ganaba la vida quedó completamente destruido. Actualmente se encuentra en el campamento transitorio César Nieves, junto a vecinos que perdieron a seres queridos, y ha visto de cerca el profundo impacto del desastre en las familias, particularmente en niñas, niños y jóvenes.

Esta base de datos tiene carácter exclusivamente informativo y de referencia, ya que el GTL únicamente recopila y consolida la información proporcionada por los socios, sin realizar procesos de validación, recomendación o selección de proveedores, ni mantener relación contractual con ellos. chunks.title: Comité de Emergencia Español: un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela la ayuda es más necesaria que nunca
chunks.text: El Comité de Emergencia Español reitera el llamamiento para mantener la ayuda a las decenas de miles de personas afectadas por los terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela hace un mes. El desafío sigue siendo incalculable tras los seísmos que dejaron más de 5.069 muertos y más de 16.740 personas heridas, además de miles de familias afectadas y comunidades con daños severos. Los esfuerzos se centran ahora en que la población pueda retomar la vida cotidiana con seguridad: volver a entornos habitables, recuperar servicios básicos, reabrir espacios comunitarios y educativos y reducir la exposición a riesgos que amenazan la salud de miles de familias. **La situación es crítica ya que las necesidades humanitarias son enormes.** El trabajo de las **8 ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español** que están respondiendo a esta emergencia, **Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision,** continúa y se centra en estos momentos en la atención a la población en situación más vulnerable, incluídos niños, y niñas, proporcionando alimentos, agua y asistencia económica, protección y refugio, atención médica y psicosocial, prevención de brotes epidémicos y apoyo educativo para la infancia, principalmente. “Un mes después de los terremotos el reto al que se enfrentan las ONG internacionales especialistas en ayuda humanitaria del Comité de Emergencia es que las familias puedan volver a una rutina segura sin que la emergencia se transforme en una crisis sanitaria.

chunks.title: Comité de Emergencia Español: un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela la ayuda es más necesaria que nunca

Evitar enfermedades y acompañar la recuperación física y emocional es ahora determinante”, **señala la directora del Comité de Emergencia Español, Sara Barbeira.** **Llamamiento a mantener la solidaridad** El **Comité de Emergencia Español, activado el 25 de junio**, canaliza la solidaridad de la sociedad española para apoyar la respuesta de las organizaciones en coordinación con entidades locales y socios sobre el terreno, especialmente en las zonas más afectadas, con La Guaira entre los estados con mayor impacto, y con efectos directos e indirectos en varios territorios del país. “Ahora empieza el trabajo más largo: evitar una crisis sanitaria, sostener la atención médica y ayudar a las familias a recuperar su vida. La solidaridad de ciudadanos y empresas españolas ha sido enorme, pero debe mantenerse para que el pueblo venezolano pueda poco a poco recuperar una cierta normalidad.

chunks.title: Comité de Emergencia Español: un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela la ayuda es más necesaria que nunca
chunks.text: “Ahora empieza el trabajo más largo: evitar una crisis sanitaria, sostener la atención médica y ayudar a las familias a recuperar su vida. La solidaridad de ciudadanos y empresas españolas ha sido enorme, pero debe mantenerse para que el pueblo venezolano pueda poco a poco recuperar una cierta normalidad. También para sanar en la manera de lo posible el trauma social de la terrible pérdida de miles de personas”, **agrega Sara Barbeira.** **Retomar la vida cotidiana: una prioridad humanitaria** Un mes después de los terremotos, las necesidades evolucionan y se vuelve clave impulsar una recuperación temprana que permita unas condiciones de vida digna y reducir riesgos secundarios. Para ello una de las prioridades de las ONG es garantizar **agua limpia, saneamiento e higiene** para prevenir enfermedades asociadas a la falta de letrinas, la contaminación del agua y la gestión deficiente de residuos. Las ONG que forman parte del Comité de Emergencia están centradas en apoyar soluciones de alojamiento temporal y mejoras en refugios, así como en reforzar la **atención sanitaria** y el acceso a medicamentos esenciales, priorizando la atención primaria.

Las ONG que forman parte del Comité de Emergencia están centradas en apoyar soluciones de alojamiento temporal y mejoras en refugios, así como en reforzar la **atención sanitaria** y el acceso a medicamentos esenciales, priorizando la atención primaria. También la atención psicosocial, especialmente para niños, niñas y familias que han sufrido pérdidas, desplazamiento o exposición a situaciones traumáticas, es fundamental. La **salud mental** de las personas afectadas es una de las grandes prioridades en esta fase. La protección de los **grupos poblaciones más vulnerables** es una de las claves de esta respuesta, protegiendo frente a violaciones de sus derechos y promoviendo entornos más seguros.

El foco se mantiene en quienes corren mayor riesgo tras el desastre, especialmente las niñas, adolescentes y mujeres, que se encuentran más expuestas a la violencia, la explotación y la interrupción de sus servicios de salud. La respuesta también incluye la puesta en marcha de **Espacios Seguros para la Infancia** para que los niños y niñas tengan un entorno seguro donde retomar rutinas que favorezcan su bienestar emocional, y de espacios temporales de aprendizaje para que puedan continuar con su educación y recuperar la normalidad. La recuperación también requerirá ampliar la cobertura hacia **comunidades receptoras** y estados que están recibiendo población desplazada, donde las vulnerabilidades preexistentes y la presión sobre los servicios básicos podrían agravar las necesidades humanitarias.

chunks.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #4: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 22 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
chunks.text: As of 22 July, AMDA’s relief team has been working to provide aid to those affected by the earthquakes that devastated Venezuela on 24 June. AMDA has been based in Caraballeda, La Guaira, one of the hardest-hit locations since the start of the quake response efforts. The below is the summary of its activities between 14-19 July: ■14 July AMDA’s second relief team (comprising a Venezuelan physician and a nurse based in Peru) arrived in Venezuela on 14 July to join the ongoing quake response in Caraballeda. Since the following day, the team began providing medical care at a temporary clinic in cooperation with local healthcare professionals and volunteers.

sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
chunks.text: The below is the summary of its activities between 14-19 July: ■14 July AMDA’s second relief team (comprising a Venezuelan physician and a nurse based in Peru) arrived in Venezuela on 14 July to join the ongoing quake response in Caraballeda. Since the following day, the team began providing medical care at a temporary clinic in cooperation with local healthcare professionals and volunteers. Because the clinic was run by volunteers, AMDA’s medical team played a vital role in maintaining the clinic's services, as staff allocation of volunteers changed from day to day. The AMDA team worked from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. each day and provided medical consultations to approximately 50 to 100 patients daily. ■18 July On 18 July, one Japanese nurse arrived at Valencia Airport in Venezuela to join the advance team. The nurse was dispatched to respond to the ongoing humanitarian needs even though more than three weeks had passed since the earthquake struck.

chunks.title: Los terremotos en Venezuela dejan una huella invisible en la salud de la niñez
chunks.text: A casi un mes de los terremotos que sacudieron a Venezuela el 24 de junio, la organización humanitaria y de desarrollo Plan International advierte que la salud física y mental de niñas, niños y adolescentes se ve cada vez más afectada por las condiciones en las zonas más golpeadas por el desastre. Las condiciones inadecuadas de vivienda, la acumulación de escombros y cambio en los arreglos de cuidado están profundizando el impacto emocional del desastre en la niñez y sus familias. Según el reporte de la agencia de Naciones Unidas responsable de coordinar la respuesta humanitaria ([OCHA]( 107 campamentos transitorios albergan actualmente a más de 23.800 personas, cerca del 86% de su capacidad total, mientras que más de 17.900 personas continúan sin vivienda. Al 19 de julio, las cifras oficiales reportaban 5.208 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.

chunks.title: Los terremotos en Venezuela dejan una huella invisible en la salud de la niñez
chunks.text: Según el reporte de la agencia de Naciones Unidas responsable de coordinar la respuesta humanitaria ([OCHA]( 107 campamentos transitorios albergan actualmente a más de 23.800 personas, cerca del 86% de su capacidad total, mientras que más de 17.900 personas continúan sin vivienda. Al 19 de julio, las cifras oficiales reportaban 5.208 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas. Las organizaciones socias de Plan International que responden en el terreno reportan que las molestias físicas sin causa clara aparecen cada vez con más frecuencia, junto con señales de estrés postraumático y una sensación constante de inseguridad, y que, al escuchar con más atención, revelan semanas de sueño interrumpido, sobresaltos y miedo acumulado. “Cuando hace brisa yo me meto para el cuarto y me escondo y me asusto”, cuenta Victoria, de nueve años, en La Guaira. Naomi, de solo cinco años, describe cómo las pesadillas recurrentes le interrumpen el sueño: “Yo estaba en la playa y un tsunami me estaba persiguiendo”.

Un dolor de cabeza, un dolor de estómago, dificultad para dormir o miedo a los ruidos fuertes pueden ser señales de angustia que la niñez no logra expresar con palabras. En esta etapa de la emergencia, la salud mental de la niñez ya no puede tratarse como una respuesta secundaria. Si no atendemos el bienestar físico y emocional en conjunto, la recuperación será imposible”, afirmó Serrano. Ella agrega que este impacto no se ve igual en todas las edades. “Niñas, niños y adolescentes de distintas edades y etapas de desarrollo no siempre tienen las palabras o los medios para explicar lo que sienten, y no siempre lo demuestran de la misma manera.

chunks.title: Los terremotos en Venezuela dejan una huella invisible en la salud de la niñez
chunks.text: Ella agrega que este impacto no se ve igual en todas las edades. “Niñas, niños y adolescentes de distintas edades y etapas de desarrollo no siempre tienen las palabras o los medios para explicar lo que sienten, y no siempre lo demuestran de la misma manera. Las niñas y los niños más pequeños pueden dejar de comer, tener dificultad para dormir, presentar episodios de llanto sin razón aparente o sobresaltarse con facilidad, mientras que las y los adolescentes son más propensos a aislarse, a estar más callados, a mostrarse más agresivos o a alejarse de quienes los rodean. Estar conscientes de estas señales y actuar sobre ellas, junto con la atención médica, es tan urgente como reconstruir un techo”. Niñas, niños y adolescentes continúan siendo agrupados en una sola categoría en la recolección de datos y las evaluaciones de necesidades, aun cuando enfrentan las crisis de manera distinta y se exponen a riesgos y desafíos diferentes.

Niñas, niños y adolescentes continúan siendo agrupados en una sola categoría en la recolección de datos y las evaluaciones de necesidades, aun cuando enfrentan las crisis de manera distinta y se exponen a riesgos y desafíos diferentes. Plan International advierte que esta distinción todavía necesita reflejarse mejor en la respuesta humanitaria. Junto con sus socios en territorio, Plan International brinda apoyo psicosocial grupal e individual a niñas, niños y adolescentes, ayuda a las familias a cubrir necesidades urgentes que salvan vidas, y fortalece los servicios de protección de la niñez, con especial atención a las niñas. Esto incluye espacios seguros donde la niñez puede comenzar a procesar lo que ha vivido, así como rutas de derivación hacia servicios especializados de salud mental.

chunks.title: Venezuela's earthquakes take a hidden toll on children's health
chunks.text: Almost one month after the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, the development and humanitarian organisation, Plan International, warns that the physical and mental health of children and adolescents is increasingly affected by conditions in the areas hardest hit by the disaster. Inadequate housing conditions, accumulation of debris, and insufficient care arrangements are deepening the emotional impact of the disaster on children and their families. According to the report from the UN agency responsible for coordinating humanitarian response ([OCHA]( 107 transitional camps are currently sheltering more than 23.800 people, close to 86% of their total capacity, while more than 17,900 people remain without housing. As of 19 July, official figures reported 5.208 deaths and 16,740 people injured.

chunks.title: Venezuela's earthquakes take a hidden toll on children's health
chunks.text: According to the report from the UN agency responsible for coordinating humanitarian response ([OCHA]( 107 transitional camps are currently sheltering more than 23.800 people, close to 86% of their total capacity, while more than 17,900 people remain without housing. As of 19 July, official figures reported 5.208 deaths and 16,740 people injured. Plan International local partners responding on the ground report that physical complaints with no clear cause are appearing more and more, alongside signs of post-traumatic stress and a constant sense of insecurity, and on closer listening, they reveal weeks of disrupted sleep, jumpiness and accumulated fear. "When it gets windy I run into my room and hide, and I get scared," says nine year old Victoria in La Guaira. Naomi, who is only five, describes how recurring nightmares are disrupting her sleep: "I was on the beach and a tsunami was chasing me." Michelle, a 25-year-old mother of three girls, sums up what she sees every day: "They're scared, they're frightened.

chunks.text: "When it gets windy I run into my room and hide, and I get scared," says nine year old Victoria in La Guaira. Naomi, who is only five, describes how recurring nightmares are disrupting her sleep: "I was on the beach and a tsunami was chasing me." Michelle, a 25-year-old mother of three girls, sums up what she sees every day: "They're scared, they're frightened. Right now, the children need psychological support to help them." Yesica Serrano, Regional Child Protection in Humanitarian Action Adviser at Plan International, is currently in Venezuela and warns that this phase of the emergency demands as much attention as the first. "Once the immediate shock of the earthquake has passed, the impact does not disappear – it stays with the children and adolescents both in body and mind. A headache, a stomach ache, difficulty sleeping or fear of loud noises can be signs of distress that children are unable to put into words.

chunks.text: "Once the immediate shock of the earthquake has passed, the impact does not disappear – it stays with the children and adolescents both in body and mind. A headache, a stomach ache, difficulty sleeping or fear of loud noises can be signs of distress that children are unable to put into words. At this stage of the emergency, children's mental health can no longer be treated as a secondary response. If we don't address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible," Serrano said. She adds that this toll doesn't look the same across ages.

chunks.title: Venezuela's earthquakes take a hidden toll on children's health
chunks.text: If we don't address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible," Serrano said. She adds that this toll doesn't look the same across ages. "Children across different ages and development stages don't always have the words or means to explain what they're feeling, and they don't always show it the same way. Younger children may stop eating, struggle to sleep, have occasional crying spells with no apparent reason or startle easily, while adolescents are more likely to withdraw, grow quiet, be more aggressive or pull away from those around them. Being consciously aware of those signals and acting on them, alongside medical care, is just as urgent as rebuilding a roof." Children and adolescents continue to be grouped into a single category in data collection and needs assessments, even though they experience crises differently and face distinct risks and challenges.

Being consciously aware of those signals and acting on them, alongside medical care, is just as urgent as rebuilding a roof." Children and adolescents continue to be grouped into a single category in data collection and needs assessments, even though they experience crises differently and face distinct risks and challenges. Plan International warns that this distinction still needs to be better reflected in the humanitarian response. With partners on the ground, the organisation is providing group and individual psychosocial support to children and adolescents, helping families meet urgent and lifesaving needs, and strengthening child protection services, with particular attention to girls. This includes safe spaces where children can begin to process what they have experienced, as well as referral pathways to specialised mental health support.

chunks.text: With partners on the ground, the organisation is providing group and individual psychosocial support to children and adolescents, helping families meet urgent and lifesaving needs, and strengthening child protection services, with particular attention to girls. This includes safe spaces where children can begin to process what they have experienced, as well as referral pathways to specialised mental health support. As the earthquake response in Venezuela enters a new phase, Plan International recognises there is now an opportunity for physical and mental health support to be more closely integrated across the displacement camps and affected communities. It also urges humanitarian actors and donors to collect and use data that distinguishes between children, adolescents and adults, helping ensure support is tailored to their different needs and reaches those most at risk. **ENDS** **For further information please contact:** Rodrigo Morales, Regional Communication Officer for Public Relations Plan International Americas Tel: +503 7885 9315 Email: **About Plan International** Plan International is an independent development and humanitarian organisation that advances children’s rights and equality for girls. chunks.title: Venezuela Emergency Response, Situation Report #4 (9 – 20 July 2026)
chunks.text: **OPERATIONAL CONTEXT** Nearly one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response in Venezuela is rapidly transitioning from the immediate emergency phase to a more structured, large-scale operation. Indeed, humanitarian needs remain immense: over 23,000 people live in transitional camps, thousands more remain displaced in host communities or informal settlements, and damaged housing and basic infrastructure continue to limit access to safe shelter, water, sanitation, healthcare and livelihoods.ii As aftershocks continue – over 1,300 registered up until now – the humanitarian response continues to expand in scale and complexity. Humanitarian actors are now planning assistance for 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the coming six months, yet significant humanitarian gaps remain, as many communities remain underserved. This requires humanitarian actors that can rapidly identify unmet needs, coordinate effectively with existing response structures and deliver assistance where it is needed most.

Strong humanitarian coordination and operational partnerships, enabling CESVI to maximise the reach and effectiveness of its response through coordinated action. 3. Evidence-based targeting of humanitarian gaps, ensuring assistance reaches underserved communities that had not previously received humanitarian assistance. Humanitarian coordination mechanisms: CESVI is actively engaged in the Shelter/NFI, WASH, and Protection Clusters, as well as OCHA-led coordination mechanisms, contributing first-hand field evidence to inter-agency planning and ensuring that assessments, targeting and assistance remain aligned with the wider humanitarian response and avoid duplication.

Established operational partnerships: The response is implemented in collaboration with national and international partners, including Ayuda en Acción, Save the Children, Huellas Foundation, Acción Campesina, the Little Sisters of the Poor, Paluz and the Italian Red Cross, enabling complementary expertise, wider operational reach and faster assistance delivery. Emergency response with a recovery perspective: CESVI combines life-saving assistance across shelter, WASH, and food security with early planning for recovery, ensuring that SitRep #4 – Venezuela Emergency Response immediate response efforts lay the foundations for longer-term recovery over the next 6 months. Further details on the planned recovery phase are available in Situation Report #3.

Further details on the planned recovery phase are available in Situation Report #3. Accountability mechanisms and protection mainstreaming: Community Feedback Mechanisms (CFM) have been established across all intervention sites in line with Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) standards, while protection considerations are mainstreamed throughout assessments and assistance delivery, with particular attention to women, children, people with disabilities and other vulnerable groups. Targeted geographic coverage: Operations focus on some of the most severely affected, yet underserved, oareas, particularly El Junquito (Capital District), Guarenas–Guatire (Miranda), and the coastal outskirts of La Guaira, where informal settlements built with precarious materials suffered disproportionate damage. 5. PRIORITY ACTIONS FOR A SUSTAINED RESPONSE While humanitarian assistance has expanded rapidly since the earthquakes, the scale of needs and the persistence of displacement require continued investment in both immediate relief and the foundations for recovery. The progress achieved during the first month of CESVI's response demonstrates what timely humanitarian action can achieve when backed by sustained support, which remains essential as the crisis continues. CESVI calls on donors, the international community and all relevant stakeholders to: o Provide immediate, flexible, and predictable funding commensurate with the vast scale and severity of the crisis to enable the scale-up and sustainment of coordinated, multisectoral humanitarian assistance, in line with evolving needs. o Promote an effective transition from emergency response to early recovery and resilience, while enabling humanitarian action to address immediate needs and critical gaps and laying the foundations for longer-term recovery and community resilience. o Support the strengthening of local supply chains and procurement systems, enabling humanitarian actors to source relief items locally wherever feasible and consequently stimulating local markets, contributing to economic recovery. o Support equitable partnerships with national and local actors, including through sustained investment in their institutional and operational capacities, to strengthen locally rooted humanitarian action and make longer-term recovery sustainable and durable. chunks.text: CESVI calls on donors, the international community and all relevant stakeholders to: o Provide immediate, flexible, and predictable funding commensurate with the vast scale and severity of the crisis to enable the scale-up and sustainment of coordinated, multisectoral humanitarian assistance, in line with evolving needs. o Promote an effective transition from emergency response to early recovery and resilience, while enabling humanitarian action to address immediate needs and critical gaps and laying the foundations for longer-term recovery and community resilience. o Support the strengthening of local supply chains and procurement systems, enabling humanitarian actors to source relief items locally wherever feasible and consequently stimulating local markets, contributing to economic recovery. o Support equitable partnerships with national and local actors, including through sustained investment in their institutional and operational capacities, to strengthen locally rooted humanitarian action and make longer-term recovery sustainable and durable. chunks.title: One month after earthquakes, Venezuela risks spiraling into deeper crisis without urgent investment in economic recovery
chunks.text: Caracas, Venezuela, July 22, 2026 — Nearly one month after devastating twin earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, the window is closing to set the country on a sustainable path toward recovery. Without immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support, the disaster risks spiraling into a deeper humanitarian crisis, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns. Venezuela was already experiencing protracted economic instability long before the ground began to shake, with [over half of the population living in extreme poverty]( Years of economic hardship drove roughly 8 million people, mainly young adults, to leave the country. This has left a critical gap in the workforce that has impacted search and rescue efforts and will continue to constrain capacity as the vital early recovery phase begins.

chunks.text: Venezuela was already experiencing protracted economic instability long before the ground began to shake, with [over half of the population living in extreme poverty]( Years of economic hardship drove roughly 8 million people, mainly young adults, to leave the country. This has left a critical gap in the workforce that has impacted search and rescue efforts and will continue to constrain capacity as the vital early recovery phase begins. Now, the economic situation threatens to unravel further. An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure to cost approximately $37 billion. Nearly 8 million people were in humanitarian need in Venezuela before the earthquakes.

chunks.text: An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure to cost approximately $37 billion. Nearly 8 million people were in humanitarian need in Venezuela before the earthquakes. In just four weeks that number has grown by 1.4 million. As response efforts scale up, access remains complicated by the indefinite closure of the Simón Bolívar International Airport and continuous aftershocks, with over 1,400 since the initial quakes. *"Beyond the destroyed buildings and people being pulled from the rubble, there is a quieter economic devastation that is becoming more visible by the day. For reconstruction efforts to have any hope of success, we must focus serious attention on restarting local economies, supporting small businesses, and getting schools back up and running,”* \*\*said IRC’s Emergency Response Lead for the Venezuela Earthquakes, Rafael Velasquez Garcia.

For reconstruction efforts to have any hope of success, we must focus serious attention on restarting local economies, supporting small businesses, and getting schools back up and running,”* \*\*said IRC’s Emergency Response Lead for the Venezuela Earthquakes, Rafael Velasquez Garcia. “\*\**With millions of futures in the balance, the time to act is now. Absolutely nothing will stop local communities from lifting each other up if they're given the resources to do so."* The IRC urges the international community to scale up humanitarian funding to support Venezuelans impacted by the earthquakes and the millions who were already in urgent need. The IRC has been working in Venezuela since 2021 to deliver programs across health, nutrition, protection, education, food security, and livelihoods.

chunks.text: Absolutely nothing will stop local communities from lifting each other up if they're given the resources to do so."* The IRC urges the international community to scale up humanitarian funding to support Venezuelans impacted by the earthquakes and the millions who were already in urgent need. The IRC has been working in Venezuela since 2021 to deliver programs across health, nutrition, protection, education, food security, and livelihoods. As soon as the earthquakes hit, the IRC started scaling up its response to support affected communities, designing and launching ten new programs in tandem with eight local partners on the ground. The IRC will continue its support in the months ahead, providing life-saving assistance and essential protection and early recovery programming to help Venezuela rebuild. Over the past month, the IRC has distributed hundreds of hygiene and water purification kits, supported our partners providing first aid and primary care to 300-400 people every day, and helped reactivate the diagnostic laboratory at the Central University of Caracas to track potential disease outbreaks. **Media contacts** Sylvan Foley ** ** IRC Global Communications ** **

chunks.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.5 (Earthquake Response), 13-20 July 2026
chunks.text: **Highlights** More than three weeks after the earthquakes of 24 June, official figures report 5,208 deaths, 16,740 people injured, and 17,907 people left without housing.1 Humanitarian needs remain significant, particularly among displaced families residing in transitional camps and communities with disrupted access to essential services. UNICEF continues to scale up multi-sectoral assistance, focusing on health, nutrition, WASH and child protection services for children and families affected by the earthquakes, reaching over 7,519 people in the initial phase of the response. Health services through mobile health teams have reached around 2,108 people, while vaccination campaigns have reached 6,466 people. More than 2,452 children have been screened for acute malnutrition.

chunks.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.5 (Earthquake Response), 13-20 July 2026
chunks.text: Health services through mobile health teams have reached around 2,108 people, while vaccination campaigns have reached 6,466 people. More than 2,452 children have been screened for acute malnutrition. WASH services are expanding at temporary shelters reaching 7,180 with critical hygiene supplies and 2,861 benefiting from access to safe drinking water. Psychosocial support and recreational activities have reached more than 2,726 children, adolescents and caregivers. Additionally, more than 4,400 people have been reached with hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available life-saving services.

chunks.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.5 (Earthquake Response), 13-20 July 2026
chunks.text: Psychosocial support and recreational activities have reached more than 2,726 children, adolescents and caregivers. Additionally, more than 4,400 people have been reached with hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available life-saving services. UNICEF will reach 150,000 people with critical emergency supplies within the coming weeks, including 49,000 with health supplies, 72,000 with micronutrients, and 29,000 with WASH items. An additional 49 tons of emergency supplies arrived on 14 July to replenish in-country emergency stockpiles. In addition to the US$137.6 million requested under the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal and aligned with the addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan 2026, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes.

chunks.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #28 (21 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 28** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **21 July 2026** **Time: 9:00 pm** **Highlights** **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June. Official toll: **5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured.** The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched** **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.** Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.** The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations.

Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.** The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

chunks.text: Adicionalmente, actores humanitarios y autoridades realizaron una reunión técnica para coordinar acciones relacionadas con abastecimiento de agua, saneamiento, gestión de residuos y calidad del agua.  CRS y Cáritas Venezuela distribuyeron 850 kits familiares de higiene, 400 kits de higiene para bebés y más de 120.000 litros de agua potable, fortaleciendo el acceso a servicios básicos para las familias afectadas. Alojamiento, Energía y Enseres  La OIM mantiene su apoyo a la gestión de los cinco campamentos transitorios cogestionados con las autoridades locales (Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande, Campo de Golf y Mare Abajo), promoviendo mejoras en los sitios, fortaleciendo la coordinación con autoridades, socios humanitarios y actores de cooperación, y respaldando los procesos de registro. A la fecha, la OIM y su socio Fundación Vivienda Popular han distribuido 3.092 sets de cocina, 3.024 lonas plásticas, 2.039 tobos, 1.675 lámparas solares, 819 kits de refugio, 672 mosquiteros y 208 linternas solares recargables.  ACNUR y sus socios implementadores continuaron fortaleciendo las condiciones de protección y alojamiento mediante la distribución de 547 kits de lámparas solares y mosquiteros que benefician a 1.495 personas, la entrega de 200 linternas solares, la instalación de 120 reflectores y lámparas solares en áreas comunitarias, espacios sanitarios y zonas de pernocta, así como la habilitación de 12 unidades modulares de alojamiento temporal en los campamentos transitorios Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande.  CRS apoyó la respuesta mediante la distribución de más de 1.600 lonas para alojamiento temporal, contribuyendo a las necesidades de refugio de familias con viviendas dañadas o destruidas Educación y desarrollo infantil temprano  UNICEF inició actividades de desarrollo de la primera infancia en campamentos transitorios, integradas a las intervenciones de protección infantil. Estas acciones alcanzaron a 82 niñas y niños menores de cinco años, incluyendo 42 niñas, así como a siete mujeres embarazadas y lactantes.  Asimismo, UNICEF brindó orientación a 66 personas cuidadoras sobre prácticas de cuidado cariñoso y sensible y desarrollo infantil temprano, con el objetivo de fortalecer el bienestar, el desarrollo y la resiliencia de niñas y niños afectados por los terremotos y que viven en contextos de desplazamiento.  Construyendo Futuros distribuyó kits escolares, juguetes y materiales recreativos, y fortaleció las capacidades de personal docente, voluntarios y actores educativos mediante actividades de formación en salvaguarda y prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual (PEAS), contribuyendo a entornos seguros para niñas, niños y adolescentes. Logística y Telecomunicaciones  Hoy, el PMA, a través del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística (GTL), facilitó la movilización de 15 TM de insumos destinados a los sectores de refugio y alojamiento, contribuyendo a fortalecer las acciones de asistencia humanitaria en respuesta a la emergencia.  Respecto a las movilizaciones internacionales de carga, hoy aterrizó en el Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía Simón Bolívar un vuelo con 41 TM de ayuda humanitaria con insumos de agua, saneamiento e higiene y alimentos de la ONG Global Empowerment Mission (GEM).  El GTL junto con Hulo coordinaron una reunión para identificar las necesidades de las organizaciones en relación con el envío de ayuda humanitaria desde Colombia hacia Venezuela.

Adicionalmente, 72 NNA participaron en actividades de apoyo psicosocial, acompañamiento lúdico y socioemocional para fortalecer sus estrategias de afrontamiento frente a los efectos de los terremotos.  ACNUR y sus socios implementadores fortalecieron además el acceso a derechos y servicios mediante mesas de información, orientación y sesiones comunitarias que alcanzaron a 1.226 personas, promoviendo el conocimiento de rutas de atención, mecanismos de protección, rendición de cuentas a las poblaciones afectadas (AAP) y prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual (PEAS). Asimismo, dos personas recibieron apoyo especializado a través de la gestión de casos de violencia basada en género (VBG).  En Playa Grande, ACNUR y su socio implementador ODISEF sostuvieron una reunión con la Defensoría del Pueblo para presentar los servicios de protección disponibles y fortalecer la articulación institucional en favor de la población afectada.  UNICEF continúa fortaleciendo los servicios de protección de la niñez mediante apoyo psicosocial, la identificación de niños, niñas y adolescentes en situación de vulnerabilidad, la gestión de casos y los servicios de referencia proporcionados a través de Espacios Amigables para la Niñez y equipos móviles de protección de la niñez en las zonas afectadas. Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 7  Para fortalecer la respuesta de protección de la niñez tras la emergencia por los terremotos, UNICEF suministró insumos y recursos esenciales a los equipos locales de protección de la niñez en La Guaira, reforzando su capacidad para prestar servicios oportunos y de calidad a los niños, niñas y familias afectadas.  En cuatro campamentos transitorios en La Guaira, cuatro Espacios Amigables para la Niñez permanecieron operativos, brindando apoyo psicosocial, actividades recreativas estructuradas y servicios de protección a 2.726 niños, niñas, adolescentes y cuidadores.  Hasta el 21 de julio, las actividades de prevención y respuesta a la violencia basada en género (VBG) lideradas por UNFPA, junto con sus socios implementadores AVESA y Tinta Violeta, alcanzaron a 1.076 personas mediante acciones de sensibilización en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves, Playa Grande y Mare Abajo.

Salud  OPS/OMS coordina la respuesta de Equipos Médicos de Emergencia, al 21 de julio registra 14 EMT desplegados y operativos, 7 desmovilizados y 1 en proceso de movilización, con presencia principalmente en La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda y Aragua. La actividad clínica acumulada reporta 21.666 consultas, 402 cirugías, 475 ingresos y 1.363 días cama ocupados, lo que evidencia el rol crítico de los EMT en la continuidad de la atención sanitaria para la población afectada.  La OPS/OMS realizó una formación teórica práctica de prevención y control de infecciones dirigida a 50 profesionales de enfermería de la Gran Caracas (La Guaira, Distrito Capital y Miranda) del Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud (MPPS).  La OPS/OMS junto a la Dirección Nacional de Salud Mental del MPPS han elaborado protocolos de actuación del punto de salud mental y del especialista en salud mental en campamentos transitorios.  La OPS/OMS continúa apoyando al Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud (MPPS) en la vigilancia activa de enfermedades prevenibles por vacunación en campamentos y comunidades afectadas, así como en la reorganización de las brigadas de vacunación en La Guaira. Asimismo, en coordinación con el MPPS, capacitó a 81 vacunadores de las ASIC 507, 508 y 509 para fortalecer las capacidades de inmunización y vigilancia epidemiológica.  La OIM continúa ampliando el acceso a servicios de salud para las poblaciones afectadas por el terremoto mediante el despliegue de equipos médicos y la prestación de atención primaria, tanto de manera directa como a través de su socio Ven Da Tu Mano.

A la fecha, se han realizado 5.552 atenciones médicas, incluyendo consultas de medicina general, medicina interna, pediatría, ginecología y obstetricia, así como entrega de medicamentos y apoyo psicológico individual.  En el campamento transitorio César Nieves, Ven Da Tu Mano (VDTM), socio de UNFPA, alcanzó a 590 personas mediante actividades de sensibilización en salud sexual y reproductiva. Asimismo, brindó atención prenatal a seis mujeres embarazadas, distribuyó 77 métodos anticonceptivos, 364 condones, 225 materiales informativos y cinco kits de higiene.  UNICEF amplió significativamente el acceso a servicios esenciales de salud en las comunidades afectadas por los terremotos mediante la provisión de suministros médicos, el despliegue de equipos móviles de salud y el apoyo a las autoridades nacionales de salud. En coordinación con socios del Clúster de Salud, UNICEF apoyó el despliegue de equipos médicos y de inmunización en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas en La Guaira.

Los fondos, canalizados a través de la Cruz Roja Canadiense y la Humanitarian Coalition, apoyarán la provisión de servicios de salud, alojamiento y agua, saneamiento e higiene para las poblaciones afectadas.  El Fondo Mundial de lucha contra el sida, la tuberculosis y la malaria aprobó un paquete de financiamiento de emergencia por 1.77 millones de dólares para apoyar los servicios de VIH y tuberculosis en Venezuela luego de los terremotos. Los recursos, que se gestionarán a través del PNUD, permitirán que 7.000 personas continúen el tratamiento del VIH, se garantice el tratamiento de la tuberculosis para 500 personas y se respalde los servicios de prevención, pruebas de detección y divulgación para 1.500 miembros de poblaciones clave en las zonas más afectadas.  La Unión Europea realizó una contribución adicional de 20 millones de euros para apoyar la acción humanitaria en el país. De este total, 10 millones de euros estarán destinados a apoyar operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, asistencia médica y el despliegue de otros expertos, así como asistencia material, en el país.

chunks.title: PAHO supports delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen routine immunization in Venezuela
chunks.text: PAHO supports delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen routine immunization in Venezuela

chunks.title: PAHO supports delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen routine immunization in Venezuela
chunks.text: Caracas, 21 July 2026 (PAHO/WHO) – A shipment of 1.15 million doses of vaccines donated by Brazil arrived in Venezuela on Monday to strengthen the country's routine immunization programme and help protect communities from vaccine-preventable diseases following the devastating earthquakes on the 24 June. The shipment includes one million doses of the pentavalent vaccine (which protects children against five serious diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B and *Haemophilus influenzae* type b), 102,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, and 48,000 doses of the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine against tuberculosis. The donation also included 20 vials of anti-arachnid antivenom. Following disasters, the risk of infectious disease outbreaks can increase as health services are disrupted and many families are displaced into temporary shelters.

chunks.title: PAHO supports delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen routine immunization in Venezuela
chunks.text: The donation also included 20 vials of anti-arachnid antivenom. Following disasters, the risk of infectious disease outbreaks can increase as health services are disrupted and many families are displaced into temporary shelters. Maintaining high vaccination coverage is essential to prevent outbreaks of diseases such as measles, diphtheria and pertussis, particularly among children and other vulnerable groups. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) supported the operation by procuring cold boxes for transporting the vaccines, electronic data loggers to continuously monitor temperatures and safeguard the cold chain, and providing additional logistical support to ensure the vaccines arrived safely and remained effective. This shipment builds on ongoing cooperation between Brazil, Venezuela and PAHO to strengthen immunization efforts.

chunks.title: PAHO supports delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen routine immunization in Venezuela
chunks.text: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) supported the operation by procuring cold boxes for transporting the vaccines, electronic data loggers to continuously monitor temperatures and safeguard the cold chain, and providing additional logistical support to ensure the vaccines arrived safely and remained effective. This shipment builds on ongoing cooperation between Brazil, Venezuela and PAHO to strengthen immunization efforts. Earlier this year, Brazil's Ministry of Health donated 100,000 doses of yellow fever vaccine and 250,000 canine rabies vaccines to Venezuela's Ministry of Health, with PAHO also providing logistical support to maintain the cold chain throughout transport. The arrival of these vaccines will support national efforts to restore and sustain essential health services while protecting communities from preventable diseases during the emergency response and recovery phase. chunks.text: ## Panorama **18 países contribuyentes** La mayor parte de la asistencia internacional desplegada tras los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio de 2026 ha sido proporcionada mediante **cooperación bilateral directa entre Estados**, incluyendo activos militares, transporte aéreo y marítimo, capacidades de ingeniería, apoyo médico y logística. **18 países** movilizaron capacidades: **2.200+ efectivos**, **35+ aeronaves de transporte**, **6 buques** y **40+ helicópteros**. **13 países** aportaron evaluación técnica y estructural; **10 países**, maquinaria e ingeniería (apuntalamiento, corte, perforación y rescate técnico). El territorio de **Puerto Rico** contribuye dentro del componente de EE.UU. Los recursos ingresaron principalmente por el **Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar (Maiquetía)** y el **Puerto de La Guaira**. ### OCHA / UNDAC Apoya a las **autoridades venezolanas** facilitando el intercambio de información y el direccionamiento para que los efectivos militares internacionales coordinen sus acciones con las autoridades nacionales.

chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 27** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **20 July 2026** **Time: 9:00 pm** **Highlights** **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June. Official toll: **5,278 people dead and 16,740 injured.** The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched** **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.** Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,278 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

chunks.text: To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched** **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.** Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,278 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes. The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

Impact on infrastructure  Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.  As part of recovery and reconstruction planning, authorities have identified 40 sites in La Guaira State, covering approximately 584,000 square metres, for the development of housing projects intended for affected populations. Most of the damage, estimated at around US$24 billion, is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools, hospitals, and public facilities.

chunks.text: National response  The Government response remains focused on assistance to affected people, as well as the establishment and management of transitional camps.  According to authorities, the response continues through 107 transitional camps for affected populations, with a total capacity of 27,822 people and a current occupancy of 23,587 people. chunks.text: In response, humanitarian organizations have mobilized relief assistance and logistical support to assist the most affected families. Tierra Viva supported 60 families through the distribution of food and hygiene kits. sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 27** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **20 de julio de 2026** **Hora: 9:00 pm** **Destacados** **Las autoridades reportan 1.405 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio. Balance oficial: **5.278 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.** El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.** **Situación general** Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.405 réplicas.** A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.278 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.** La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas.

Apoya la respuesta humanitaria para atender el terremoto en Venezuela Haz tu donación de forma segura y rápida ahora: Información de Contacto Para mayor información, por favor contactar a la Oficina de OCHA Venezuela: Vanessa May – Jefa de Oficina a.i. - Alfonso Zabaleta – Oficial de Asuntos Humanitarios - Jennifer Moreno – Oficial de Información Pública – Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA)

chunks.title: WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies - Mid-Year Update | July 2026
chunks.text: ## **Overview** In the first half of 2026, the CFE continued to enable WHO to respond rapidly to health emergencies worldwide. WHO released more than US$ 10 million from the CFE to address the health consequences of 12 emergencies, including five disease outbreaks, three complex crises, and four natural disasters. As a key source of WHO’s flexible, early financing for emergencies, the CFE ensures that life-saving operations can begin immediately, often before other donor funding is mobilized. Twelve Member States and the UN Foundation have pledged or contributed more than US$ 17 million to the CFE so far this year.

chunks.title: WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies - Mid-Year Update | July 2026
chunks.text: Within 48 hours, WHO released US$ 3.9 million from the CFE, providing the immediate financing needed to launch and scale up response operations mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which continues to account for the majority of cases and operational requirements. In the first three weeks of the response, WHO activated its incident management system and deployed more than 100 experts through its staff and global partner networks. Leveraging its global logistics hubs, WHO delivered 75 metric tonnes of life-saving supplies, including personal protective equipment, diagnostics and clinical equipment. Clinical management capacity expanded rapidly, with isolation and treatment centres established for suspected and confirmed cases within days, reaching over 500 beds by the end of June. At the same time, WHO strengthened other key response pillars working with the Ministry of Health and partners, including infection prevention and control, community engagement, surveillance, and preparations for critical therapeutic clinical trials.

Readiness measures were expanded in eight priority countries to help prevent further spread.
