Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por 299 millones de dólares, destinada a atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.** Este llamado se suma a la meta de 5,5 millones de personas que ya contemplaba atenderse con el Plan este 2026, para lo que se requieren 632 millones de dólares. De misión en el país, la Comisaria Europea de Gestión de Crisis, Hadja Lahbib, realizó una visita a La Guaira junto con el Coordinador Humanitario de las Naciones Unidas y representantes de agencias humanitarias para conocer de primera mano las necesidades de la población afectada y la respuesta que se está brindando.

Impacto en infraestructura  Las autoridades reportan al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 edificios colapsados.  Como parte de la planificación para la recuperación y reconstrucción, las autoridades identificaron 40 terrenos en el estado La Guaira, equivalentes a aproximadamente 584.000 metros cuadrados, para el desarrollo de proyectos habitacionales destinados a la población afectada. Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 2  Una primera evaluación de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres (UNDRR) señala que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura suman unos 37 mil millones de dólares. La mayoría, unos 24 mil millones de dólares, se concentrarían en viviendas, comercios, escuelas, hospitales e instalaciones públicas. Entre tanto, estimaciones preliminares de PNUD indican daños físicos directos por 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 6 % del PIB.

Hasta el 16 de julio, 41 campamentos se encuentran instalados en Caracas, 28 en Miranda, 28 en La Guaira, y 10 en Aragua.  Las autoridades avanzan en un proceso de registro único de las familias afectadas en campamentos transitorios, mediante la recopilación de datos biométricos y de contacto para apoyar la gestión de la asistencia, los programas de apoyo social y las soluciones habitacionales.  El Gobierno venezolano anunció la creación de un fondo inicial de reconstrucción equivalente a 200 millones de dólares.  Disponible la línea de apoyo psicológico para las personas afectadas: 0800-AYUDA-01.  Se habilitó un formulario digital del Consejo Nacional para las Personas con Discapacidad (Conapdis) para coordinar una respuesta oportuna e inclusiva en las zonas afectadas.  Se habilitaron mecanismos para la localización de personas desaparecidas ( y el reporte de personas afectadas (0-800-RESCATE).  Las actividades escolares permanecen suspendidas en los municipios afectados de los estados Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro y Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua y Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); Distrito Capital (Libertador); y Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello y Pedro Gual).  Al 14 de julio de 2026, las autoridades nacionales habían reportado la recepción de 82 aportes de ayuda humanitaria internacional, equivalentes a aproximadamente 3.624 toneladas de asistencia provenientes de 36 países, organizaciones y entidades donantes. Entre los mayores contribuyentes se encuentran Colombia, Trinidad y Tobago, México, Panamá, China y empresas chinas, Estados Unidos y Brasil.  La ayuda recibida incluye alimentos, agua potable, medicamentos, insumos médicos, vacunas, equipos hospitalarios, artículos de higiene, colchonetas, mantas, carpas, mobiliario, plantas potabilizadoras, herramientas, baterías y suministros para alojamiento temporal, contribuyendo a fortalecer la atención sanitaria, la seguridad alimentaria, el acceso a agua y saneamiento, y la asistencia a las familias afectadas por el terremoto.

Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 4  OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales, continúa coordinando la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias, priorizando acciones en salud, alojamiento, alimentación, agua, saneamiento e higiene, logística y protección.  Al 14 de julio de 2026, 100 organizaciones nacionales, internacionales, agencias de Naciones Unidas, organizaciones locales, instituciones públicas y actores del Movimiento de la Cruz Roja reportaron 2.200 actividades de respuesta en 57 municipios de 14 estados, abarcando 11 sectores humanitarios.  La mayor concentración de la respuesta se registra en La Guaira, con 77 organizaciones y 1.128 actividades, seguida por el Distrito Capital con 62 organizaciones y 536 actividades, y Miranda con 37 organizaciones y 337 actividades. Los sectores con mayor volumen de intervenciones son salud (550 actividades), agua, saneamiento e higiene (476), protección (281), protección de niñas, niños y adolescentes (230) y seguridad alimentaria (204), reflejando una respuesta multisectorial orientada a atender necesidades críticas, fortalecer la protección de las poblaciones afectadas y apoyar la recuperación temprana en las zonas impactadas por el terremoto  El equipo UNDAC/OCHA desplegado en Venezuela apoyó a la coordinación de los equipos USAR, el establecimiento de mecanismos iniciales de coordinación en La Guaira a través del OSOCC y, de manera más amplia, el fortalecimiento de la capacidad operativa de la oficina de OCHA en Venezuela, incluyendo gestión de información, evaluaciones de necesidades y apoyo técnico especializado. A través del OSOCC, facilitó la coordinación entre el gobierno, Naciones Unidas, organizaciones y otros actores clave, promoviendo una respuesta humanitaria integrada, basada en evidencia y alineada con las prioridades nacionales.  Asimismo, los especialistas de iMMAP y MapAction continuarán brindando apoyo técnico a la comunidad humanitaria nacional e internacional en Venezuela, fortaleciendo las capacidades de gestión de información, análisis geoespacial, cartografía humanitaria y apoyo logístico. Este acompañamiento también contribuirá al trabajo de OCHA en Venezuela, apoyando la coordinación entre actores, el análisis de necesidades y la toma de decisiones basadas en evidencia para fortalecer la preparación y respuesta ante futuras emergencias.  OCHA continuó fortaleciendo la coordinación con el sector privado para apoyar las acciones de respuesta y recuperación temprana, promoviendo la articulación con actores especializados en áreas como logística, gestión de escombros, rehabilitación de infraestructura y planificación de la reconstrucción, a través de los mecanismos de coordinación existentes entre las Naciones Unidas y el sector privado.  Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del PNUD.

chunks.text: Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene  En el campamento transitorio Playa Grande, CISP, socio implementador de UNICEF, suministró 12.000 litros de agua y mantuvo operativos cinco puntos de lavado de manos, cuatro estaciones de lavado de ropa y 10 baños portátiles. Asimismo, distribuyó 80 bolsas para desechos, realizó jornadas de recolección de residuos que abarcaron 74 contenedores, ejecutó labores de limpieza y mantenimiento de las instalaciones sanitarias, completó la instalación de las duchas para hombres y desarrolló actividades de promoción de higiene que alcanzaron a 106 personas, incluyendo a 23 niñas, niños y adolescentes mediante sesiones sobre lavado de manos e higiene en contextos de emergencia. Logística y Telecomunicaciones  Arribaron al Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar dos vuelos humanitarios, uno coordinado por Airlink, el Departamento de Estado de EE.UU. y Amazon, y otro organizado por UNHRD y financiado por ECHO, con 85.25 toneladas métrica (TM) de ayuda humanitaria para nueve organizaciones, de las cuales el PMA, a través del Grupo de Trabajo de Logística (GTL), apoyó en la movilización y almacenamiento de 42.66 TM de carga humanitaria correspondientes a cuatro de estas organizaciones, agilizando los movimientos de carga en el aeropuerto.  A la fecha, el GTL ha apoyado, junto con OCHA, la coordinación de la llegada de 525.36 TM de ayuda humanitaria por vía aérea al Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar. Los recursos serán implementados por organizaciones miembros del DEC y sus socios locales para apoyar la respuesta humanitaria.  Parte del apoyo brindado por UNDAC incluye una especialista en coordinación con el sector privado para fortalecer la participación empresarial en la respuesta y recuperación.

chunks.text: ## HIGHLIGHTS As of 14 July, authorities reported at least 4,734 fatalities, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people without shelter following the earthquakes. EMERGENCY UPDATE #3: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES 5 July – 14 July zaiD anaiD/RCHNU © EMERGENCY UPDATE #3: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES OPERATIONAL CONTEXT Two weeks after the earthquakes, the response is increasingly focused on sustaining temporary accommodation, restoring essential services and expanding protection and referral support for people unable to return safely to their homes. As efforts transition from emergency relief to early recovery and reconstruction, priorities are expanding to include safe housing rehabilitation, earthquake-resistant rebuilding and the restoration of damaged infrastructure. UNHCR will continue to provide protection services, support access to documentation, psychosocial assistance, referrals and protection monitoring, as well as reestablishment of services provided by the Ombudsman Office.

chunks.text: La Evaluación Rápida de Necesidades (RNA), un esfuerzo interagencial para generar evidencia oportuna e identificar necesidades en la fase inicial de la emergencia, se realizó entre el 1 y el 3 de julio, dentro de los siete días posteriores a los terremotos. Complementada con información secundaria, análisis especializados e imágenes satelitales, la evaluación confirma una crisis multisectorial en los siete estados afectados:**La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón y Yaracuy.** Los resultados muestran un deterioro de las condiciones de vida y de los servicios básicos, la pérdida de medios de vida y capacidad de compra de los hogares, y un impacto significativo sobre la vivienda, con efectos en el alojamiento, movilidad y cohesión comunitaria. Las mayores afectaciones se concentran en La Guaira, Miranda y el Distrito Capital, evidenciando la necesidad de una respuesta humanitaria multisectorial y sostenida.

chunks.text: Media update from the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) three weeks after the earthquakes on the distress children continue to experience and the need for psychosocial support. Press release [Venezuela]( Published 16. Jul 2026 **Elena Vicario, NRC Country Director for Venezuela said:** “Weeks on from the earthquakes, children’s distress remains profound. For thousands of children, this moment of fear will be etched in their memory forever.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #3: Children’s distress profound after earthquakes | NRC
chunks.text: Jul 2026 **Elena Vicario, NRC Country Director for Venezuela said:** “Weeks on from the earthquakes, children’s distress remains profound. For thousands of children, this moment of fear will be etched in their memory forever. Many of the safe places where they learned, played and grew no longer exist. Children have lost not only their homes and schools, but also friends, neighbours, teachers and family members. “The need for psychosocial support is urgent.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #3: Children’s distress profound after earthquakes | NRC
chunks.text: Children have lost not only their homes and schools, but also friends, neighbours, teachers and family members. “The need for psychosocial support is urgent. Without it is harder for children to recover from the traumatic experience and they will continue to live with the sense of danger generated by the earthquakes. This can affect their capacity to learn, thrive and achieve their full potential. For many children every loud noise can feel as though the tragedy is happening all over again.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #3: Children’s distress profound after earthquakes | NRC
chunks.text: This can affect their capacity to learn, thrive and achieve their full potential. For many children every loud noise can feel as though the tragedy is happening all over again. A child who receives timely support can find the words to understand and express what they are feeling and gradually regain a sense of calm and hope. “One mother told our team how, after spending five days outdoors, a heavy storm arrived. As thunder rolled overhead, children began hugging one another and crying, convinced that another earthquake was coming.

chunks.text: “One mother told our team how, after spending five days outdoors, a heavy storm arrived. As thunder rolled overhead, children began hugging one another and crying, convinced that another earthquake was coming. The fear and anxiety were immediate and visible. “Many schools are closed because of damage, or because they are being used as temporary shelters, and there is now a need for temporary learning spaces. NRC has started providing psychosocial support in temporary shelters.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #3: Children’s distress profound after earthquakes | NRC
chunks.text: “Many schools are closed because of damage, or because they are being used as temporary shelters, and there is now a need for temporary learning spaces. NRC has started providing psychosocial support in temporary shelters. Within the first days of our education response, we reached over 100 children, creating spaces where they can express themselves, play, regain routines and begin to process what they have lived through. We hope to set up 10 temporary learning spaces where we can support 600 children as they gradually overcome the initial shock and reduce the constant sense of fear and alertness. “The solidarity of the Venezuelan people has played an important part in the first weeks after the earthquakes.

However, I have noticed that adolescents are often left out.

We need that impact to fade little by little, working together.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #7 (July 15, 2026)
chunks.text: Project HOPE continues expanding its earthquake response across northern Venezuela, adapting operations to meet evolving health and humanitarian needs while reducing the risk of secondary public health emergencies. Over the past several days, Project HOPE expanded services into a new community in La Guaira, continued scaling mobile medical services, and provided more than 1,300 additional primary healthcare consultations, despite severe weather temporarily disrupting operations in some locations. Disease surveillance; water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) remain central priorities as displaced families continue to face difficult living conditions. **Situation Overview** Humanitarian needs remain significant as recovery efforts continue across northern Venezuela. The official death toll has risen to nearly 4,500 people while more than 17,000 remain displaced or without permanent housing.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake Response, July–December 2026 – Addendum to the 2026 UNICEF HAC Appeal
chunks.text: On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela, adding a new layer of humanitarian needs to an already fragile context. Two weeks after the earthquakes, official figures reported 4,490 deaths, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people left without housing. The earthquakes have created a major child-focused humanitarian emergency on top of already significant needs. Children and families have lost homes, schools, access to safe water, health services, and protection systems, while aftershocks continue to heighten risks and complicate recovery.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake Response, July–December 2026 – Addendum to the 2026 UNICEF HAC Appeal
chunks.text: The earthquakes have created a major child-focused humanitarian emergency on top of already significant needs. Children and families have lost homes, schools, access to safe water, health services, and protection systems, while aftershocks continue to heighten risks and complicate recovery. UNICEF requires **US$65.7 million to reach 470,000 people; of which 167,000 are children**. UNICEF’s earthquake response and is fully aligned with the addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) in Venezuela, which targets **1.3 million people affected by the earthquake** across 7 states. Before the earthquakes, UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) Appeal targeted 2.3 million people, including 1.2 million children, with a focus on addressing critical needs in health care, nutrition, safe water, sanitation, education, and child protection services.

chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 22** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **15 July 2026** **Time: 9:00 pm** **Highlights** Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,200 aftershocks.** Official toll: **4,829 people dead and 16,740 injured.** **An additional appeal for US$299 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.** The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,284 aftershocks.** Twenty-one days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **4,829 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency**. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.** The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.** This is in addition to the 5.5 million people already targeted under the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires US$632 million in funding.

As of 15 July, 40 camps are located in Caracas, 28 in Miranda, 28 in La Guaira, and 10 in Aragua.  Authorities are advancing a unified registration process for affected families in transitional camps through the collection of biometric and contact information to support assistance management, social support programmes and housing solutions.  The Government of Venezuela announced the creation of an initial reconstruction fund equivalent to US$200 million.  A psychosocial support hotline remains available for affected people: 0800-AYUDA-01.  A digital form has been launched by the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS) to support a timely and inclusive response in affected areas.  Mechanisms have been established to locate missing persons ( and to report affected individuals (0-800-RESCATE).  School activities remain suspended in affected municipalities across the states of Aragua (Santiago Mariño, Girardot, Ocumare de la Costa de Oro and Tovar); Carabobo (Juan José Mora, Puerto Cabello, Naguanagua and Valencia); Falcón (José Laurencio Silva); La Guaira (Vargas); the Capital District (Libertador); and Miranda (Chacao, Baruta, El Hatillo, Sucre, Plaza, Zamora, Acevedo, Brión, Buroz, Páez, Andrés Bello and Pedro Gual). Situation by state Capital District (Caracas) and Miranda  A coordination meeting was held with authorities from the Miranda State Government and InterCluster members to share the results of the multisectoral needs assessment conducted in seven transitional camps. chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 22** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **15 de julio de 2026** **Hora: 9:00 pm** **Destacados** Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), l**as autoridades reportan más de 1.200 réplicas.** Balance oficial: **4.829 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.** **Se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones para ampliar la respuesta a los terremotos y atender las necesidades de** **1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.** El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas. **Situación general** Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.284 réplicas.** A 21 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **4.829 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia.** Asimismo, indicaron que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.** La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por 299 millones de dólares, destinada a atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.** Este llamado se suma a la meta de 5,5 millones de personas que ya contemplaba atenderse con el Plan este 2026, para lo que se requieren 632 millones de dólares.

Mantuvo conversaciones con el gobierno, representantes del sector privado y socios internacionales para identificar posibles áreas de cooperación en la recuperación temprana y la respuesta humanitaria. chunks.title: Venezuela: UNOPS apoyará a las comunidades afectadas por los recientes terremotos

chunks.text: **CARACAS, 15 July 2026.—** UNOPS has just concluded a mission to Venezuela to support response recovery efforts following the devastating earthquake. **Dalila Gonçalves**, **UNOPS Regional Director for Latin America and the Caribbean**, led the mission. She engagedin discussions with the government, private-sector representatives, and international partners to identify potential areas of cooperation in early recovery and humanitarian response. "Our solidarity is with the people of Venezuela. The communities’ needs are immense and the damage is colossal.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #03 (Reporting period: 08 - 14 July 2026)
chunks.text: *This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.* **Summary Points** LTC Telecoms is coordinating telecommunications response efforts in Venezuela, working with government authorities, mobile network operators, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), and other partners to identify connectivity gaps, restore critical communications, and prioritize support in the most affected areas. LTC Telecoms and partners expanded emergency connectivity services at priority displacement sites, including Playa Grande, César Nieves Stadium Transitional Camp, and Caraballeda, providing shared internet access and strengthening communications for affected communities and humanitarian responders.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #03 (Reporting period: 08 - 14 July 2026)

LTC Telecoms and partners expanded emergency connectivity services at priority displacement sites, including Playa Grande, César Nieves Stadium Transitional Camp, and Caraballeda, providing shared internet access and strengthening communications for affected communities and humanitarian responders. Despite ongoing restoration efforts, power disruptions, damaged telecommunications infrastructure, and connectivity challenges continue to affect communities in La Guaira, Petare, Catia, and other earthquake-affected areas, underscoring the need for continued telecommunications support.

Situation Overview Between 08 and 13 July, Venezuela remained in a severe humanitarian emergency following the twin magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes that struck the north-central region on 24 June, just 40 seconds apart. The earthquakes affected at least seven states, including La Guaira, Capital District, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, and Yaracuy, causing widespread damage to homes, public infrastructure, schools, hospitals, electricity and telecommunications networks, and other essential services. The response continues to transition from large-scale search and rescue operations to humanitarian relief, emergency shelter, protection services, health support, and early recovery planning.

chunks.text: The humanitarian situation remained severe, with casualty figures continuing to rise and assessments identifying significant multisectoral needs affecting an estimated 1.3 million people. OCHA continued coordinating international assistance and supporting response efforts. Priority needs include emergency shelter, medical care, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, child protection, and the restoration of telecommunications and other critical infrastructure. During the reporting period, UN Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher concluded a four-day visit to Venezuela, calling for sustained international support to meet urgent humanitarian needs and support recovery efforts. Authorities maintained emergency coordination mechanisms and continued managing transitional camps across affected areas.

chunks.text: During the reporting period, UN Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher concluded a four-day visit to Venezuela, calling for sustained international support to meet urgent humanitarian needs and support recovery efforts. Authorities maintained emergency coordination mechanisms and continued managing transitional camps across affected areas. While responsibility for urban search and rescue activities was increasingly transferred to Venezuelan Civil Protection authorities, international response teams remained deployed to support recovery efforts, assessments, and humanitarian operations. Telecommunications Overview The 24 June earthquakes caused significant damage to telecommunications infrastructure across La Guaira, Greater Caracas, and parts of Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, and Falcón States. While Venezuela's core telecommunications networks remain operational, damage to power systems, fibreoptic infrastructure, mobile network facilities, and transmission equipment disrupted connectivity in several affected areas.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #03 (Reporting period: 08 - 14 July 2026)
chunks.text: Telecommunications Overview The 24 June earthquakes caused significant damage to telecommunications infrastructure across La Guaira, Greater Caracas, and parts of Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, and Falcón States. While Venezuela's core telecommunications networks remain operational, damage to power systems, fibreoptic infrastructure, mobile network facilities, and transmission equipment disrupted connectivity in several affected areas. Ongoing aftershocks, infrastructure damage, and access constraints continued to affect service reliability and restoration efforts. Although emergency repairs restored partial services in major population centres, intermittent outages and reduced service quality persisted in some earthquake-affected areas. Reliable telecommunications services remained critical to humanitarian operations, enabling coordination among responders, information sharing, and access to assistance for affected communities.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #03 (Reporting period: 08 - 14 July 2026)
chunks.text: Although emergency repairs restored partial services in major population centres, intermittent outages and reduced service quality persisted in some earthquake-affected areas. Reliable telecommunications services remained critical to humanitarian operations, enabling coordination among responders, information sharing, and access to assistance for affected communities. Mobile network operators Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, and Digitel remained operational across most of the country; however, localized service disruptions and reduced network performance continued to be reported in affected areas. Restoration efforts remained ongoing as authorities and service providers worked to repair damaged infrastructure and stabilize connectivity. The electricity sector continued to face operational challenges due to damage to transmission and distribution infrastructure.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #03 (Reporting period: 08 - 14 July 2026)
chunks.text: Restoration efforts remained ongoing as authorities and service providers worked to repair damaged infrastructure and stabilize connectivity. The electricity sector continued to face operational challenges due to damage to transmission and distribution infrastructure. Power disruptions affected households, health facilities, water systems, telecommunications equipment, and temporary displacement sites, slowing recovery efforts and complicating the restoration of essential services. Continued investment in telecommunications and power infrastructure repairs, alongside emergency connectivity solutions, will be critical to restoring reliable communications, supporting humanitarian operations, and enabling longer-term recovery in earthquake-affected communities. LTC Telecoms Activities Coordination Page 2 of 5 Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area | Since 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed to Caracas to support inter-agency coordination, telecommunications assessments, and the restoration of critical communications services. Working with OCHA, Comisión Nacional de Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL), CANTV, Movistar, Digitel, and other partners, LTC Telecoms is supporting the establishment of a telecommunications coordination mechanism to map incoming assets, identify connectivity gaps, avoid duplication, and prioritize support in the most affected areas. As of 13 July, efforts remain focused on high-impact locations including Petare, Catia, and La Guaira, where power outages, network disruptions, and infrastructure damage continue to affect connectivity. Planned and ongoing interventions include shared internet services, public Wi-Fi, satellite communications, and solar-powered charging facilities to support humanitarian coordination, information-sharing, and access to services.

Backup solutions, including UPS units, generators, EcoFlow batteries, and solar panels, remain essential to maintain service continuity during outages. Connectivity congestion: High numbers of Starlink units and unmanaged routers may reduce service quality and affect community access. Fuel movement restrictions: Generator operations are constrained by challenges associated with transporting fuel between sites. Evolving site requirements: Population growth at existing sites and the emergence of new locations, such as Playa Verde, require continuous reassessment of connectivity and power needs.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #12 (13 to 14 July 2026)
chunks.text: The twelfth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 13 to 14 July. **Highlights** Between 13 and 14 July, IOM continued scaling up its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira, with interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, and information management. To date, IOM has reached 5,774 unique individuals through 8,844 instances of assistance and services, mainly in health and MHPSS, shelter and site coordination, WASH, and protection. IOM distributed essential items, advanced the installation and organization of transitory camps, and supported the relocation of 31 households from the José María Vargas Sports Centre to other accommodation sites in Caracas. **IOM Activities** IOM continues supporting transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira through shelter, site coordination, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, mobility monitoring and inter-agency coordination. IOM and its partners distributed 517 tarpaulins, 515 kitchen sets and 476 buckets.

At the Tanaguarena Golf Course, 120 essential item kits were distributed and the arrival of large-capacity tents was coordinated. The organization of spaces and services also continued at Mare Abajo II and Playa Grande. At César Nieves Stadium and Playa Grande, water supply, toilet cleaning, shower installation, waste management and hygiene promotion activities continued.

IOM will also continue registration and the monitoring of needs and mobility, as well as support to the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group to consolidate information and coordinate interventions.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #12 (13 y 14 de julio 2026)
chunks.text: El duodécimo Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, con información correspondiente al período del 13 al 14 de julio. **Aspectos destacados** Entre el 13 y el 14 de julio, la OIM continuó ampliando su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas de La Guaira, con intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, salud, protección, agua, saneamiento e higiene, y gestión de información. A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a 5.774 personas únicas mediante 8.844 asistencias y servicios, principalmente en salud y SMAPS, alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, WASH y protección. La OIM distribuyó artículos esenciales, avanzó en la instalación y organización de campamentos transitorios y apoyó la reubicación de 31 núcleos familiares desde el Polideportivo José María Vargas hacia otros espacios en Caracas. **Actividades de la OIM** La OIM continúa apoyando campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas en La Guaira mediante alojamiento, coordinación de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, monitoreo de la movilidad y coordinación interagencial. La OIM y sus socios distribuyeron 517 lonas, 515 sets de cocina y 476 baldes.

La OIM y sus socios distribuyeron 517 lonas, 515 sets de cocina y 476 baldes. En el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena se entregaron 120 kits de artículos esenciales y se coordinó el ingreso de carpas de gran capacidad. También continuó la organización de espacios y servicios en Mare Abajo II y Playa Grande. En el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande continuaron las actividades de abastecimiento de agua, limpieza de baños, instalación de duchas, gestión de residuos y promoción de la higiene.

El monitoreo también identificó la movilidad de familias afectadas desde La Guaira hacia Amazonas y Santa Elena de Uairén. **Respuesta planificada de la OIM** La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la gestión y adecuación de campamentos transitorios, la instalación de carpas y servicios básicos, la atención en salud y salud mental, el triaje y las derivaciones de protección, y las medidas de prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual. También continuará el registro y monitoreo de necesidades y movilidad, así como el apoyo al Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales para consolidar información y coordinar las intervenciones.

chunks.title: EU provides €20 million in humanitarian funding following earthquakes in Venezuela
sources: European Commission's Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations
chunks.text: The European Union is releasing an additional €10 million in humanitarian funding to help the most affected communities in Venezuela, following the recent earthquakes. The other €10 million, subject to the approval of the Budgetary Authority, support the search and rescue, medical and other expert teams' operations, along with in-kind assistance deployed in the country. The announcement comes as Commissioner for Preparedness and Crisis Management Hadja **Lahbib** visits Venezuela as a sign of the EU's unwavering support for the country in facing this crisis. The Commissioner will be in Caracas tomorrow, where she will meet with EU-funded aid partners and local authorities that are coordinating the emergency response, as well as with one of the European medical teams deployed through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism.

The Commissioner will be in Caracas tomorrow, where she will meet with EU-funded aid partners and local authorities that are coordinating the emergency response, as well as with one of the European medical teams deployed through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. Today's announcement add to the [€5 million]( life-saving assistance already approved at the end of June, and to the €52 million allocated at the beginning of the year to respond to the humanitarian consequences of the socio-economic crisis in [Venezuela]( EU humanitarian aid is solely channelled through partners such as UN agencies and international NGOs, which work with local partners. Additionally, as part of the EU Humanitarian Air Bridge launched in June, 2 EU-funded flights have already landed in Venezuela, bringing nearly 80 tonnes of essential supplies. Through the EU [Civil Protection Mechanism]( around 750 responders and experts, as well as relief items, have been mobilised from 18 countries.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 21** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **14 July 2026** **Time: 9:00 pm** **Highlights** Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,200 aftershocks.** Official toll: **4,734 people dead and 16,740 injured.** A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.** **An additional appeal for US$298 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.** The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,275 aftershocks.** Twenty days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **4,734 people dead, 16,740 injured and 6,462 rescued** since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their home**. The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance.

The funding will provide humanitarian assistance in key sectors, including food security, health care, shelter and non-food items, through WFP, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and IOM.  The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52 million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.  Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.  Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.  Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance, water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP, UNHCR and Save the Children.  Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and the Danish Red Cross.  The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and their local partners to support the humanitarian response.  As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 21** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **14 de julio de 2026** **Hora: 9:00 pm** **Destacados** Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de 1.200 réplicas.** Balance oficial: **4.734 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.** **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.** **Se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$298 millones para ampliar la respuesta a los terremotos y atender las necesidades de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.** El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas. **Situación general** Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.275 réplicas.** A 20 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **4.734 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, indicaron que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.** La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por 298 millones de dólares, destinada a atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses**.

Esto incluye equipos en proceso de desmovilización.  OCHA continuó fortaleciendo la coordinación con el sector privado para apoyar las acciones de respuesta y recuperación temprana, promoviendo la articulación con actores especializados en áreas como logística, gestión de escombros, rehabilitación de infraestructura y planificación de la reconstrucción, a través de los mecanismos de coordinación existentes entre las Naciones Unidas y el sector privado.  Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del PNUD.

chunks.title: Quick Note - Environmental Issues - June 2026 Earthquakes Venezuela
chunks.text: Purpose This note summaries environmental policies and challenges associated with the response to the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes. The information provided can be used to integrate environmental issues into plans and operations. This note focuses on shelter, formal and informal sheltering sites and housing, land and property (HLP), but is relevant for WASH-related efforts and activities involving infrastructure and energy as well. Weather and Hazard Overview: Heavy Rains and Landslides The impacted area is entering the normal annual peak in rainfall1 and can be affected by hurricanes or tropical low-pressure waves which can trigger intense rains. The potential for heavy rains needs to be monitored on a daily basis.2 In addition, landslide and mud flow mapping is needed, given a potential for increased events associated with seismic activity, as a results of heavy rains, or both.3 Experts in Venezuela can be expected to provide detailed technical support on these hazards.

The potential for heavy rains needs to be monitored on a daily basis.2 In addition, landslide and mud flow mapping is needed, given a potential for increased events associated with seismic activity, as a results of heavy rains, or both.3 Experts in Venezuela can be expected to provide detailed technical support on these hazards. Screening for Environmental Impacts and Issues Screening humanitarian operations for critical environmental impacts is essential to reducing harm to disaster survivors. While direct surveys of the disaster-affected are preferred, valuable screening results are possible through scraping environment-related information from personal observations, field reports and other assessments. The two screening tools which can be used for this process are the Rapid Environmental Impact Assessment process, providing a broad view of environmental issues, and the Nexus Environmental Assessment Tool (NEAT) +, providing a more operational and project-level 1 See on weather patterns. 2 See for local forecasts in Spanish. 3 Also 2026 Venezuela Earthquakes - Rapid Imagery Assessment for Hazardous Landslides and An Integrated Approach for Debris-Flow Risk Mitigation in the North Coastal Range of Venezuela. 14 July 2026 result.4 In the absence of field data collection, both tools can be used as table-top exercises.

Clearing this debris is essential to rapid rebuilding and recovery. Comprehensive guidance on safe and environmentally sound debris management can be found in Disaster Waste Management Guidelines5. Disaster waste management contingency planning provides step-by-step details to plan debris operations. It is also important to consider the significance of a family’s housing, land and property assets6 which can be extracted from the earthquake debris to reduce the need for immediate and long-term relief and recovery support and reduce volumes going to disposal sites A background note on asbestos, a hazardous material likely to be found in debris, can be found here.

It is also important to consider the significance of a family’s housing, land and property assets6 which can be extracted from the earthquake debris to reduce the need for immediate and long-term relief and recovery support and reduce volumes going to disposal sites A background note on asbestos, a hazardous material likely to be found in debris, can be found here. Debris management, whether large or small, should include effective yet relatively simple personal and operations-level protection from asbestos and other hazardous dust for workers and neighboring populations (which alone can trigger health issues and can contain hazardous compounds) and direct exposure to hazardous items during the removal, transport and processing of debris. Large scale projects to clear debris and deconstruct earthquake-damaged buildings are expected. In parallel, community-based, labor-intensive debris clearance can be highly effective in residential low-rise-building neighborhoods.

chunks.text: Large scale projects to clear debris and deconstruct earthquake-damaged buildings are expected. In parallel, community-based, labor-intensive debris clearance can be highly effective in residential low-rise-building neighborhoods. This approach provides opportunities to recover personal possessions and household and other items from damaged buildings, locally reuse, repurpose, recycle or monetize debris, improve the sense of control by disaster survivors and, where cash or vouchers are used as compensation for debris clearance, improve disaster survivors’ self-recovery capacities. Energy Access to sufficient energy for normal activities, a challenge before the earthquakes, is expected to be a significant issue for the foreseeable future. The Venezuela Working Group on Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation has given attention to energy before the recent earthquakes and can be a source of information going forward.

Considering the issues with energy before the earthquakes and likely to emerge from communal sites and for household needs, a post disaster energy needs-and-options assessment should be conducted. This assessment can focus on the evolution of short (weeks) and longer term (months) needs and supply options during building repairs and the transition to permanent shelter solutions. Additional information on energy options is available from the Global Platform for Action in Sustainable Energy in Displacement Settings. WASH With damage to water and sanitating infrastructure and the creation of communal sites, specific steps are required to ensure adequate potable water and safe disposal of solid and liquid waste.

chunks.text: Additional information on energy options is available from the Global Platform for Action in Sustainable Energy in Displacement Settings. WASH With damage to water and sanitating infrastructure and the creation of communal sites, specific steps are required to ensure adequate potable water and safe disposal of solid and liquid waste. Where possible, solid and liquid waste should be kept separate from earthquake debris to reduce health risks and facilitate debris processing. Given the ongoing rainy season, consideration should be given to collecting rainwater for nonpotable uses using gutters and collection tanks. This approach can be used in both communal shelters and affected residential neighborhoods, with a potential short-term reduction in piped or trucked supply requirements.

Disease vectors are likely to increase with an expected increase in nesting sites and food sources. Integrated pest management approaches should be implemented in communal sites and affected neighborhoods to reduce the risk of vector-borne diseases. Reducing Environmental Impacts of Vector Control Chemicals in Emergencies provides technical guidance on vector control in humanitarian settings.

chunks.text: The Circular Economy, Emergency Procurement, and Packaging A circular economy approach, where procurement and distribution are part of a cradle-tograve plan to reuse, repair, repurpose or recycle the assistance, is becoming a good practice standard for humanitarian aid. A circular economy approach may not currently be possible for all physical humanitarian aid. However, a minimum expectation is that organizations providing aid understand: What will happen to the aid item once it is no longer usable, and Whether there are systems in place to repair, reuse, repurpose or recycle the item with minimal threat to the environment. The Logistics Cluster WREC project can provide guidance on this approach. In general, relief item procurement should be done as close to the point of need as possible to reduce transport costs and impacts on the environment.

In general, relief item procurement should be done as close to the point of need as possible to reduce transport costs and impacts on the environment. The basic approach is to remove packaging which is linked to the commercial sale of an item, such as plastic sleeves for tools or excessive plastic wrapping or boxing intended to assure zero damage during transit. While packaging still needs to protect relief items these items are not for sale and the level of damage protection during transport can be reduced. Efforts to reduce the environmental impacts of packing include an expectation that all packaging will be either collected at or after distribution and processed (reused, repurposed or recycled) or that those receiving relief items will reuse, repurpose or recycle the packaging. Discussing existing formal and informal reuse, repurposing and recycling systems with local informants can identify whether packaging becomes waste or becomes an asset for affected families.

chunks.title: Quick Note - Environmental Issues - June 2026 Earthquakes Venezuela
chunks.text: Donated Relief Items The Venezuela response is likely to generate a considerable volume of relief supplies from private individuals and solidarity groups. Historically, these relief supplies have overloaded logistics and storage capacities and, in the case of drugs, required special processing. These challenges draw resources away from humanitarian operations and can lead to environmental impacts by overloading disposal sites and, in the case of drugs, requiring specialized incineration. Relief items should not be sent to Venezuela which (1) have not been specifically requested as part of ongoing assistance programs, or (2) do not meet humanitarian standards (see above). As it can be difficult to prevent the arrival of unsolicited relief items, an online system for matching donated items to actual needs on the ground before shipment may help reduce negative impacts and a need to purchase relief items locally or internationally.

Nature-Based Risk Management Options Given that a significant part of the affected area is also subject to landslides and debris and mud flows, medium term programs using a nature-based approach to hazard management should be 8 IOM’s catalogue requires a log in through an IOM account. 14 July 2026 considered. The nature-based approach is generally less costly with lower maintenance requirements than typical hard structure interventions. Nature-based approaches can involve significant community participation, providing opportunities for livelihood support and proactive risk reduction.

Nature-based approaches can involve significant community participation, providing opportunities for livelihood support and proactive risk reduction. Given the likely years-long timeline for rebuilding housing, nature-based hazard management programming can provide a long-termer mechanism for supporting affected individuals. ##

Por ello, se continúa recopilando la data a través del formulario, a la vez, se notificó que, para los procesos de registro de movilización de carga humanitaria, deberá notificarse a su vez en la web difundida por las autoridades nacionales.

chunks.text: From 9-10 July (local time), AMDA’s joint relief team continued providing medical assistance at a temporary clinic in Caraballeda, La Guaira, one of the areas severely affected by the 24 June quakes. The details are as follows: ■9 July Representing a diverse mix of nationalities, AMDA President Dr. Takushi Sato, Japanese nurse Hideaki Yamazaki, two physicians from AMDA Peru, local Venezuelan doctors, a Venezuelan doctor based in Peru, a Mexican physician, and many others treated approximately 300 patients throughout the day. The AMDA team provided medical services including patient consultations, trauma care, and ultrasound examinations. In some cases, Dr. Sato and Venezuelan physicians discussed patients' conditions and jointly determined the most appropriate course of treatment.

Meanwhile, many patients visited the temporary clinic from the early morning. A patient who had undergone a surgical procedure by the AMDA team the previous day returned to the clinic for a follow-up examination, allowing the team to monitor the patient's recovery.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Following Venezuela's twin earthquakes on 24 June 2026, CORE (Community Organized Relief Effort) and the Wayuu Taya Foundation conducted a rapid needs assessment across 24 sites in seven states between 26 June and 6 July. The assessment found housing damage at 20 of 24 sites assessed, with the highest-priority locations concentrated in La Guaira and Distrito Capital. Communities identified personal hygiene products, shelter and housing, and baby products as their top unmet needs. In addition, limited sanitation and water access have contributed to a rise in water-borne illness.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Communities identified personal hygiene products, shelter and housing, and baby products as their top unmet needs. In addition, limited sanitation and water access have contributed to a rise in water-borne illness. Displaced families are sheltering in a mix of formal camps, informal settlements, and with relatives, with informal sites facing the greatest gaps in WASH and aid coverage. It is recommended to continue first-line assistance, debris clearance, phased shelter rehabilitation, and WASH interventions, while incorporating voucher-based and other market-linked approaches alongside in-kind and service-based assistance to support recovery.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela JULY 2026 OVERVIEW On June 24, a Mw 7.2 foreshock, followed by a Mw 7.5 mainshock, struck near Yumare, west of Caracas, on Venezuela's National Day, when more residents were at home, increasing casualties. As of July 7th, Venezuelan authorities reported at least 3,535 fatalities. Caracas neighborhoods Los Palos Grandes and Altamira suffered severe damage, including the complete collapse of a 22-story building, and nearby, La Guaira was declared a disaster zone. Damage extends across nine states; beyond outright collapses, many buildings remain standing but unsafe, with water and gas service cut and structures unassessed.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Caracas neighborhoods Los Palos Grandes and Altamira suffered severe damage, including the complete collapse of a 22-story building, and nearby, La Guaira was declared a disaster zone. Damage extends across nine states; beyond outright collapses, many buildings remain standing but unsafe, with water and gas service cut and structures unassessed. In response, CORE (Community Organized Relief Effort) and the Wayuu Taya Foundation mobilized a multimodal emergency program, including the distribution of shelf-stable food kits and hygiene kits, debris removal, and search-and-recovery site support. Our teams have conducted a rapid needs assessment, summarized below, to ensure an evidence-based, well-targeted response. Assessments are ongoing — this document outlines preliminary findings.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Our teams have conducted a rapid needs assessment, summarized below, to ensure an evidence-based, well-targeted response. Assessments are ongoing — this document outlines preliminary findings. KEY ASSESSMENT DATA 24 14,820 3,019 SITES ASSESSED / 7 STATES PEOPLE AFFECTED HOUSEHOLDS AFFECTED Figures reflect the population and sites covered by this rapid assessment, not the full earthquake-affected population. METHODOLOGY The assessment combined three methods: Key Informant Interviews with 28 camp managers/community leaders (17 female, 11 male), conducted in person by three local staff over six days (June 26–July 6, 2026). A participant survey on top unmet needs and preferred assistance modality, administered during in-kind distributions, and direct observation of shelters and market functionality to inform cash and voucher feasibility.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: METHODOLOGY The assessment combined three methods: Key Informant Interviews with 28 camp managers/community leaders (17 female, 11 male), conducted in person by three local staff over six days (June 26–July 6, 2026). A participant survey on top unmet needs and preferred assistance modality, administered during in-kind distributions, and direct observation of shelters and market functionality to inform cash and voucher feasibility. Coverage included 24 localities from 9 municipalities in 7 states (See Table 1). 2 NEEDS ASSESSMENT I WWW.CORERESPONSE.ORG KEY FINDINGS An estimated 14,820 people from 3,019 households were affected (See Figure 1). Of 24 sites assessed, 10 were rated as high priority, 7 medium, and 7 low. 21 fatalities were reported, mostly in La Guaira (20), where rescue operations remained active at the time of assessment. Distrito Capital accounted for the largest share of affected people (5,519 or 37% of the total), followed by Aragua (4,304 or 29%).

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Of 24 sites assessed, 10 were rated as high priority, 7 medium, and 7 low. 21 fatalities were reported, mostly in La Guaira (20), where rescue operations remained active at the time of assessment. Distrito Capital accounted for the largest share of affected people (5,519 or 37% of the total), followed by Aragua (4,304 or 29%). The 10 high-priority sites were concentrated in La Guaira and Distrito Capital, where multiple residential buildings collapsed entirely. Moderate-severity damage, significant but without total collapse, was most common in Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, and Yaracuy. Respondents identified their top three unmet needs as personal hygiene products (60%), shelter and housing (48%), and baby products (37%).

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Moderate-severity damage, significant but without total collapse, was most common in Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón, and Yaracuy. Respondents identified their top three unmet needs as personal hygiene products (60%), shelter and housing (48%), and baby products (37%). Our assessment teams also noted that sanitation facilities were limited and access to safe water beyond the bottled water being distributed to families was limited, resulting in an increase in the number of reported water-borne diseases in the assessed camp. Food was available at all sites and was not reported by the community as a need at this time. Medical teams were also available at most sites, though our teams have received requests for medical supplies to support the work of existing medical teams.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Food was available at all sites and was not reported by the community as a need at this time. Medical teams were also available at most sites, though our teams have received requests for medical supplies to support the work of existing medical teams. SHELTER DAMAGE: Housing damage was observed at 20 of 24 sites, ranging from cracked structures to complete collapse. Affected buildings are predominantly confined masonry concrete block walls with reinforced concrete columns and beams, and roofs that are a mix of reinforced concrete and corrugated galvanized iron (CGI/zinc) sheeting. Our teams assessed damage consistent with earthquake damage patterns, spanning a spectrum from light cracking (cosmetic/repairable), through moderate structural damage (repairable with retrofit), to severe damage or complete collapse (unsafe).

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Affected buildings are predominantly confined masonry concrete block walls with reinforced concrete columns and beams, and roofs that are a mix of reinforced concrete and corrugated galvanized iron (CGI/zinc) sheeting. Our teams assessed damage consistent with earthquake damage patterns, spanning a spectrum from light cracking (cosmetic/repairable), through moderate structural damage (repairable with retrofit), to severe damage or complete collapse (unsafe). Common damage includes wall cracking, out-of-plane failure of block walls, spalled concrete columns with exposed reinforcement, collapsed or damaged cinder block, and partial roof or slab collapse. Our assessment teams also noted that a lot of the damage is invisible from above. In larger metro areas like Caracas, many buildings appear stable from a distance and satellite imagery, but closer inspection reveals varying levels of cracking and structural damage.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: Our assessment teams also noted that a lot of the damage is invisible from above. In larger metro areas like Caracas, many buildings appear stable from a distance and satellite imagery, but closer inspection reveals varying levels of cracking and structural damage. These unseen impacts do not register in top-down assessments. Near Morón and in La Guaira, damage is concentrated in single-family and one- to two-story homes; a meaningful share are repairable and could be rapidly rehabilitated to return families home quickly. 3 NEEDS ASSESSMENT I WWW.CORERESPONSE.ORG WATER, SANITATION, AND HYGIENE (WASH): Potable water is one of the most persistent unmet needs, affecting both formal centers and informal settlements, where conditions are more critical. Sanitation is also affected, with broken pipes, portable toilets in poor condition, and unsafe shared bathrooms.

chunks.text: Near Morón and in La Guaira, damage is concentrated in single-family and one- to two-story homes; a meaningful share are repairable and could be rapidly rehabilitated to return families home quickly. 3 NEEDS ASSESSMENT I WWW.CORERESPONSE.ORG WATER, SANITATION, AND HYGIENE (WASH): Potable water is one of the most persistent unmet needs, affecting both formal centers and informal settlements, where conditions are more critical. Sanitation is also affected, with broken pipes, portable toilets in poor condition, and unsafe shared bathrooms. These gaps have already led to health impacts, including scabies, lice, and diarrhea (IPOSTEL camp), gastrointestinal issues (Plaza del Foro), and skin/ stomach conditions (Palabra de Dios, Parque Caraballeda OPP 33). DISPLACEMENT & CAMPS: Displaced families are finding shelter through a mix of formal and informal arrangements. Many are staying with neighbors and relatives; some have set up tents outside their homes, and others are living in formal or informal camps.

chunks.title: Rapid Community Needs Assessment: Earthquake in Caracas, Venezuela | July 2026
chunks.text: DISPLACEMENT & CAMPS: Displaced families are finding shelter through a mix of formal and informal arrangements. Many are staying with neighbors and relatives; some have set up tents outside their homes, and others are living in formal or informal camps. Many families were also sheltering with neighbors and relatives across assessed sites. Two categories of camp are forming, distinguished by the level of institutional support present: » Formal camps: Five established sites (Guayana Esequiba, Parque del Oeste, Manuel Gual, Campo de Golf, Venetur Tibisay) house over 9,100 people and provide full-service coverage, including central kitchens, security presence, medical services, and in some cases, psychosocial services. » Informal sites: A large share of displaced individuals remain in informal or unspecified arrangements and prefer this option to returning to compromised homes. These sites show strong self-organization (e.g., resident watch shifts at Plaza del Foro), but little or no state presence.

These sites show strong self-organization (e.g., resident watch shifts at Plaza del Foro), but little or no state presence. Residents depend on neighbor donations while WASH and shelter gaps remain significant. Aid distribution is also uneven within this group: when assistance is provided, it does not reach all households equally. The assessment team also noted that these sites are largely open-air, leaving families exposed to mosquitoes, sun, and the elements, driving the need for vector protection, sun protection, and shelter reinforcement.

These homes are usually 1-2 floors and built incrementally. Most of these homes do not comply with earthquake-resistant codes, and they pose severe lifesafety risks during seismic events. These are primarily due to informal construction, which uses heavy, brittle materials like unreinforced clay bricks and adobe. A large section of rural homes closer to the fault lines have wall cracking, out-of-plane wall collapse, and severe roof caving.

chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 20** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **13 de julio de 2026** **Hora: 9:00 pm** **Destacados** Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de 1.200 réplicas.** Balance oficial: **4.561 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.** **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.** **Se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$298 millones para ampliar la respuesta a los terremotos y atender las necesidades de1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.** El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas. **Situación general** Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.254 réplicas.** A 19 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **4.561 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, indicaron que **17.907 personas permanecen sin vivienda.** La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por 298 millones de dólares, destinada a atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses**.

Situación por estado Distrito Capital (Caracas) y Miranda  Equipos de primera línea que prestan atención en los campamentos transitorios participaron el 13 de julio en una formación sobre salud mental y apoyo psicosocial (SMAPS), coordinada por los grupos técnicos de SMAPS y las Áreas de Responsabilidad de Protección de la Niñez y Violencia Basada en Género (VBG), con el apoyo del Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud, Cecodap y Cedesex. chunks.text: Se prevé la articulación con Tinta Violeta para asistir al menos a 10 familias en situación de vulnerabilidad.  Delta Amacuro: Actores humanitarios distribuyeron 20 kits de alimentación y 20 kits de higiene para 20 familias, además de unos 30 kits para niñas y niños, con el apoyo de World Vision International, Médicos Sin Fronteras y la Federación Luterana Mundial. Se realizaron jornadas de evaluación coordinadas por la Autoridad Única de Salud, Kape-Kape y Tinta Violeta y se instaló una mesa de coordinación interinstitucional integrada por las autoridades regionales, el sector salud y OCHA.  Monagas: La Alcaldía de Maturín apoyó a familias procedentes de La Guaira acogidas por redes familiares, incluido un grupo de 12 personas desplazadas desde el sector Ciudad Caribe que prevé recibir a cuatro familiares adicionales. La asistencia comprendió la entrega de enseres, medicamentos y artículos para adecuar las viviendas de acogida, incluidos colchones, ventiladores y materiales de construcción.  Táchira: La OIM y ODISEF atendieron a 11 personas en movilidad en el terminal de San Cristóbal (5 mujeres, 3 hombres y 3 NNA), con sesiones psicoeducativas, orientaciones legales, atención de salud, primeros auxilios psicológicos y la entrega de kits de higiene. Se priorizó a una persona mayor y una mujer lactante. Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 4  Sucre: Se desplegó un equipo técnico de ingenieros para apoyar la evaluación, inspección y seguimiento de las infraestructuras afectadas en La Guaira y Caracas, contribuyendo a los procesos de análisis de daños y recuperación.  Zulia: Continúa la atención a la población desplazada en el terminal de pasajeros de Maracaibo y en los municipios receptores, operada por la Gerencia de Atención al Ciudadano y ASONACOP con la Cruz Roja, HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ y Cáritas, y en articulación con los Consejos de Protección y de Derechos de NNA.  En los estados Nueva Esparta, Trujillo y Lara se mantienen las acciones de coordinación, acopio y monitoreo previamente informadas, con seguimiento del Foro Local de Coordinación a la atención y los riesgos de protección.

Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 4  Sucre: Se desplegó un equipo técnico de ingenieros para apoyar la evaluación, inspección y seguimiento de las infraestructuras afectadas en La Guaira y Caracas, contribuyendo a los procesos de análisis de daños y recuperación.  Zulia: Continúa la atención a la población desplazada en el terminal de pasajeros de Maracaibo y en los municipios receptores, operada por la Gerencia de Atención al Ciudadano y ASONACOP con la Cruz Roja, HIAS, CESVI, ASOREZ y Cáritas, y en articulación con los Consejos de Protección y de Derechos de NNA.  En los estados Nueva Esparta, Trujillo y Lara se mantienen las acciones de coordinación, acopio y monitoreo previamente informadas, con seguimiento del Foro Local de Coordinación a la atención y los riesgos de protección. Coordinación humanitaria  OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales, continúa coordinando la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias, priorizando acciones en salud, alojamiento, alimentación, ASH, logística y protección.  UNDAC y OCHA continuaron apoyando a Protección Civil en el fortalecimiento de capacidades de coordinación y gestión de información para emergencias, incluyendo intercambio técnico sobre mecanismos de coordinación USAR y herramientas de seguimiento operativo.  OCHA continuó fortaleciendo la coordinación con el sector privado para apoyar las acciones de respuesta y recuperación temprana, promoviendo la articulación con actores especializados en áreas como logística, gestión de escombros, rehabilitación de infraestructura y planificación de la reconstrucción, a través de los mecanismos de coordinación existentes entre las Naciones Unidas y el sector privado.  Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del PNUD. Conforme a la metodología internacional de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.  Se informó la activación de un mecanismo especial para la tramitación expedita de una “Visa de Trabajo para Situaciones Especiales”, gestionada a través del Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores. El procedimiento podrá realizarse en línea, bajo la coordinación del Despacho del Viceministro para Temas Multilaterales y la Oficina de Relaciones Consulares, y estará dirigido a trabajadores extranjeros de organizaciones internacionales, así como a funcionarios de las Naciones Unidas, que se desplieguen en Venezuela en el marco de la respuesta a la emergencia ocasionada por los terremotos.

chunks.text: Conforme a la metodología internacional de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.  Se informó la activación de un mecanismo especial para la tramitación expedita de una “Visa de Trabajo para Situaciones Especiales”, gestionada a través del Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores. El procedimiento podrá realizarse en línea, bajo la coordinación del Despacho del Viceministro para Temas Multilaterales y la Oficina de Relaciones Consulares, y estará dirigido a trabajadores extranjeros de organizaciones internacionales, así como a funcionarios de las Naciones Unidas, que se desplieguen en Venezuela en el marco de la respuesta a la emergencia ocasionada por los terremotos. Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria Seguridad Alimentaria  Desde el inicio de la respuesta, el PMA y sus socios han alcanzado a más de 64.000 personas con asistencia alimentaria esencial en La Guaira. El 13 de julio, el PMA distribuyó 390 canastas alimentarias familiares en las comunidades de Urimare, en Playa Grande, beneficiando a 1.160 personas, además de otras 35 canastas destinadas a apoyar la preparación de alimentos en albergues temporales ubicados en Carayaca y Catia La Mar, alcanzando a 140 personas. Las canastas contienen alimentos básicos no perecederos, incluidos harina de maíz, arroz, pasta, lentejas, caraotas, aceite vegetal y sal, cubriendo aproximadamente el 75 por ciento de los requerimientos alimentarios de un hogar durante 30 días.  Paralelamente, continuó la distribución de comidas calientes en los campamentos temporales de La Guaira, donde se sirvieron 7.233 raciones, incluidas 1.364 en la comunidad de Playa Grande, 2.883 en el Estadio de Béisbol César Nieves y 2.986 en el Polideportivo José María Vargas, contribuyendo a garantizar el acceso continuo a alimentos para las familias desplazadas y afectadas.
