En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, se brindaron 132 consultas médicas y de SMAPS. Las actividades de protección incluyeron seis casos asistidos mediante triaje de protección, sensibilización sobre PEAS, apoyo psicosocial, análisis de riesgo de explotación y abuso sexual, y colocación de materiales informativos sobre PEAS en áreas clave del campamento. A la fecha, se han movilizado seis vuelos con carga humanitaria, incluidos cinco enviados por DHR del Gobierno de los Estados Unidos en coordinación con la OIM, y un vuelo con suministros de la OIM desde Panamá, con apoyo de DHL. **Respuesta planificada de la OIM** La OIM continuará enfocándose en la coordinación y gestión de sitios, registro, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, recopilación de datos, DTM y coordinación interagencial en campamentos transitorios priorizados y comunidades afectadas. El financiamiento adicional a través del Llamamiento de Fondos de USD 98 millones de la OIM permitiría ampliar la asistencia de alojamiento de emergencia, la entrega de artículos esenciales, el apoyo a la recuperación temprana, los servicios de protección, la atención de salud y salud mental, el monitoreo de movilidad y la gestión de información.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #9 (8 July 2026)
chunks.text: The ninth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as of 8 July. It also includes IOM’s Flash Appeal funding priorities to scale up urgent assistance. **Highlights** IOM launched a USD 98 million Appeal to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities between July and December 2026, prioritizing shelter, early recovery, health, WASH, protection, data, DTM and coordination. At César Nieves Stadium, registration resumed, with 20 new families registered, bringing the total to 482 families, or 1,479 people. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM’s Emergency Medical Team provided 132 health and mental health consultations.

chunks.text: At César Nieves Stadium, registration resumed, with 20 new families registered, bringing the total to 482 families, or 1,479 people. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM’s Emergency Medical Team provided 132 health and mental health consultations. To date, IOM has reached 4,011 unique individuals with 6,713 assistance and distribution services, mainly in health, shelter and protection. **IOM activities** IOM continues supporting prioritized transitory camps in La Guaira, including César Nieves Stadium, José María Vargas Sports Complex and Playa Grande, with site coordination, registration, WASH, protection, health and inter-agency coordination. At César Nieves Stadium, registration and food distribution coordination continued, while WASH improvements advanced through toilet signage by sex and shower installation. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, 132 medical and MHPSS consultations were provided.

chunks.text: At César Nieves Stadium, registration and food distribution coordination continued, while WASH improvements advanced through toilet signage by sex and shower installation. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, 132 medical and MHPSS consultations were provided. Protection activities included six cases assisted through protection triage, PSEA sensitization, psychosocial support, SEA risk analysis and placement of PSEA information materials in key camp areas. Six humanitarian cargo flights have been mobilized to date, including five sent by DHR of the Government of the United States in coordination with IOM, and one flight with IOM supplies from Panama, supported by DHL. **IOM planned response** IOM will continue focusing on site coordination and management, registration, WASH, health and Mental Health, protection, data collection, DTM and inter-agency coordination in prioritized transitory camps and affected communities. Additional funding through IOM’s USD 98 million Appeal would enable the scale-up of emergency shelter assistance, core relief items, early recovery support, protection services, health and mental health care, mobility monitoring and information management.

chunks.title: “They’re flinching at the slightest noise” - Children’s mental wellbeing at stake two weeks on from devastating earthquake
chunks.text: **Caracas, 9 July 2026 –** Children are showing signs of mental distress in the wake of last month’s devastating earthquakes in Venezuela, with parents and psychologists reporting children flinching at the slightest noise, finding it difficult to sleep, and showing more signs of irritability and aggression. Children who have undergone such stressful experiences will often show their stress through behaviour changes and need support to recover, said Save the Children. Save the Children has established safe spaces for children within the earthquake zone where families can bring their children to play and regain a sense of normalcy and strengthen their resilience, while also being assessed for more severe psychosocial distress or other protection concerns. Counsellors at these spaces have reported some children are showing signs of acute distress including anger, while children as young as seven or eight are saying they are scared of what the future holds.

chunks.title: “They’re flinching at the slightest noise” - Children’s mental wellbeing at stake two weeks on from devastating earthquake
chunks.text: Save the Children has established safe spaces for children within the earthquake zone where families can bring their children to play and regain a sense of normalcy and strengthen their resilience, while also being assessed for more severe psychosocial distress or other protection concerns. Counsellors at these spaces have reported some children are showing signs of acute distress including anger, while children as young as seven or eight are saying they are scared of what the future holds. Some parents have told our staff that their children now become anxious when they see the cracks in the ground, while others are struggling to sleep at night and are flinching when they hear loud sounds such as rumbles of thunder. Some older children told Save the Children staff that they had to protect and rescue younger family members while they escaped from the earthquake, despite feeling deeply scared themselves, and continue to carry this anxiety with them. Around 1.8 million people including about 680,000 children have been impacted by the earthquakes that struck Venezuela two weeks ago, many of whom witnessed their friends and family members die before their eyes, with mental and health and psychosocial support identified by the UN and NGOs as one of the key needs facing affected people. \[1\] Children who have experienced extremely distressing events are at risk of long-lasting impacts for months or even years to come unless they receive mental health and psychosocial support at the onset of the distressful event, said Save the Children. **Two-year-old Daisy\*** was with her parents when the earthquake struck their home in Caracas.

Save the Children is also running safe spaces where children can access mental health support and continue learning while schools remain closed, and where those with more significant needs can be referred for individual support. chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #2 (9th July 2026)
chunks.text: Two weeks after the 24 June seismic doublet (magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, 39 seconds apart), Venezuela's emergency has shifted from acute search and rescue into sustained, multi-sector humanitarian operations, even as rescuers occasionally still find survivors and already-weakened buildings continue to collapse. The official death toll stands at 3,535, with 16,740 people injured and nearly 18,000 displaced. Authorities now report more than 940 aftershocks. Buildings damaged are reported between 856 (government) and 2,501 (OCHA/ partner tracking), including 190 confirmed collapses.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #2 (9th July 2026)
chunks.text: Authorities now report more than 940 aftershocks. Buildings damaged are reported between 856 (government) and 2,501 (OCHA/ partner tracking), including 190 confirmed collapses. More than 55,000 people remain unaccounted for on the national missing-persons platform, of which 123 are children. Authorities report 80 operational transitional camps supporting the displaced population. Independent satellite-based analysis (ANOVA Policy Research, with Microsoft AI for Good) suggests population exposure in La Guaira's coastal corridor may be up to three times higher than official figures capture, due to outdated census frameworks and under-counted floating population.

Of an estimated 403,784 residents across seven La Guaira parishes, roughly 73,500 lived in structures with observable damage, and 37,600 in structures with severe damage or collapse — the group most likely to need transitional or permanent housing. The UNDRR assessment estimates approximately USD 37 billion in direct damage economy-wide, of which roughly USD 24 billion is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools, hospitals, and public facilities, alongside a separate preliminary UNDP estimate of USD 6.7 billion, equivalent to 6% of GDP.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes leave children at greater risk of violence
chunks.text: 9 July 2026 The earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June have left children increasingly vulnerable to trafficking, sexual exploitation, violence and other forms of abuse, as families struggle to recover from the devastation. ### Trafficking networks target children in emergencies Yesica Serrano, Regional Child Protection in Humanitarian Action Adviser at Plan International, speaking from Caracas stressed that criminal trafficking networks often seek to take advantage of the chaos that follows emergencies, targeting girls and boys who have been separated from their families, lost their care givers or have missing relatives or who are otherwise left vulnerable by the crisis. “During emergencies, the protective care environment for children weakens. Caregivers are under immense stress, looking for ways to cope with their situation, may lose a certain level of alertness and vigilance over the care of children. And it is in these lapses that trafficking networks and other perpetrators of abuse take advantage of these moments of vulnerability to target and recruit children,” said Serrano from Caracas.

chunks.text: Caregivers are under immense stress, looking for ways to cope with their situation, may lose a certain level of alertness and vigilance over the care of children. And it is in these lapses that trafficking networks and other perpetrators of abuse take advantage of these moments of vulnerability to target and recruit children,” said Serrano from Caracas. As an aggravating factor, recruitment of children through social media is common in Latin America, and during emergencies, when children are more connected online and caregivers are focused on rebuilding their lives and other basic needs, attention to the content children consume decreases, which increases the risk of exposure to harmful content. ### Children vulnerable to multiple forms of abuse Family separation is among the most significant child protection risks following a disaster. When caregivers have died, are hospitalised, or lose contact with children during evacuation children can be left without the care and protection they need. Children who are alone or whose family support networks have been disrupted face heightened risks of trafficking and sexual exploitation.

chunks.title: Venezuela Earthquakes leave children at greater risk of violence
chunks.text: When caregivers have died, are hospitalised, or lose contact with children during evacuation children can be left without the care and protection they need. Children who are alone or whose family support networks have been disrupted face heightened risks of trafficking and sexual exploitation. Adolescent girls and boys are more exposed to child labour, trafficking for the purposes of sexual exploitation, and recruitment by criminal groups, through coercion or false promises, presenting themselves as an alternative solution to meet their needs. “Emergencies do not affect all children equally. Girls and adolescent girls face increased risks of sexual exploitation, violence and child labour, particularly linked to domestic work, while adolescents in general are more exposed to the possible risk of recruitment by criminal groups.” Said Carmen Elena Alemán, Regional Director for Plan International in Latin America and the Caribbean. ### How Plan works to keep children safe Plan International works to prevent these risks alongside its partner organisations, providing group-based psychosocial support to caregivers to prevent violence and strengthen protective family environments, and working directly with children to reduce their risk factors for violence, abuse, exploitation, and neglect, and to support their psycho-emotional recovery.

chunks.text: “Emergencies do not affect all children equally. Girls and adolescent girls face increased risks of sexual exploitation, violence and child labour, particularly linked to domestic work, while adolescents in general are more exposed to the possible risk of recruitment by criminal groups.” Said Carmen Elena Alemán, Regional Director for Plan International in Latin America and the Caribbean. ### How Plan works to keep children safe Plan International works to prevent these risks alongside its partner organisations, providing group-based psychosocial support to caregivers to prevent violence and strengthen protective family environments, and working directly with children to reduce their risk factors for violence, abuse, exploitation, and neglect, and to support their psycho-emotional recovery. In addition, we are distributing hygiene kits and dignity kits as well as essential household items, providing safe spaces and psychosocial support in communities across 2 affected states, and conducting emergency education and primary health care activities, with a special focus on girls and adolescents. The organisation calls on various stakeholders to ensure that the humanitarian response in Venezuela incorporates child protection measures from the very beginning: family tracing and reunification processes in coordination with the relevant authorities; strengthened oversight in shelters and collective housing sites; and accessible reporting mechanisms adapted to children’s needs. chunks.title: Situational Report - Response to Venezuela Earthquakes (July 8th, 2026)
chunks.text: **Highlights** The humanitarian crisis continues to evolve following the twin earthquakes of 24 June. According to OCHA (7 July), 3,685 people have died, 16,740 have been injured, more than 1,000 aftershocks have been recorded and 6,462 people have been rescued, with La Guaira remaining the hardest-hit state. Authorities also report that 17,907 people have been left without housing, increasing humanitarian needs across affected communities. The response is progressively shifting from life-saving search and rescue to sustained humanitarian assistance, with temporary camps expanding and growing needs in health, shelter, safe water, sanitation, protection and education.

chunks.text: Project HOPE continues to expand its earthquake response across northern Venezuela as humanitarian operations transition from rescue efforts to sustained health and humanitarian assistance activities. Our team is scaling up mobile medical services, strengthening support for primary health facilities, expanding water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions, and increasing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) to meet growing needs. As the response evolves, protecting communities from secondary public health emergencies — including infectious disease outbreaks — is an increasingly important priority.

Venezuela Earthquakes — July 7, 2026 Page 2 of 3 Disease surveillance has become an increasing priority and Project HOPE teams are closely monitoring for potential future outbreaks of cholera, dengue, typhoid fever, hepatitis A, diarrheal diseases, Zika, Chikungunya, and malaria — which often emerge when disasters disrupt WASH systems. Project HOPE clinical teams are treating patients presenting with respiratory infections, diarrhea, skin conditions, hypertension, asthma, and earthquake-related injuries, and one presumptive malaria case has been referred for testing. Maternal health needs are an increasing concern as pregnant women face disruptions in care and access barriers.

Mental Health & Psychosocial Support With mental health needs continuing to soar, Project HOPE is expanding psychological first aid and MHPSS services so that survivors, displaced families, and frontline responders can adequately cope with trauma Project HOPE’s psychological first aid services in Venezuela are currently being offered both in-person during on-site activities and remotely via telephone. chunks.text: Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Support WASH interventions continue to scale, with Project HOPE distributing more than 1,000 hygiene kits, delivering safe drinking water to affected communities, providing water purification tablets, supporting health facilities with infection prevention and control supplies, and preparing for future water and sanitation repairs. Deliveries of cleaning and disinfection supplies were completed at four supported health centers in Distrito Capital. These deliveries will benefit an estimated 300-500 people at each center. Project HOPE has worked in Venezuela since 2019, strengthening access to health services, medicines, and health education, while supporting local health workers and community-based responses to humanitarian needs. Project HOPE has a team of over 100 in the country, and additional Project HOPE emergency response team members are mobilizing to support the most urgent health and humanitarian needs.

chunks.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
chunks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY On the 24th of June 2026, two earthquakes of 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes affected the centre-north of Venezuela, with particularly severe consequences in the states of La Guaira and Grand Caracas. After 12 days, the emergency continues to evolve in a context marked by internal displacement, temporary shelter arrangements for affected populations in formal or informal collective spaces, persistent disruptions in access to services, and growing demand for humanitarian assistance and protection mechanisms. The available information shows that protection needs continue to rise among the population affected by the earthquakes. In addition, the effects of the emergency are not strictly limited to the areas directly impacted, as population displacements have been observed toward host communities and other states in the country, including Bolívar, Delta Amacuro, Anzoátegui, Sucre, Zulia, Táchira, and Apure.

chunks.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
chunks.text: The available information shows that protection needs continue to rise among the population affected by the earthquakes. In addition, the effects of the emergency are not strictly limited to the areas directly impacted, as population displacements have been observed toward host communities and other states in the country, including Bolívar, Delta Amacuro, Anzoátegui, Sucre, Zulia, Táchira, and Apure. The loss of homes, displacement, stays in temporary government-managed shelters and informal accommodation sites, as well as the disruption or weakening of family, community, institutional, and protection networks, have increased exposure to protection risks and reduced the coping capacity of affected communities. Assessments conducted identify significant concerns related to mental health and psychosocial support needs, family separation, inadequate privacy and security in accommodation facilities, and the loss of personal documentation, which may affect access to assistance and essential services. These risks disproportionately affect children and adolescents, women, older persons, persons with disabilities, and other individuals with specific protection needs.

PROTECTION RISK ANALYSIS The emergency context continues to exacerbate protection risks for the affected population. In the hardest-hit areas, the destruction of homes, buildings, and essential infrastructure has thoroughly transformed the living conditions of communities, leading to displacement, the establishment of temporary shelters, and the disruption of support and protection networks. Exposure to physical risks also persists due to the presence of damaged structures and the continued presence of some people in affected areas, particularly those who are still participating in search efforts or waiting for missing family members to be found. The extent of the loss of lives has also increased the need for the identification of the deceased persons and the processing of the relevant legal documentation.

The extent of the loss of lives has also increased the need for the identification of the deceased persons and the processing of the relevant legal documentation. MAIN RISKS IDENTIFIED 1. FAMILY SEPARATION AND IMPACT ON CHILD PROTECTION MECHANISMS While assessments have not highlighted a large-scale presence of unaccompanied or separated children and adolescents, concerns persist regarding temporary separations from family members and difficulties in reestablishing contact among members of the nuclear family. Ongoing efforts to search for and identify missing persons, coupled with the sustained impact of human and material losses, continue to affect care dynamics as well as family and community protection mechanisms.

chunks.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
chunks.text: FAMILY SEPARATION AND IMPACT ON CHILD PROTECTION MECHANISMS While assessments have not highlighted a large-scale presence of unaccompanied or separated children and adolescents, concerns persist regarding temporary separations from family members and difficulties in reestablishing contact among members of the nuclear family. Ongoing efforts to search for and identify missing persons, coupled with the sustained impact of human and material losses, continue to affect care dynamics as well as family and community protection mechanisms. As a result, risks related to supervision, care, and access to protective environments for children and adolescents persist. Furthermore, the use of educational facilities as temporary shelters poses challenges for the gradual restoration of the usual protective environments for children and adolescents, as shelter, protection, and educational needs converge within a single space. 2. PSYCHOLOGICAL/EMOTIONAL ABUSE OR INFLICTED EMOTIONAL SUFFERING Assessments continue to reveal a significant emotional impact among the affected population.

chunks.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
chunks.text: Furthermore, the use of educational facilities as temporary shelters poses challenges for the gradual restoration of the usual protective environments for children and adolescents, as shelter, protection, and educational needs converge within a single space. 2. PSYCHOLOGICAL/EMOTIONAL ABUSE OR INFLICTED EMOTIONAL SUFFERING Assessments continue to reveal a significant emotional impact among the affected population. The main manifestations reported include anxiety, fear, sleep disturbances, and emotional exhaustion, together with persistent concerns about the safety and well-being of family members. Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) needs remain among the primary protection concerns identified throughout the response. This impact is also observed among caregivers, community leaders, frontline responders, and managers of temporary shelters, some of whom are themselves directly affected by the emergency and show signs of emotional overload.

chunks.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
chunks.text: Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) needs remain among the primary protection concerns identified throughout the response. This impact is also observed among caregivers, community leaders, frontline responders, and managers of temporary shelters, some of whom are themselves directly affected by the emergency and show signs of emotional overload. In addition, individuals requiring specialized mental health care have been identified, including cases that need psychiatric follow-up or continued access to medication, whose needs have not yet been fully met. Among children, observations made during field visits suggest that the experiences they lived through during the emergency continue to be reflected in their play and social interactions, highlighting the persistence of severe emotional distress. At the same time, in some shelter settings there appears to be a tendency to normalize manifestations of stress, anxiety, and emotional suffering, which could contribute to the under identification of mental health and psychosocial support needs. 3.

At the same time, in some shelter settings there appears to be a tendency to normalize manifestations of stress, anxiety, and emotional suffering, which could contribute to the under identification of mental health and psychosocial support needs. 3. GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE Displacement and the prolonged stay of affected people in temporary camps and other collective accommodation arrangements continue to create risk factors for gender-based violence (GBV), particularly for women, girls, and adolescents. Assessments have identified concerns related to a lack of privacy, insufficient lighting, exposure to strangers, and difficulties in ensuring safe spaces within some shelters. Furthermore, these spaces have demonstrated shortcomings from a gender and protection perspective, with limited privacy in water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, as well as weaknesses in access control and registration mechanisms.

Furthermore, these spaces have demonstrated shortcomings from a gender and protection perspective, with limited privacy in water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, as well as weaknesses in access control and registration mechanisms. Added to this, daily and sustained interactions between the affected population, response actors, support staff, security personnel, and military personnel can create risks of exploitation, abuse, harassment, or unequal power dynamics, especially for women, girls, and adolescents. Taken together, these factors require continuous monitoring and the strengthening of prevention, mitigation, and response measures against gender-based violence, exploitation, and abuse. 4. DISCRIMINATION AND STIGMATISATION, DENIAL OF ACCESS TO RESOURCES, OPPORTUNITIES, SERVICES, AND/OR HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE Risks of exclusion for part of the affected population persist in terms of access to assistance, essential services, and protection mechanisms.

chunks.title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
chunks.text: Taken together, these factors require continuous monitoring and the strengthening of prevention, mitigation, and response measures against gender-based violence, exploitation, and abuse. 4. DISCRIMINATION AND STIGMATISATION, DENIAL OF ACCESS TO RESOURCES, OPPORTUNITIES, SERVICES, AND/OR HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE Risks of exclusion for part of the affected population persist in terms of access to assistance, essential services, and protection mechanisms. While the response focuses primarily on formally designated temporary shelters, some individuals and families remain in informal settlements, open spaces, or damaged structures, in many cases to safeguard their belongings or stay close to their communities. The limited provision of assistance and services in these areas tends to increase risks of exclusion, particularly for older adults, people with disabilities, people with limited mobility, people with chronic illnesses, and people with mental health and psychosocial support needs, as well as for children and adolescents. This situation also raises protection concerns for women, girls, and adolescents, who may face increased exposure to risks of gender-based violence, including exploitation, abuse, and other forms of violence, in contexts characterised by precarious housing conditions, the absence of formal protection mechanisms, and the limited availability of specialised services.

chunks.text: The limited provision of assistance and services in these areas tends to increase risks of exclusion, particularly for older adults, people with disabilities, people with limited mobility, people with chronic illnesses, and people with mental health and psychosocial support needs, as well as for children and adolescents. This situation also raises protection concerns for women, girls, and adolescents, who may face increased exposure to risks of gender-based violence, including exploitation, abuse, and other forms of violence, in contexts characterised by precarious housing conditions, the absence of formal protection mechanisms, and the limited availability of specialised services. Finally, Indigenous groups have also been identified among the population living outside formal shelters, reinforcing the need to ensure inclusive, culturally appropriate, and equitable mechanisms for access to assistance and protection. SECTOR PRIORITIES As the emergency evolves, strengthening protection mechanisms in temporary shelters, informal settlements, and affected communities remains essential, especially for people who continue to face barriers to accessing formal response systems. Likewise, strengthening the capacities of shelter facility managers and their support teams is essential to address protection risks and foster safer and more inclusive environments.

In line with the internationally recognized PDNA methodology, the corresponding coordination efforts with relevant counterparts will be advanced.  During a meeting held on 4 July between government authorities and humanitarian organizations, authorities announced the activation of a special mechanism to expedite the processing of a “Work Visa for Special Situations” through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

chunks.text: It is intended for foreign personnel of international organizations, as well as United United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) OCHA | 5 Nations staff, deploying to Venezuela in support of the response to the earthquake emergency. Initial humanitarian response Food Security  WFP distributed 4,750 individual ready-to-eat rations in the parishes of Catia La Mar, Carlos Soublette, Naiguatá, and Urimare, providing immediate food assistance to earthquake-affected populations. It also supported 2,400 people with 600 family food baskets in communities across Caraballeda. These baskets contain dry commodities such as maize meal, pasta, pulses, vegetable oil, and salt, covering 75 percent of their food requirements for 30 days.  WFP provided 7,240 hot meals (lunch and dinner) for 3,620 people, in partnership with World Central Kitchen, across three temporary shelters: the José María Vargas sports stadium, the Cesar Nieves baseball stadium, and the Playa Grande community. 39,021 people have been reached with food assistance since the beginning of the response. Health  In Polideportivo Vargas Transitional Camp, IOM provided 127 health consultations through a mobile health outreach activity, including psychological support, general medicine, paediatrics and internal medicine services, and facilitated three referrals through established referral pathways.  UNICEF supported immunization activities in the Polideportivo Vargas and Estadio César Nieves transitional camps, where 45 and 23 vaccine doses were administered, respectively.  UNFPA provided sexual and reproductive health services in the Polideportivo Vargas and Estadio César Nieves transitional camps, including awareness-raising on contraceptive use, distribution of contraceptives, and HIV and syphilis testing.  In Playa Grande Transitional Camp, Project HOPE provided 27 medical consultations and seven psychosocial support consultations.

chunks.text: Focal point:  The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed to support the response through CERF.  The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and the Red Cross.  Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.  The Inter-American Development Bank Group (IDB Group) announced a donation package of at least US$1 million to support immediate humanitarian assistance, to be implemented in coordination with Cáritas Venezuela, as well as damage and loss assessments.  PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support health response and early recovery activities over the next six months and released US$1.5 million from the Contingency Fund for Emergencies. WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50 million to scale up food assistance and support emergency logistics and communications activities. UNHCR requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.  The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52 million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.  Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.  Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.  Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance, water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP, UNHCR and Save the Children.  Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and the Danish Red Cross.  The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom Government through UK Aid Match.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 15** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **8 de julio de 2026** **Hora: 9:00 pm** **Destacados** Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de 1.100 réplicas.** Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado. Balance oficial: **3.811 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.** **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.** **Tom Fletcher, jefe humanitario de las Naciones Unidas, hizo un llamado a los Estados Miembros y donantes para transformar la solidaridad en apoyo concreto.** **Se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$296 millones para ampliar la respuesta a los terremotos y atender las necesidades** **multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.** El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas. **Situación general** Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.102 réplicas.** A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.811 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, las autoridades reportan que unas **17.907 personas quedaron sin vivienda**.

Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria Seguridad Alimentaria  El PMA distribuyó 4.750 raciones individuales listas para el consumo en las parroquias de Catia La Mar, Carlos Soublette, Naiguatá y Urimare, proporcionando asistencia alimentaria inmediata a las poblaciones afectadas por los terremotos. Además, brindó apoyo a 2.400 personas mediante la entrega de 600 cestas alimentarias familiares en comunidades de Caraballeda. Estas cestas contienen alimentos secos como harina de maíz, pasta, leguminosas, aceite vegetal y sal, y cubren el 75 % de las necesidades alimentarias durante 30 días.  El PMA proporcionó 7.240 comidas calientes (almuerzo y cena) a 3.620 personas, en alianza con World Central Kitchen, en tres campamentos transitorios en La Guaira: el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Estadio César Nieves y la comunidad de Playa Grande. 39.021 personas han recibido asistencia alimentaria desde el inicio de la respuesta a la emergencia.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #8 (7 July 2026)
chunks.text: The eighth Situation Report provides an update on the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and summarizes IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts as of 7 July. The second page of the report also includes key funding priorities to sustain and scale up urgent assistance. **Highlights** Official figures report 3,685 fatalities, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 people rescued and 17,907 people without housing following the 24 June earthquakes. A total of 856 buildings have also been reported as affected, including 190 total collapses. A total of 87 transitory camps have been reported, with installed capacity for 20,227 people and 14,634 people currently accommodated.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #8 (7 de julio de 2026)
chunks.text: El octavo Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume la respuesta en curso y planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales al 7 de julio. La segunda página del reporte también incluye prioridades clave de financiamiento para sostener y ampliar la asistencia urgente. **Aspectos destacados** Las cifras oficiales reportan 3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740 heridas, 6.462 rescatadas y 17.907 personas sin vivienda tras los terremotos del 24 de junio. También se reportan 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 colapsos totales. Se reportan 87 campamentos transitorios, con una capacidad instalada para 20.227 personas y 14.634 personas actualmente alojadas.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #8 (7 de julio de 2026)
chunks.text: También se reportan 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 colapsos totales. Se reportan 87 campamentos transitorios, con una capacidad instalada para 20.227 personas y 14.634 personas actualmente alojadas. La OIM continúa apoyando alojamiento, coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios, registro, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, participación comunitaria, gestión de información y coordinación interagencial. A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado 3.638 personas únicas con 6.253 asistencias y distribuciones, principalmente en salud, CCCM/alojamiento y protección. Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar condiciones en campamentos transitorios, ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, fortalecer el registro y las derivaciones, y abordar riesgos de protección y salud pública. **Actividades de la OIM** La OIM continúa apoyando la coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios clave en La Guaira, incluidos el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande.

Asimismo, fortaleció acciones de protección, participación comunitaria, derivaciones seguras, atención inicial de casos y coordinación interagencial, incluyendo la colocación de materiales informativos en áreas clave de los campamentos. **Respuesta planificada de la OIM** La OIM continuará priorizando alojamiento temporal, coordinación y gestión de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, datos y evaluaciones de necesidades. Las acciones previstas incluyen mejorar condiciones de alojamiento mediante carpas, literas, espacios cubiertos seguros y planificación de sitios; ampliar el acceso a agua segura, saneamiento e higiene; fortalecer servicios médicos y psicosociales; y continuar las derivaciones de protección, rendición de cuentas y mitigación de riesgos de violencia contra la mujer. El financiamiento adicional permitiría a la OIM ampliar el alojamiento de emergencia, los artículos esenciales, WASH, protección, salud y servicios de salud mental, al tiempo que se fortalecen el registro, la gestión de información, el monitoreo de movilidad y la coordinación en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas.

chunks.title: Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: Transitional Camps (06 July 2026)
chunks.text: Following the earthquakes that occurred on 24 June 2026, La Guaira State reported some of the most severe impacts and one of the highest levels of population displacement. In support of the response led by national, state and municipal authorities, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is coordinating the management of three transitory camps — Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Estadio Playa Grande — where, together with other humanitarian actors, it provides assistance services. This coordination facilitates the provision of basic services, identification, case assistance and referrals for people with specific needs. This document presents information on the occupancy and general characteristics of these three temporary accommodation sites.

chunks.title: República Bolivariana de Venezuela: Campamentos Transitorios (06 de julio de 2026)
chunks.text: Tras los terremotos ocurridos el 24 de junio de 2026, el estado La Guaira registró algunas de las afectaciones más severas y uno de los mayores desplazamientos de población reportados. En apoyo a la respuesta liderada por las autoridades nacionales, estadales y municipales, la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM) coordina la gestión de tres Campamentos Transitorios —Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Estadio Playa Grande— donde, junto con otros actores humanitarios, brinda servicios de asistencia. Esta articulación facilita la provisión de servicios básicos, la identificación, así como la atención de casos y derivación de personas con necesidades específicas. Este documento presenta información sobre la ocupación y las características generales de estos tres sitios de alojamiento temporal.

La Cancillería habilitó un formulario web “ donde además de recibir donaciones monetarias, permite solicitar el permiso de llegada de donaciones que lleguen a Venezuela vía aérea y marítima. Sin embargo, esta web está orientada a donaciones y las organizaciones que requieren autorización y una comunicación del Coordinador Residente a Cancillería, deben realizar su solicitud a través de los formularios del GTL. El GTL, en coordinación con OCHA, ha extendido el reporte de movilización aérea de carga humanitaria a todas las organizaciones (nacionales, internacionales y del Sistema de Naciones Unidas), con el fin de consolidar diariamente esta información, permitiendo que OCHA envíe una Nota Verbal a Cancillería. chunks.title: IOM Venezuela Flash Appeal: 2026 Earthquake Response (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: **SITUATION OVERVIEW** On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 struck the north-central region of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (henceforth referred to as Venezuela), triggering widespread devastation across several states, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, and Falcón. The earthquakes, followed by hundreds of aftershocks, caused significant loss of life, with 3,535 people reported dead and over 16,740 injured, as of 6 July. Damage to more than 2,500 infrastructure assets, including 38 hospitals, has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, water supply, and transport systems, placing considerable strain on national response capacities. The disaster is unfolding in a context of pre-existing structural vulnerabilities, limited access to basic services, weakened public systems, and protracted humanitarian needs.

chunks.title: IOM Venezuela Flash Appeal: 2026 Earthquake Response (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: Damage to more than 2,500 infrastructure assets, including 38 hospitals, has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, water supply, and transport systems, placing considerable strain on national response capacities. The disaster is unfolding in a context of pre-existing structural vulnerabilities, limited access to basic services, weakened public systems, and protracted humanitarian needs. As a result, the earthquakes have triggered an acute-on-chronic emergency, deepening existing vulnerabilities and increasing humanitarian needs across affected areas. Thousands of families have been displaced and are sheltering in collective centres (e.g. schools, sports centres), spontaneous settlements, self-managed sites, and open spaces due to the destruction or structural damage of homes and continued fear of further collapses. While initial response efforts by national authorities and international actors have focused on search and rescue, emergency medical assistance, and rapid assessments, significant gaps remain across key sectors.

chunks.title: IOM Venezuela Flash Appeal: 2026 Earthquake Response (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: Thousands of families have been displaced and are sheltering in collective centres (e.g. schools, sports centres), spontaneous settlements, self-managed sites, and open spaces due to the destruction or structural damage of homes and continued fear of further collapses. While initial response efforts by national authorities and international actors have focused on search and rescue, emergency medical assistance, and rapid assessments, significant gaps remain across key sectors. These include safe and adequate shelter, core relief items, access to healthcare and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, protection, site-level coordination and management, and reliable data for operational targeting. Needs are particularly acute in overcrowded and informal displacement settings, where limited infrastructure, weak service provision, and the absence of structured site management increase risks of communicable disease outbreaks, violence against women and girls (VAWG) and other vulnerable groups, family separation, and other protection concerns. To date, a significant share of the humanitarian response has been concentrated in La Guaira, Distrito Capital, and Miranda, where large-scale interventions have been prioritized.

chunks.title: IOM Venezuela Flash Appeal: 2026 Earthquake Response (July - December 2026)
chunks.text: Needs are particularly acute in overcrowded and informal displacement settings, where limited infrastructure, weak service provision, and the absence of structured site management increase risks of communicable disease outbreaks, violence against women and girls (VAWG) and other vulnerable groups, family separation, and other protection concerns. To date, a significant share of the humanitarian response has been concentrated in La Guaira, Distrito Capital, and Miranda, where large-scale interventions have been prioritized. However, Falcón, Aragua, and Carabobo have also reported significant impacts. In these areas, infrastructure damage, service disruption, and comparatively lower operational coverage point to unmet needs and emerging gaps in assistance, particularly among populations in dispersed and hard-to-reach locations. Ensuring that these areas are reached will be critical for a coherent, equitable, and needs-based response, while also laying out the foundation for early recovery and longer-term resilience-building efforts.

chunks.title: Atrocity Alert No. 490: Sudan, Lebanon and Venezuela
sources: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
chunks.text: ## Atrocity Alert is a weekly publication by the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect highlighting situations where populations are at risk of, or are enduring, mass atrocity crimes. ### **GROWING RISK OF ATROCITIES AMID ESCALATING CONFLICT IN EL OBEID, SUDAN** Intensifying clashes in and around El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, are raising serious concerns over the heightened risk of atrocity crimes against civilians. Over the past few weeks, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have reportedly built-up their presence by encircling the city and begun a siege from at least three directions, with a potential offensive appearing imminent. Repeated drone strikes have already led to widespread civilian casualties. Estimates indicate that approximately 500,000 civilians in El Obeid are at risk of large-scale atrocities, including more than 100,000 internally displaced persons.

chunks.text: Repeated drone strikes have already led to widespread civilian casualties. Estimates indicate that approximately 500,000 civilians in El Obeid are at risk of large-scale atrocities, including more than 100,000 internally displaced persons. On 29 June the Yale School of Public Health’s Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL) [reported]( satellite evidence covering the period 25 May to 25 June, indicating widespread and escalating damage to protected civilian infrastructure, including electricity generation facilities, fuel storage sites, multiple gas stations and the main market. Yale HRL concludes that the damage “is consistent with intentional bombardment of civilian infrastructure necessary for the sustainment of life.” Control over El Obeid and the wider region has remained highly contested, with frontlines [shifting repeatedly]( between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The emerging pattern of encirclement, siege warfare and sustained strikes on civilian infrastructure mirrors RSF tactics previously [documented]( in El Fasher, North Darfur, where similar methods were used to isolate the city, degrade essential services and intensify pressure on civilian populations through sustained bombardment and encirclement.

chunks.title: Au Venezuela, une urgence humanitaire majeure à la suite de séismes dévastateurs
chunks.text: ## Deux séismes majeurs ont frappé le nord du Venezuela, faisant des milliers de morts et de disparus. La destruction de nombreuses infrastructures aggrave considérablement un système de santé déjà fragile. Pour répondre à cette crise, Médecins du Monde France vient en appui aux équipes de Médecins du Monde Espagne, déjà déployées sur le terrain. Le 24 juin 2026, les séismes de magnitudes 7,2 et 7,5 ont particulièrement touché la capitale Caracas et l’État de La Guaira.

Nous sommes prêts à mobiliser rapidement depuis la [Colombie]( où nous sommes opérationnels, une équipe de médecins, d’infirmiers, de psychologues et de logisticiens, ainsi que des kits médicaux pouvant **permettre la prise en charge d’environ 1 500 personnes.** Cette intervention contribuera à : Assurer des **soins de santé primaires** en première ligne et **distribuer les médicaments** nécessaires, **Stabiliser les urgences** en orientant les patientes et patients vers des **structures adaptées,** Fournir un **accompagnement en santé mentale**.

chunks.title: CADENA mobilises emergency response for earthquake-affected communities in Venezuela
chunks.text: [*CADENA International*]( a HelpAge network member with offices across Latin America, has launched an emergency response in Venezuela following the 24 June earthquakes. Its efforts focus on search and rescue, healthcare, relief distributions, psychosocial support and rapid needs assessments.* *The organisation has deployed international search and rescue specialists, and is delivering emergency supplies including household water filters and solar lamps, working closely with local authorities and humanitarian partners on the ground.* ## **Reaching older people and other at-risk groups** Among the estimated 1.8 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, around 250,000 older people are expected to require targeted support. Older people represent approximately 14% of the population and are among those facing the greatest risks following the disaster, particularly those living with disabilities, chronic health conditions, mobility limitations, social isolation, or the loss of caregivers. ## **Responding to urgent needs on the ground** Initial assessments conducted by CADENA found overcrowded shelters, families sleeping outdoors due to fear of aftershocks, limited access to safe drinking water, shortages of basic medical supplies, and growing protection concerns. Teams also reported that many older people had lost essential assistive devices and were struggling to access services and humanitarian assistance.

Teams also reported that many older people had lost essential assistive devices and were struggling to access services and humanitarian assistance. To address these needs, CADENA is providing emergency relief items, supporting access to safe water, and helping affected households meet their most urgent basic needs. The organisation is prioritising households with older people, particularly those facing additional risks linked to disability, chronic illness, damaged housing, or lack of family support. ## **Providing healthcare and psychosocial support** Volunteer medical brigades are providing primary healthcare services in affected communities, while additional medical teams and supplies are being mobilised to strengthen the response. Particular attention is being given to ensuring continuity of care for older people and others who rely on regular medication and treatment for chronic conditions.

Particular attention is being given to ensuring continuity of care for older people and others who rely on regular medication and treatment for chronic conditions. At the same time, CADENA is delivering mental health and psychosocial support through specialist staff and trained volunteers. Community-based activities and psychological first aid are helping survivors cope with trauma, grief, stress and uncertainty following the earthquakes. Older people, who may be experiencing heightened isolation and distress, are a key focus of these efforts.

A CADENA team member conducts a psychosocial assessment with an earthquake survivor. ## **Scaling up for recovery** CADENA is preparing to expand its emergency response in the coming weeks. Planned activities include the distribution of water, hygiene and shelter kits, food assistance, protection activities, disaster risk awareness initiatives, healthcare support, and continued mental health and psychosocial services. The aim is to ensure that older people and other at-risk groups are not left behind as affected communities move from emergency response towards recovery.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #2: Families need safe water and sanitation to reduce health risks | NRC
chunks.text: *Media update by Beatriz Ochoa, the Norwegian Refugee Council’s (NRC) Regional Head of Advocacy for Latin America two weeks after earthquakes in Venezuela:* 08. Jul 2026 “Two weeks after the earthquakes struck Venezuela, many families who lost their homes have told me they are concerned about how they will meet their most basic needs. Thousands of people continue to live in temporary shelters, schools, parks and other public spaces. Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services is now becoming increasingly important to prevent health problems and the spread of disease.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #2: Families need safe water and sanitation to reduce health risks | NRC
chunks.text: Thousands of people continue to live in temporary shelters, schools, parks and other public spaces. Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services is now becoming increasingly important to prevent health problems and the spread of disease. “Many families are living in densely populated settings, with limited privacy, exposure to high temperatures and seasonal rains, and sometimes insufficient access to showers, soap and adequate sanitation facilities. “I have seen families doing everything they can to maintain dignity in extremely difficult conditions. In one temporary shelter, I saw families organising themselves to keep common spaces clean, including through makeshift toilets and basic waste management arrangements.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #2: Families need safe water and sanitation to reduce health risks | NRC
chunks.text: “I have seen families doing everything they can to maintain dignity in extremely difficult conditions. In one temporary shelter, I saw families organising themselves to keep common spaces clean, including through makeshift toilets and basic waste management arrangements. Their determination is remarkable, but families should not have to shoulder this burden alone. “We urgently need support from international donors so we and other humanitarian organisations can provide access to safe water, toilets, hygiene supplies, and clear public health information to help reduce the risk of diarrhoeal diseases, skin infections and other preventable health problems among displaced families. “Water is being delivered by tanker trucks to many temporary shelters, but families often lack appropriate containers to store it safely.

chunks.title: Venezuela on-the-record update #2: Families need safe water and sanitation to reduce health risks | NRC
chunks.text: “We urgently need support from international donors so we and other humanitarian organisations can provide access to safe water, toilets, hygiene supplies, and clear public health information to help reduce the risk of diarrhoeal diseases, skin infections and other preventable health problems among displaced families. “Water is being delivered by tanker trucks to many temporary shelters, but families often lack appropriate containers to store it safely. Access to bottled water, showers and toilets remains limited in some locations. These challenges can be particularly difficult for older people, people with disabilities, pregnant women and families with young children. "As displacement becomes more protracted, and the days turn into weeks, I have seen families beginning to organise daily life in temporary shelters, including preparing and cooking meals together.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: *This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.* **Summary Points** On 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator arrived in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination, support rapid connectivity assessments, and help identify priority communications needs for the humanitarian response. Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid connectivity assessment survey across affected areas to map available communications services, identify coverage gaps, and prioritize shared connectivity solutions for humanitarian partners.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.* **Summary Points** On 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator arrived in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination, support rapid connectivity assessments, and help identify priority communications needs for the humanitarian response. Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid connectivity assessment survey across affected areas to map available communications services, identify coverage gaps, and prioritize shared connectivity solutions for humanitarian partners. Organizations operating in affected areas are encouraged to complete the survey to help identify priority connectivity needs and gaps. On 06 July, LTC Telecoms assessed three displacement shelters in La Guaira and identified unreliable power supply and internet connectivity gaps as the main operational constraints. Connectivity support, including Starlink terminals and solar power systems, is being deployed to strengthen communications for responders.

Situation Overview Venezuela continues to face a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June, just 40 seconds apart. The worst-affected areas include La Guaira State, Greater Caracas, and parts of Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, and Falcón States. Hundreds of aftershocks have continued to affect impacted communities, hampering rescue efforts and increasing risks to damaged infrastructure. Response activities remain focused on life-saving assistance, including shelter, health, protection, infrastructure restoration, and support to thousands of affected households. 1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: Hundreds of aftershocks have continued to affect impacted communities, hampering rescue efforts and increasing risks to damaged infrastructure. Response activities remain focused on life-saving assistance, including shelter, health, protection, infrastructure restoration, and support to thousands of affected households. 1 The ETC and Logistics Cluster have been merged into the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), following the humanitarian reset in 2025. Bringing logistics and emergency telecommunications under one coordination structure, the WFP-led LTC is the backbone of the entire humanitarian response, enabling humanitarian action to move, communicate, coordinate, and deliver lifesaving assistance. Page 1 of 6 Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area | The Government of Venezuela has declared the most affected areas, particularly La Guaira, disaster zones and continues to lead response efforts through the deployment of emergency services, military assets, and international assistance. As of 05 July, authorities reported that more than 6,400 people had been rescued since the onset of the emergency.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: Page 1 of 6 Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area | The Government of Venezuela has declared the most affected areas, particularly La Guaira, disaster zones and continues to lead response efforts through the deployment of emergency services, military assets, and international assistance. As of 05 July, authorities reported that more than 6,400 people had been rescued since the onset of the emergency. Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams remain active in affected areas, while authorities continue to expand temporary accommodation for displaced populations, conduct debris removal operations, and carry out structural safety assessments. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) is coordinating international emergency assistance and supporting humanitarian response efforts. Priority needs include emergency shelter, medical care, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, child protection, and the restoration of telecommunications and other critical infrastructure.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) is coordinating international emergency assistance and supporting humanitarian response efforts. Priority needs include emergency shelter, medical care, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, child protection, and the restoration of telecommunications and other critical infrastructure. As of 06 July, response operations are gradually shifting from search-and-rescue activities toward recovery and humanitarian assistance. However, significant challenges persist, including displacement, infrastructure damage, recurring aftershocks, and growing humanitarian needs. Relief and recovery efforts are expected to continue for several months.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: However, significant challenges persist, including displacement, infrastructure damage, recurring aftershocks, and growing humanitarian needs. Relief and recovery efforts are expected to continue for several months. Telecommunications Overview The 24 June earthquakes caused significant damage to telecommunications infrastructure across La Guaira, Greater Caracas, and parts of Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, and Falcón States. Although Venezuela’s core national telecommunications networks remain operational, damage to power systems, fibre-optic infrastructure, mobile base stations, and transmission facilities has disrupted connectivity in several affected areas. Ongoing aftershocks, infrastructure damage, and access constraints continue to affect service reliability and restoration efforts.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: Although Venezuela’s core national telecommunications networks remain operational, damage to power systems, fibre-optic infrastructure, mobile base stations, and transmission facilities has disrupted connectivity in several affected areas. Ongoing aftershocks, infrastructure damage, and access constraints continue to affect service reliability and restoration efforts. Telecommunications disruptions have been driven by both direct infrastructure damage and prolonged power outages, affecting emergency communications, humanitarian coordination, public information dissemination, and contact between separated family members. La Guaira, the hardest-hit area, experienced the most severe connectivity disruptions. Mobile network operators Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, and Digitel remain operational across most of the country; however, coverage degradation, service interruptions, and network capacity constraints have been reported in earthquake-affected areas.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: La Guaira, the hardest-hit area, experienced the most severe connectivity disruptions. Mobile network operators Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, and Digitel remain operational across most of the country; however, coverage degradation, service interruptions, and network capacity constraints have been reported in earthquake-affected areas. Damage to cellular towers, backhaul links, and power systems has reduced network performance, particularly in densely populated urban and coastal communities. Emergency responders continue to rely on temporary communications solutions while network restoration activities are underway. Localized damage to fibre-optic and fixed telecommunications infrastructure, including transmission routes and utility corridors, has further affected connectivity.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: Emergency responders continue to rely on temporary communications solutions while network restoration activities are underway. Localized damage to fibre-optic and fixed telecommunications infrastructure, including transmission routes and utility corridors, has further affected connectivity. Fixed broadband services remain particularly impacted in areas where power and transmission networks were damaged. As of 06 July, operators continue restoration efforts in the most severely affected locations. While most national networks remain operational outside the disaster zone, service availability and quality in heavily affected areas remain dependent on infrastructure repairs, power restoration, and improved site access.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)

While most national networks remain operational outside the disaster zone, service availability and quality in heavily affected areas remain dependent on infrastructure repairs, power restoration, and improved site access. Telecommunications recovery is expected to continue for several weeks and will remain critical to humanitarian operations, public safety, and broader recovery efforts. chunks.text: Page 2 of 6 Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area | LTC Telecoms Activities Coordination LTC Telecoms began monitoring telecommunications networks immediately following the earthquakes through established partner coordination channels to identify connectivity gaps and assess potential support requirements. Global LTC Telecoms provided inputs to the WFP Venezuela Concept of Operations (CONOPS) and continues to support response efforts. On 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator arrived in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination and support rapid telecommunications assessments in priority response areas. The coordinator is leading efforts to identify telecommunications service availability, connectivity gaps, and operational requirements to inform targeted connectivity support for humanitarian response operations. Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid telecommunications and connectivity survey across affected areas.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: The coordinator is leading efforts to identify telecommunications service availability, connectivity gaps, and operational requirements to inform targeted connectivity support for humanitarian response operations. Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid telecommunications and connectivity survey across affected areas. The assessment is mapping operational locations and available connectivity services, including Starlink, Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT), Broadband Global Area Network (BGAN), mobile networks, and fixed fibre broadband services. Findings will support a spatial analysis of connectivity coverage, helping to identify service gaps and prioritise locations for shared connectivity solutions that enable life-saving humanitarian operations. To support government-led and inter-agency efforts to restore critical communications, LTC Telecoms is establishing a telecommunications coordination mechanism in Caracas in collaboration with OCHA, the National Telecommunications Commission (CONATEL), CANTV, Movistar, Digitel, and international partners.

chunks.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
chunks.text: Findings will support a spatial analysis of connectivity coverage, helping to identify service gaps and prioritise locations for shared connectivity solutions that enable life-saving humanitarian operations. To support government-led and inter-agency efforts to restore critical communications, LTC Telecoms is establishing a telecommunications coordination mechanism in Caracas in collaboration with OCHA, the National Telecommunications Commission (CONATEL), CANTV, Movistar, Digitel, and international partners. Coordination efforts will focus on mapping incoming telecommunications assets, identifying connectivity gaps, avoiding duplication, and prioritising support to the most affected areas. Planned support will focus on high-impact locations including Petare, Catia, La Guaira, and other communities where widespread power outages, network disruptions, and damage to critical infrastructure are limiting access to essential services. Proposed interventions include the provision of community connectivity services, public Wi-Fi, satellite communications, and solar-powered charging facilities at shelters, distribution sites, hospitals, urban search-and-rescue bases, and operational airports.

National connectivity dropped sharply from more than 90 percent to approximately 59–65 percent immediately following the Page 4 of 6 Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) – Telecoms Area | earthquakes before partially recovering to around 77 percent within the following 24–48 hours. As of 03 July, La Guaira remained the most affected area, with connectivity operating at reduced capacity. chunks.text: **Reporte de situación N.º 14** **Terremotos en Venezuela** **7 de julio de 2026** **Hora: 9:00 pm** **Destacados** Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de mil réplicas**. Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado. Balance oficial: **3.685 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.** **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.** **Tom Fletcher, jefe humanitario de las Naciones Unidas, inició una visita oficial a Venezuela para apoyar los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso.** El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas. **Situación general** Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.076 réplicas.** A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia.

chunks.text: Carabobo y Yaracuy (zona del epicentro)  En Carabobo, las principales afectaciones continúan concentrándose en el municipio Juan José Mora (parroquia Morón). En Yaracuy, particularmente en el municipio Veroes y otras localidades cercanas a la zona epicentral, se reportan viviendas destruidas o en condición de alto riesgo. Evaluaciones recientes identifican necesidades prioritarias en protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (ASH) y seguridad alimentaria. Acciones de respuesta: Cinco (5) organizaciones (Cruz Roja Venezolana, CESAP, Tierra Viva, Cáritas Morón y Empodérame) brindan respuesta en salud, alimentación, agua y distribución de ayuda humanitaria. Falcón (Tucacas – Municipio Silva)  En el marco del proyecto Salud+, la Organización Panamericana de la Salud (OPS/OMS) programó una misión al municipio José Laurencio Silva (Tucacas y Boca de Aroa) para valorar daños estructurales y operativos de la red hospitalaria y ambulatoria, evidenciar y priorizar las necesidades de salud inmediatas de la población afectada, y fortalecer la articulación con la Cruz Roja Venezolana, OCHA, las alcaldías de Silva y Miranda y Protección Civil, para la optimización de la respuesta.  OCHA y Protección Civil Falcón continúan coordinando acciones para fortalecer los procesos de levantamiento de información sobre daños y necesidades en las comunidades afectadas.

Además, las autoridades informaron del acondicionamiento de un espacio en las instalaciones del VEN 911, en San Félix, para la atención de familias afectadas en caso de necesitarse.  En el estado Delta Amacuro, se registró la llegada de aproximadamente 50 personas, para quienes se mantienen en marcha acciones de preparación y articulación con la comunidad humanitaria, particularmente en los sectores de asistencia alimentaria y distribución de kits familiares. Asimismo, se realizó una revisión preliminar de las necesidades prioritarias de la población afectada, identificándose requerimientos adicionales para complementar los kits de asistencia, incluyendo artículos de higiene personal, sábanas y agua potable. Se avanzó en la coordinación con las autoridades de Salud para fortalecer la atención psicosocial de las personas afectadas por los terremotos, tanto a nivel domiciliario como mediante actividades grupales en establecimientos de salud.  En el estado Monagas, las autoridades reportaron la llegada de 347 personas (106 familias) afectadas por los terremotos provenientes principalmente de La Guaira, las cuales han sido recibidas por redes familiares y comunitarias. chunks.text: Organizaciones locales como ASOMAYOR ampliaron el acceso a servicios de salud y apoyo diagnóstico para las familias desplazadas. Adicionalmente, la empresa CONFERRY, en coordinación con autoridades locales, implementó un puente humanitario para el traslado de personal médico, rescatistas, equipos de respuesta y grupos familiares desde y hacia las zonas afectadas,  En el estado Zulia, continúa la llegada y el tránsito de familias desplazadas desde La Guaira, Caracas y Petare. Según el seguimiento de ASONACOP y ODISEF en el terminal de Maracaibo (al 6 de julio), se identificó y asistió a varias familias con destinos dentro del estado (Machiques, Villa del Rosario y San Francisco) y en tránsito hacia Colombia (Maicao y Santa Marta), con predominio de mujeres, niñas, niños y adolescentes y personas mayores. Una de las familias estaba integrada por 13 personas, en su mayoría niñas, niños y adolescentes. La atención incluyó orientación jurídica y apoyo psicosocial, referencia médica al ambulatorio del terminal (por cuadros de mareo, náuseas, dolor abdominal en niñas, dolor articular y cefalea), entrega de alimentos servidos, agua e hidratación, medicamentos, ropa, actualización de documentos y articulación del transporte hacia los destinos.
