Se reportan casos de pérdida total de vivienda y de pérdidas humanas en el núcleo familiar. Coordinación humanitaria  El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, llegó a Venezuela el 7 de julio para una visita de cuatro días, durante la cual se reunirá con personas afectadas por los terremotos, personal humanitario, autoridades y otros actores clave, con el fin de conocer de primera mano el impacto de la emergencia, los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso y los avances hacia la siguiente fase de la respuesta. A su llegada, realizó un recorrido por zonas afectadas en La Guaira y posteriormente sostuvo un encuentro con la presidenta encargada, Delcy Rodríguez, el canciller Yván Gil, y el presidente de la Asamblea Nacional Jorge Rodríguez.

chunks.text: Coordinación humanitaria  El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, llegó a Venezuela el 7 de julio para una visita de cuatro días, durante la cual se reunirá con personas afectadas por los terremotos, personal humanitario, autoridades y otros actores clave, con el fin de conocer de primera mano el impacto de la emergencia, los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso y los avances hacia la siguiente fase de la respuesta. A su llegada, realizó un recorrido por zonas afectadas en La Guaira y posteriormente sostuvo un encuentro con la presidenta encargada, Delcy Rodríguez, el canciller Yván Gil, y el presidente de la Asamblea Nacional Jorge Rodríguez. En la reunión también participaron el Coordinador Humanitario, Gianluca Rampolla del Tindaro, y la Jefa de Oficina de OCHA Venezuela, Vanessa May.  OCHA, junto con el Coordinador Humanitario y en articulación con las autoridades nacionales, coordina la respuesta humanitaria con las Naciones Unidas y organizaciones socias, priorizando acciones en salud; alojamiento; alimentación; agua, saneamiento e higiene; logística; y protección.  La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano (USAR) fue transferida a Protección Civil de Venezuela, que asumirá la coordinación de los equipos nacionales e internacionales desplegados en las zonas afectadas. El proceso incluyó el traspaso de información operativa y la capacitación sobre las metodologías de coordinación USAR utilizadas durante la respuesta. Paralelamente, los equipos internacionales han iniciado progresivamente su desmovilización; no obstante, varios equipos, particularmente de América Latina, permanecen desplegados en las zonas afectadas.  El Grupo de Coordinación Interclúster (ICCG) participó en el Taller de Análisis Conjunto Interagencial convocado por OCHA para consolidar la evidencia generada por las evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades y construir una comprensión común de las necesidades humanitarias derivadas de los terremotos, orientando la priorización y planificación de la respuesta.  Autoridades venezolanas solicitaron la activación de la Evaluación de las Necesidades Posteriores al Desastre (PDNA), en el marco del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y con el acompañamiento del PNUD.

Conforme a la metodología internacionalmente de la PDNA, se avanzará en las coordinaciones correspondientes con las contrapartes relevantes.  Las autoridades nacionales han agilizado los procedimientos migratorios y administrativos para facilitar el ingreso al país de equipos internacionales de búsqueda y rescate, personal de Naciones Unidas, representantes de medios de comunicación y otros especialistas desplegados para apoyar las operaciones de respuesta a la emergencia. Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 5 Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria Seguridad Alimentaria  Desde el inicio de la respuesta, el PMA ha brindado asistencia alimentaria a 30.983 personas. Solo el 7 de julio, el PMA distribuyó 5.500 kits de alimentos listos para el consumo en Catia La Mar y Naiguatá, proporcionando asistencia alimentaria inmediata a las poblaciones afectadas por los terremotos.  Paralelamente, el PMA entregó 100 cestas alimentarias familiares para apoyar la preparación de comidas en cocinas comunitarias que operan en alojamientos temporales, incluidas 40 cestas en el campamento temporal Chato Candela, en el Distrito Capital (parroquia Caruao), y 70 cestas en el alojamiento temporal Luis Hurtado Higuera, en El Junquito.

chunks.text: Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 5 Acciones iniciales de Respuesta Humanitaria Seguridad Alimentaria  Desde el inicio de la respuesta, el PMA ha brindado asistencia alimentaria a 30.983 personas. Solo el 7 de julio, el PMA distribuyó 5.500 kits de alimentos listos para el consumo en Catia La Mar y Naiguatá, proporcionando asistencia alimentaria inmediata a las poblaciones afectadas por los terremotos.  Paralelamente, el PMA entregó 100 cestas alimentarias familiares para apoyar la preparación de comidas en cocinas comunitarias que operan en alojamientos temporales, incluidas 40 cestas en el campamento temporal Chato Candela, en el Distrito Capital (parroquia Caruao), y 70 cestas en el alojamiento temporal Luis Hurtado Higuera, en El Junquito. Agua, saneamiento e higiene  En Playa Grande, la OIM coordinó con CISP (socio implementador de UNICEF) autoridades y actores presentes la definición y distribución de espacios para duchas diferenciadas para mujeres y hombres.  UNICEF apoyó el acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. En Polideportivo Vargas, 1.700 personas mantuvieron acceso a kits de higiene, 60 baños operativos, 16 puntos de lavado de manos y un suministro diario de 20.000 litros de agua, complementado con la movilización de 15 estaciones de duchas y la disponibilidad de 100 contenedores de residuos movilizados por el Ministerio de Obras Públicas. En Estadio César Nieves, 1.253 personas contaron con acceso a kits de higiene, 30 baños operativos, ocho puntos de lavado de manos y 20.000 litros diarios de agua, con el apoyo del Ministerio de Energía y otras organizaciones; además, se instaló una planta potabilizadora para establecer un punto permanente de agua segura.

Las acciones incluyeron reuniones interagenciales de coordinación, seguimiento al funcionamiento de los servicios, actualización de censos y registros de población, planificación de reubicaciones internas, fortalecimiento de mecanismos de control de acceso y apoyo a la organización comunitaria y las normas de convivencia.  En el Estadio César Nieves, se confirmó la entrega de artículos no alimentarios (baldes, lonas y sets de cocina) a 500 familias, mientras que en Playa Grande se completó la instalación de una carpa de gran capacidad y se inició la reubicación ordenada de familias hacia espacios más adecuados de alojamiento.

En el campamento transitorio “Polideportivo Vargas”, se trabaja con la Defensoría del Pueblo, el Servicio de Atención a Niñas, Niños y Adolescentes (NNA), el Consejo Municipal de Derechos de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes (CMDNNA), Consejo de Protección de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes de Caracas (CPNNA). Se realizó la remisión de 7 casos al sistema de protección del NNA.  ACNUR brindó servicios de protección a 97 personas en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Estadio Playa Grande, mediante orientación legal, primeros auxilios psicológicos, promoción de derechos, gestión documental y mesas de información. Asimismo, al menos 32 personas fueron remitidas de forma segura a servicios especializados y 21 niños, niñas y adolescentes en situación de riesgo o indocumentación recibieron asesoría jurídica, de los cuales 18 casos fueron referidos a los sistemas de protección infantil y servicios de salud.  ACNUR fortaleció las condiciones de protección y seguridad en los campamentos mediante la instalación de 29 reflectores y lámparas solares en áreas comunes del Polideportivo Vargas y el Estadio Playa Grande.  ACNUR impulsó acciones de coordinación y fortalecimiento institucional en los tres campamentos, incluyendo reuniones técnicas con la Defensoría del Pueblo, el Sistema de Protección Integral de Niños, Niñas y Adolescentes (SPINNA), agencias de las Naciones Unidas y actores humanitarios, para abordar temas relacionados con PEAS, identificación de necesidades de protección, normas de convivencia y mecanismos de atención a la población afectada.  UNFPA desarrolló actividades de prevención y respuesta a la violencia basada en género (VBG) en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas y Estadio César Nieves, alcanzando a 84 personas mediante sensibilizaciones sobre mensajes clave de VBG y difusión de servicios especializados. Además, siete equipos adicionales se encuentran en proceso de despliegue y se espera que inicien operaciones próximamente, mientras un equipo concluyó su misión y se encuentra en fase de desmovilización.  Entre el Ministerio de Salud, la Célula de Información y Coordinación Médica (CICOM) y los EMT desplegados, se acordó integrar a la Red EMT en las acciones de vigilancia epidemiológica, con el Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA) OCHA | 7 fin de fortalecer la detección temprana y el monitoreo de riesgos para la salud en las zonas afectadas.  Se mantiene la entrega de bolsas para el manejo digno y seguro de personas fallecidas al Servicio Nacional de Medicina y Ciencias Forenses (SENAMECF). Hasta la fecha, se han distribuido 3.000 con el fin de reforzar la capacidad institucional para la gestión de fallecidos en el contexto de la emergencia.  El Clúster de Salud y la co-coordinación sectorial fortalecen la gestión de información, los mecanismos de recolección y análisis de datos, y las prioridades informativas que contribuyan a la toma de decisiones y a una mejor coordinación de la respuesta.  El Grupo Técnico de Trabajo de Salud Mental y Apoyo Psicosocial (GTT SMAPS) continúa fortaleciendo la articulación y coordinación de las intervenciones de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial en el marco de la respuesta a la emergencia.  UNFPA brindó servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva en los campamentos transitorios Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves y Estadio Playa Grande, incluyendo actividades de promoción de servicios, sensibilizaciones sobre el uso de condones y sesiones educomunicativas. sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 14** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **07 July 2026** **Time: 9:00 pm** **Highlights** Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,000 aftershocks.** At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state. Official toll: **3,685 people dead and 16,740 injured.** A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.** **Tom Fletcher, the United Nations humanitarian chief, began an official visit to Venezuela to support ongoing response efforts.** The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1.076 aftershocks.** More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **3,685 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued** since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately **17,907 people lost their homes.** The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and the assistance to affected populations.

chunks.text: In this context, United Nations UnderSecretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher began a visit to Venezuela to gain first-hand insight into the impact of the emergency and the ongoing response efforts. Impact on infrastructure  Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.  An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion. chunks.text: Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)  In Playa Grande, IOM coordinated with CISP (UNICEF’s implementing partner), authorities and other actors present to define and allocate separate shower facilities for women and men.  UNICEF supported access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in the Polideportivo Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande temporary camps. At Polideportivo Vargas, 1,700 people maintained access to hygiene kits, 60 operational toilets, 16 handwashing stations and a daily supply of 20,000 litres of water, complemented by the mobilization of 15 shower stations and the availability of 100 waste containers provided by the Ministry of Public Infrastructure. At Estadio César Nieves, 1,253 people had access to hygiene kits, 30 operational toilets, eight handwashing stations and 20,000 litres of water per day, with support from the Ministry of Energy and other organizations. In addition, a water treatment plant was installed to establish a permanent source of safe water. At Playa Grande, the camp maintained 18 operational portable toilets and received United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) OCHA | 7 10,000 litres of water through water trucks, in addition to hygiene kits distributed by Action Against Hunger.

Following the emergency, reported funding for the plan reached US$300 million.  As part of the support provided by UNDAC, the team includes a private sector coordination specialist to strengthen business engagement in response and recovery efforts. Focal point:  The Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$15 million to support a multisectoral response, alongside the activation of the Venezuela Humanitarian Fund (VHF). Norway contributed to support the response through CERF.  The United States announced a US$100 million contribution to the VHF, in addition to a further US$100 million in bilateral funding for response operations implemented by IOM, WFP, UNICEF, International Medical Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, Proyecto Esperanza and the Red Cross.  Germany and the Republic of Korea contributed US$5 million and US$1.25 million, respectively, to the VHF to support humanitarian action in the country. Other Member States and donors have expressed their intention to support the response through the Fund.  The Inter-American Development Bank Group (IDB Group) announced a donation package of at least US$1 million to support immediate humanitarian assistance, to be implemented in coordination with Cáritas Venezuela, as well as damage and loss assessments.  PAHO/WHO launched an emergency appeal for nearly US$24 million to support health response and early recovery activities over the next six months and released US$1.5 million from the Contingency Fund for Emergencies.

WFP launched an initial appeal for US$50 million to scale up food assistance and support emergency logistics and communications activities. UNHCR requires US$14.8 million to support up to 30,000 affected people over the next six months.  The European Union allocated €5 million to support the emergency response, in addition to the €52 million already allocated this year for humanitarian operations in the country.  Australia announced a US$2 million contribution to support the provision of food, shelter, healthcare and access to safe water through IFRC and WFP.  Switzerland announced a contribution of CHF 2.5 million to support the response.  Sweden allocated SEK 25 million to support the humanitarian response through food assistance, water, temporary shelter, protection and family reunification programmes implemented by WFP, UNHCR and Save the Children.  Denmark announced an additional contribution of DKK 11 million to support the humanitarian response, including DKK 10 million through UNHCR and DKK 1 million through DanChurchAid and the Danish Red Cross.  The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) announced an initial allocation of £7.5 million for the earthquake response in Venezuela, including £2 million contributed by the United Kingdom Government through UK Aid Match. The funds will be implemented by DEC member agencies and their local partners to support the humanitarian response.  OCHA continues to coordinate with donors and partners to ensure rapid, strategic and needs-based allocation of resources.

chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: Venezuela is facing a severe humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck the country's central-northern region on 24 June. At least 3,342 people have been killed and 16,470 injured. With tens of thousands of people still unaccounted for, the death toll is expected to increase as search and rescue efforts continue. An estimated 36,700 pregnant women have been affected by the earthquakes, including approximately 4,000 who are expected to give birth in the next month.

chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: With tens of thousands of people still unaccounted for, the death toll is expected to increase as search and rescue efforts continue. An estimated 36,700 pregnant women have been affected by the earthquakes, including approximately 4,000 who are expected to give birth in the next month. The health system is under severe strain, with 38 health facilities damaged, significantly limiting access to essential maternal health services for women and newborns. Maintaining emergency obstetric and newborn care is therefore an urgent humanitarian priority. The disruption of essential services, overcrowded shelters, family separation, and rising psychosocial distress are exacerbating protection risks, particularly for women, adolescent girls, persons with disabilities, and older persons.

The disruption of essential services, overcrowded shelters, family separation, and rising psychosocial distress are exacerbating protection risks, particularly for women, adolescent girls, persons with disabilities, and older persons. In addition, more than 10,000 people are currently residing in temporary shelters, where privacy, lighting and protection measures remain insufficient. Strengthening gender-based violence prevention and ensuring safe access to survivor-centred services is critical. UNFPA is scaling up its responses to ensure continued access to maternal health services, emergency obstetric care, family planning, clinical management of rape, and gender-based violence prevention and response services.

chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: Earthquakes in Venezuela Flash Update 26 June - 6 July 2026 Highlights Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 that struck the central-northern region of the country on 24 June. Nearly 1,000 aftershocks have been recorded, while search and rescue operations and humanitarian assistance continue across affected areas. Official reports indicate that at least 3,342 people have died and more than 16,470 have been injured.1 The states most affected remain La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and other neighbouring areas. More than 2,500 infrastructures have sustained damage, including 38 health facilities, while thousands of people remain displaced or accommodated in temporary shelters.

The disruption of essential services, overcrowding in shelters, family separation and increased psychosocial distress are heightening protection risks, particularly for women, adolescent girls, persons with disabilities and older persons. UNFPA Flash Update I Venezuela I 26 June - 6 July 2026 Situation Overview Twelve days after the earthquakes, Venezuela remains in an active emergency response phase. Authorities report more than 1,000 aftershocks, although their frequency and intensity have gradually decreased. Search and rescue operations continue alongside damage assessments and the restoration of essential services. chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: Search and rescue operations continue alongside damage assessments and the restoration of essential services. Official figures indicate 3,342 fatalities and 16,470 injuries, although figures are expected to continue to rise with tens of thousands of people still missing. More than 26,000 people are directly affected and over 17,345 have lost their homes. Currently, 10,702 people are currently residing across 79 temporary camps, which have been established across the most affected areas. The health system remains under considerable pressure.

chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: Currently, 10,702 people are currently residing across 79 temporary camps, which have been established across the most affected areas. The health system remains under considerable pressure. Thirty-eight health facilities have sustained damage, including major hospitals in Caracas, limiting access to essential care for women and newborns. Disruptions to electricity, transport and communications continue to affect humanitarian operations and service delivery. Protection concerns are increasing as displacement, overcrowding in shelters, family separation, and economic hardship weaken traditional support networks.

Women and girls face heightened risks of GBV, particularly in collective shelters where privacy, lighting and protection measures remain insufficient. Psychosocial distress and mental health needs are widespread among affected populations and first responders alike. UNFPA Flash Update I Venezuela I 26 June - 6 July 2026 UNFPA Response Sexual and reproductive health: UNFPA continues to support national authorities, humanitarian partners and local organizations to ensure access to life-saving SRH and protection services for women, girls and adolescents affected by the earthquakes. Response efforts have expanded from the initial deployment of emergency supplies to the delivery of integrated services in temporary shelters, and strengthened support to health facilities in the affected areas. In La Guaira, UNFPA and its implementing partner are delivering the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for Sexual and Reproductive Health in Emergencies at the José María Vargas temporary shelter. Women and adolescent girls are receiving modern contraceptives, menstrual hygiene kits, condoms, counselling, and information on sexually transmitted infection prevention, pregnancy danger signs, sexual violence and available referral services.

chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: In La Guaira, UNFPA and its implementing partner are delivering the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for Sexual and Reproductive Health in Emergencies at the José María Vargas temporary shelter. Women and adolescent girls are receiving modern contraceptives, menstrual hygiene kits, condoms, counselling, and information on sexually transmitted infection prevention, pregnancy danger signs, sexual violence and available referral services. Pregnant women and survivors of sexual violence are being identified and safely referred through established pathways in coordination with the public health system. UNFPA has also begun distributing emergency reproductive health supplies to support the continuity of essential services in affected areas. This includes post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) kits for the clinical management of rape, reproductive health commodities and emergency obstetric supplies provided to referral hospitals and humanitarian health partners.

chunks.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
chunks.text: UNFPA has also begun distributing emergency reproductive health supplies to support the continuity of essential services in affected areas. This includes post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) kits for the clinical management of rape, reproductive health commodities and emergency obstetric supplies provided to referral hospitals and humanitarian health partners. Gender-based violence: As lead agency for Gender-Based Violence coordination, UNFPA is coordinating inter-agency prevention and response interventions, including dignity kit distributions, psychosocial support, case management and legal assistance for survivors. Initial safety assessments in collective shelters have identified inadequate lighting in some areas as an important protection concern for women and girls, informing ongoing GBV risk mitigation measures and the prioritization of additional dignity kits3 and safety interventions. Coordination Mechanisms UNFPA continues to actively participate in national and inter-agency coordination mechanisms led by the Government of Venezuela and OCHA, contributing to needs assessments, humanitarian analysis, information management and collective response planning.

chunks.text: Initial safety assessments in collective shelters have identified inadequate lighting in some areas as an important protection concern for women and girls, informing ongoing GBV risk mitigation measures and the prioritization of additional dignity kits3 and safety interventions. Coordination Mechanisms UNFPA continues to actively participate in national and inter-agency coordination mechanisms led by the Government of Venezuela and OCHA, contributing to needs assessments, humanitarian analysis, information management and collective response planning. UNFPA is working closely with health, protection, shelter and mental health actors to ensure that SRH and GBV remain recognized as life-saving components of the emergency response. Particular attention is being given to integrating GBV risk mitigation measures within collective shelters and temporary camps. Partnerships with women's organizations, youth networks and community-based actors remain central to delivering an inclusive, locally-led and accountable humanitarian response. 3 Dignity kits contain essential items to maintain hygiene and health as well as increase safety.

chunks.text: Particular attention is being given to integrating GBV risk mitigation measures within collective shelters and temporary camps. Partnerships with women's organizations, youth networks and community-based actors remain central to delivering an inclusive, locally-led and accountable humanitarian response. 3 Dignity kits contain essential items to maintain hygiene and health as well as increase safety. They include a torch, sanitary pads, soap, shampoo, underwear, toothbrushes and toothpaste, toilet paper, comb, and a leaflet with key messages on GBV and available support services. UNFPA Flash Update I Venezuela I 26 June - 6 July 2026 Funding Status UNFPA estimates that approximately US$10 million will be required during the first three months of the response to sustain life-saving SRH and GBV interventions, including the implementation of the MISP, support to pregnant women, essential supplies, specialized services, coordination, rapid assessments, and partnerships with local organizations. Additional resources remain urgently needed to expand access to maternal health services, strengthen GBV prevention and response programmes, and protect the rights and dignity of women and girls affected by the earthquakes.

"Across the affected communities, we are witnessing extraordinary resilience. Health personnel, midwives, social workers and community volunteers continue to provide life-saving services under extremely difficult conditions, often while dealing with the impact of the earthquakes on their own families. Their dedication is inspiring.

chunks.text: Health personnel, midwives, social workers and community volunteers continue to provide life-saving services under extremely difficult conditions, often while dealing with the impact of the earthquakes on their own families. Their dedication is inspiring. At the same time, the needs of women, girls and adolescents are growing every day, and sustained support is essential to ensure that no one is left without access to protection, sexual and reproductive healthcare, and hope for recovery." — Eugenia Sekler, Head of Office, UNFPA Venezuela For more information Eugenia Sekler Norha Restrepo (Media Enquiries) Head of Office Regional Communications Adviser

chunks.text: Informe Diario de Situación Respuesta al Terremoto del 24 de junio de 2026 Fecha del informe: 07 de julio de 2026 Hora de corte: 19:00 horas Cifras Clave O re r p g o a r n t i e z s a ciones con S IT e S n sibilización en SSR e C re o a n li s z u a l d ta a s s médicas M dis é t t r o ib d u o í s d o an s ticonceptivos Consultas médicas Pruebas rápidas de VIH y EESS evaluados 2 Organizaciones / Instituciones fortalecidas Consultas de salud Resumen Las acciones reportadas durante la jornada se concentraron en la provisión de servicios de salud sexual y reproductiva, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, atención primaria en salud, distribución de insumos esenciales, evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades y fortalecimiento de la coordinación técnica de la respuesta. En los espacios de alojamiento temporal de La Guaira se desarrollaron actividades de sensibilización comunitaria sobre salud sexual y reproductiva, prevención de infecciones de transmisión sexual y uso de métodos anticonceptivos, alcanzando a 126 personas, además de la distribución de 16 métodos anticonceptivos modernos y la realización de pruebas rápidas de VIH y sífilis. Las intervenciones en salud mental y apoyo psicosocial incluyeron atención a población afectada en campamentos y comunidades, así como apoyo al personal de respuesta. Adicionalmente, se realizaron 15 consultas de salud mental en Playa Verde y Los Corales y se efectuaron evaluaciones en establecimientos de salud para identificar necesidades operativas y oportunidades de apoyo.

chunks.title: Clúster Salud Venezuela: Informe Diario de Situación - Respuesta al Terremoto del 24 de junio de 2026 (07 de julio de 2026)
chunks.text: Las intervenciones en salud mental y apoyo psicosocial incluyeron atención a población afectada en campamentos y comunidades, así como apoyo al personal de respuesta. Adicionalmente, se realizaron 15 consultas de salud mental en Playa Verde y Los Corales y se efectuaron evaluaciones en establecimientos de salud para identificar necesidades operativas y oportunidades de apoyo. Las actividades de coordinación y evaluación permitieron completar el levantamiento de información en 22 centros de atención para personas mayores ubicados en el Área Metropolitana de Caracas y La Guaira, así como la distribución de insumos médicos y suministros para fortalecer la atención en establecimientos y puntos de respuesta. Asimismo, una jornada de atención primaria en salud realizada en la Urbanización José Antonio Páez, Catia La Mar, brindó 67 atenciones médicas, identificando como principal preocupación el acceso limitado a agua potable segura, con requerimientos asociados a abastecimiento, almacenamiento y tratamiento de agua para reducir riesgos sanitarios en la comunidad. chunks.title: Venezuela, Americas | Earthquake: Emergency Appeal - Operational Strategy (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: ## DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 302 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states.

chunks.title: Venezuela, Americas | Earthquake: Emergency Appeal - Operational Strategy (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. They were also felt in parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and Brazil, reaching as far as Martinique and the Brazilian Amazon, more than 1,700 km from the epicentres. The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency and designated La Guaira a disaster zone, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations is concentrated. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. According to the initial statistical model developed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), there was a 50 per cent probability that the number of casualties (deaths and injuries) would range between 1,000 and 10,000, and a 30 per cent probability that it would exceed 10,000. International response teams from at least 17 countries have deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the 2 OCHA Situation Report No. 9 Earthquakes in Venezuela coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG). According to OCHA, as of 2 July2, 2,595 people had been confirmed dead and 12,400 injured.

According to OCHA, as of 2 July2, 2,595 people had been confirmed dead and 12,400 injured. A further 12,841 people had been displaced after their homes were severely damaged. In total, 2,501 structures were affected, including 38 hospitals, 189 buildings that collapsed completely, and 855 buildings that either partially collapsed or sustained significant damage. La Guaira remains the worst-affected state.

chunks.text: Key response activities include search and rescue, health care and first aid, damage and needs assessments, restoring family links (RFL), water, hygiene, and sanitation (WASH), logistics, branch mobilisation, and information management. In the area of health care and first aid, the Venezuelan Red Cross has delivered over 1,900 medical consultations via field hospital and mobile units, while strengthening referral systems, epidemiological surveillance and vaccination coordination. In WASH, these interventions have been scaled up through the operation of the WATSAN system providing safe water to operational sites and affected communities, alongside installation of sanitation facilities (showers, latrines and handwashing units) in field hospitals and shelters. In parallel, the National Society continues managing over 2,500 RFL cases and additional tracing requests through fixed and mobile connectivity points, while expanding PGI and psychosocial support services for affected people in camps and host communities. Additionally, the Venezuelan Red Cross is maintaining a monitoring system of 109 shelters across five states, deploying digital data collection tools, and supporting operational planning.

Logistics operations have included reception and distribution of relief items, stock management and transport coordination, while field teams continue to provide hydration, hygiene supplies and operational support to response personnel and affected communities. 1.2 Capacity and response at the national level The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency and designated La Guaira as a Disaster Zone. Response operations are being coordinated by the Emergency Joint Staff and include search and rescue activities led by Civil Protection teams and the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB), working alongside international teams deployed in the affected areas. In addition, the public and private health systems has been activated to provided mass casualty care and humanitarian assistance through the distribution of essential supplies, food, and water; the deployment of field hospitals to reinforce the existing hospital network; the establishment of temporary shelters in La Guaira and Caracas; and the activation of platforms for reporting missing persons and housing damage.

By 28 June, the Advance Team composed by three health care specialists of the Spanish Red Cross completed the assessment, confirming the deployment of a full team of 17 healthcare specialists, including experts in emergency and pre-hospital care, trauma care, epidemiology, hygiene promotion, midwifery, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), among other health-related specialties. The ERU Clinic will be based in La Guaira and is expected to become fully operational by 7 July. Following the initial needs assessment, an additional request was made for a Logistics ERU, which will be deployed by the Swiss Red Cross and include general logistics and warehouse management specialists.

The magnitude of the event, the continuation of aftershocks, and the extent of infrastructure damage have exceeded local capacities in the most affected areas, especially in La Guaira and the Caracas metropolitan area. The national and international response continues to expand, but significant gaps remain in access to affected communities, consolidation of information, sectorisation of assistance, and coverage of basic needs in open spaces, makeshift shelters, and population concentration points. In health, the public and private network remains under pressure due to trauma care, patient referrals from La Guaira to Caracas, and the continuity of essential services for people with chronic illnesses, pregnant women, girls, boys, older persons, and persons with disabilities.

OPERATIONAL CONSTRAINTS There are significant gaps in humanitarian access to critical locations with urgent humanitarian needs, due to main connecting roads being affected by the earthquake, gas leak exposure at certain key points with explosion risk, the risk of dust inhalation from collapsed infrastructure, which could endanger the health of humanitarian personnel, and reports of unrest and security risks due to the absence of basic essential resources, including food and medicine. Response agencies are working to establish a clear, unified coordination command post to enable effective information management for decision-making, as well as the consolidation of unified damage and needs assessments to understand the true magnitude of the disaster.

Response agencies are working to establish a clear, unified coordination command post to enable effective information management for decision-making, as well as the consolidation of unified damage and needs assessments to understand the true magnitude of the disaster. To date, these challenges have hindered information management and the consolidation of data needed to strengthen decision-making. Additionally, the health system has reached its maximum care capacity, with shortages of sufficient personnel to support the humanitarian response required for the emergency. Finally, at the Operations Camp in La Guaira, challenges remain in establishing sanitation and hygiene infrastructure, as well as a stable connectivity network, which is preventing information from arriving in a timely manner.

chunks.text: OPERATIONAL STRATEGY Vision This operation aims to support the VRC in addressing the immediate, short- and medium-term needs of Venezuelans affected by the earthquake. The initiative targets 300,000 people in Greater Caracas and La Guaira through a coordinated response. The operation seeks to reduce pressure on vulnerable communities and overwhelmed services in the most affected areas including Carabobo, Aragua, Miranda, and Falcón, as communications and assessments improve, with special emphasis on supporting people with multiple and complex vulnerabilities to (re)establish sustainable livelihoods and access health, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, community-based health and first aid (CBHFA), and shelter. By June 2028, the emergency operation will complement the VRC’s ongoing and future interventions, with support from the IFRC and coordination with Movement partners and other stakeholders. Special attention will be paid to ensuring complementarity with the responses provided by the authorities and other actors, leveraging the VRC’s privileged position and access to avoid duplication of services delivered by humanitarian agencies and to maximise results.

Transition toward long-term planning During the emergency phase, interventions include temporary shelter, essential primary health care – including mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) referral pathways and services – as well as food and household item distribution and cash assistance. Anticipated climate risks and operational adjustments As mentioned in the Risks and Vulnerabilities sections, El Niño conditions may intensify rainfall variability and climate extremes in Venezuela. This is a part of the Atlantic hurricane season, during which storms and heavy rainfall may occur, increasing the risk of flash floods, landslides, drainage failures, and disease outbreaks. This compounds risks in areas where infrastructure, roads, water systems, and health services have already been damaged by the earthquake.

chunks.text: This is a part of the Atlantic hurricane season, during which storms and heavy rainfall may occur, increasing the risk of flash floods, landslides, drainage failures, and disease outbreaks. This compounds risks in areas where infrastructure, roads, water systems, and health services have already been damaged by the earthquake. It could further affect earthquake-impacted communities, disrupt humanitarian operations, and hinder recovery efforts; therefore, it represents a potential overlap of the earthquake response with additional climate-related emergencies during the lifetime of the operation. If rainfall forecasts materialise, affected communities could face simultaneous or sequential shocks: damaged or unsafe housing exposed to heavy rains; temporary shelters under pressure from flooding, heat, or poor drainage; disrupted WASH systems unable to meet increased demand; health facilities managing trauma care while also responding to waterborne or vector-borne diseases; and access routes becoming intermittently blocked by landslides, flooding, or infrastructure deterioration. Due to the above, the operation will integrate preparedness, contingency planning, and risk reduction measures to strengthen resilience against future shocks.

PLANNED OPERATIONS The operation will focus on providing comprehensive humanitarian assistance and recovery support to people affected by the earthquake, addressing immediate needs, and supporting the early recovery of impacted communities. Actions will prioritise health care, including psycho-social support, first aid, pre-hospital care, and support to health services; access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene; provision of basic conditions in shelters and temporary spaces; and support for the progressive recovery of housing and livelihoods, with a focus on dignity, protection, and equitable access. From the earliest phases, the operation will incorporate a recovery perspective to support affected people in the transition from emergency assistance toward safer, more dignified, and sustainable solutions. As the context stabilises, and as damage, needs, market, and basic service assessments progress, the operation will expand housing recovery activities, rehabilitation of essential community services, restoration of livelihoods, strengthening of community capacities, and risk reduction in the face of aftershocks and other secondary hazards.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #7 (6 de julio de 2026)
chunks.text: El séptimo Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume la respuesta en curso y planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales al 6 de julio. La segunda página del reporte también incluye prioridades clave de financiamiento para sostener y ampliar la asistencia urgente. **Aspectos destacados** Las cifras oficiales reportan 3.535 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas, 6.462 personas rescatadas y 17.854 personas sin vivienda tras los terremotos del 24 de junio. También se reportan 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 colapsos totales. Se reportan 82 campamentos transitorios.

chunks.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #7 (6 de julio de 2026)
chunks.text: También se reportan 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 colapsos totales. Se reportan 82 campamentos transitorios. Las últimas cifras disponibles indican una capacidad instalada para 14.599 personas, con 10.702 personas actualmente alojadas. La OIM continúa apoyando alojamiento temporal, coordinación y gestión de sitios, registro, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, participación comunitaria, gestión de información y coordinación interagencial. Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar las condiciones en los campamentos transitorios, ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, fortalecer el registro y las derivaciones, y abordar riesgos de protección y salud pública. **Actividades de la OIM** La OIM continúa apoyando la coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios clave en La Guaira, incluidos el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande.

Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar las condiciones en los campamentos transitorios, ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, fortalecer el registro y las derivaciones, y abordar riesgos de protección y salud pública. **Actividades de la OIM** La OIM continúa apoyando la coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios clave en La Guaira, incluidos el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. El apoyo se centró en mejoras del sitio, coordinación de servicios, registro, conectividad, participación comunitaria, derivaciones de protección y distribuciones de artículos esenciales, incluida la asistencia a 360 familias en el Estadio César Nieves y comunidades aledañas. El 6 de julio, los equipos de salud y SMAPS apoyados por la OIM brindaron 353 atenciones médicas y psicosociales en los tres sitios. La OIM también continuó apoyando el mapeo de campamentos transitorios y el registro para orientar la planificación operativa, al tiempo que fortaleció las actividades de protección, orientación legal, derivaciones y sensibilización sobre riesgos de protección en emergencias. **Respuesta planificada de la OIM** La OIM continuará priorizando alojamiento temporal, coordinación y gestión de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, datos y evaluaciones de necesidades.

chunks.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #7 (6 July 2026)
chunks.text: The seventh Situation Report provides an update on the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and summarizes IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts as of 6 July. The second page of this also includes key funding priorities to sustain and scale up urgent assistance. Highlights Official figures report 3,535 fatalities, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 people rescued and 17,854 people without housing following the 24 June earthquakes. A total of 856 buildings have been reported as affected, including 190 total collapses.

A total of 856 buildings have been reported as affected, including 190 total collapses. A total of 82 transitory camps have been reported. The latest available figures indicate installed capacity for 14,599 people, with 10,702 people currently accommodated. IOM continues supporting temporary accommodation, site coordination and management, registration, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, community engagement, information management and inter-agency coordination.

chunks.text: IOM activities IOM continued supporting coordination and management of key transitory camps in La Guaira, including Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande. Support focused on site improvements, service coordination, registration, connectivity, community engagement, protection referrals and essential item distributions, including assistance to 360 families at Estadio César Nieves and surrounding communities. chunks.text: Esta infografía presenta información clave sobre la presencia operacional y las actividades de respuesta humanitaria ante el terremoto en Venezuela durante el año 2026. El reporte consolida de forma visual los datos de los socios líderes e implementadores que reportan sus actividades a través de la plataforma 3W, facilitando la coordinación y visibilidad del impacto en el terreno. Al 7 de julio de 2026, el panorama general de la respuesta destaca las siguientes cifras: **Sectores activos:** 11 sectores humanitarios en funcionamiento. **Organizaciones:** 59 organizaciones reportando actividades. **Actividades:** 1,044 actividades ejecutadas o en desarrollo. **Cobertura geográfica:** Presencia en 38 municipios del país.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **CIFRAS CLAVE** 3,5K personas fallecidas tras dos poderosos terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela el 24 de junio 6,4K personas rescatadas tras dos poderosos terremotos que azotaron Venezuela el 24 de junio 750K personas podrían necesitar asistencia alimentaria entre junio y agosto en Honduras **VENEZUELA: TERREMOTO** Más de una semana después de los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio en la región centro-norte de Venezuela, las autoridades informan de 3.535 personas fallecidas, 16.740 heridas y 6.462 rescatadas, con casi 1.000 réplicas registradas. Al menos siete estados se han visto afectados, siendo La Guaira la zona más afectada. Aproximadamente 17.845 personas han perdido sus hogares, y 80 campamentos transitorios —concentrados en Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira— operan ahora al 73% de su capacidad. La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano fue transferida formalmente de equipos internacionales a la Protección Civil de Venezuela, aunque varios equipos internacionales siguen desplegados para apoyar los esfuerzos de recuperación.

chunks.title: Latinoamérica y El Caribe Resumen de Situación Semanal al 7 de julio 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: Aproximadamente 17.845 personas han perdido sus hogares, y 80 campamentos transitorios —concentrados en Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira— operan ahora al 73% de su capacidad. La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano fue transferida formalmente de equipos internacionales a la Protección Civil de Venezuela, aunque varios equipos internacionales siguen desplegados para apoyar los esfuerzos de recuperación. El 1 de julio comenzó un período de luto nacional de siete días. Las necesidades prioritarias siguen concentradas en la protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH) y seguridad alimentaria, especialmente entre las familias desplazadas y aquellas en las zonas más cercanas al epicentro. La respuesta humanitaria sigue ampliándose en todos los sectores, con servicios de salud, protección y apoyo psicosocial que llegan a varios cientos de personas afectadas a través de consultas, asesoramiento y gestión de casos en los campamentos transitorios.

chunks.text: Las necesidades prioritarias siguen concentradas en la protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH) y seguridad alimentaria, especialmente entre las familias desplazadas y aquellas en las zonas más cercanas al epicentro. La respuesta humanitaria sigue ampliándose en todos los sectores, con servicios de salud, protección y apoyo psicosocial que llegan a varios cientos de personas afectadas a través de consultas, asesoramiento y gestión de casos en los campamentos transitorios. Los socios de WASH están ampliando la infraestructura de saneamiento y la distribución de kits de higiene, mientras que continúan las mejoras en los campamentos transitorios. La evaluación inicial del UNDRR estima que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura ascienden a aproximadamente 37.000 millones de dólares, mientras que la estimación preliminar del PNUD sobre los daños físicos directos es de 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalente al 6% del PIB. Apoya [aquí al Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela]( Más información en: [ReliefWeb Response]( **ECUADOR: INUNDACIÓN** El 3 de julio, fuertes lluvias provocaron el desbordamiento del río Zamora, lo que desencadenó graves inundaciones en Guadalupe, en el municipio de Zamora, en la provincia amazónica de Zamora Chinchipe. Los informes preliminares de la Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos de Ecuador (SNGR) indican 5 personas fallecidas, 10 desaparecidas y 38 heridas, incluidos bomberos implicados en operaciones de evacuación y rescate. Se estima que 300 personas han sido afectadas y 200 desplazadas, con daños en viviendas, carreteras, suministro de agua, electricidad, telecomunicaciones, cultivos y medios de vida. Las autoridades nacionales y locales han activado mecanismos de coordinación de emergencia, establecido un albergue temporal para familias desplazadas y lideran operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades y la prestación de asistencia humanitaria. **CENTROAMÉRICA: SEGURIDAD ALIMENTARIA** FEWS NET pronostica precipitaciones por debajo de la media y condiciones secas persistentes en la mayor parte de Centroamérica hasta principios de julio, a pesar del aumento de las precipitaciones a principios de junio, que no compensaron los déficits a largo plazo.

Se prevé que la mayoría de las zonas productoras de granos básicos reciban no más del 45% de la precipitación media histórica entre el 16 de junio y el 10 de julio, con los déficits más pronunciados, de hasta el 65%, concentrados en Guatemala y Nicaragua. En Honduras, ya se han registrado resultados de Crisis (Fase 3 de la CIF) en el Corredor Seco y en el departamento de Choluteca, en la costa del Pacífico. FEWS NET estima que entre 500.000 y 749.999 personas necesitarán asistencia alimentaria humanitaria a nivel nacional, con picos entre junio y agosto.

chunks.title: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 7 July 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: **KEY FIGURES** 3.5K people dead after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela on 24 June 6.4K people rescued after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela on 24 June 750K people may require food assistance between June-August in Honduras **VENEZUELA: EARTHQUAKE** More than a week after the 24 June magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes in Venezuela’s north-central region, authorities report 3,535 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued, with nearly 1,000 aftershocks recorded. At least seven states have been affected, with La Guaira remaining the hardest hit. Approximately 17,845 people have lost their homes, and 80 transitional camps - concentrated in Caracas, Miranda, and La Guaira - are now operating at 73 per cent capacity. Coordination of Urban Search and Rescue operations has formally transferred from international teams to Venezuela’s Civil Protection, though several international teams remain deployed to support recovery efforts.

chunks.title: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 7 July 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
chunks.text: Approximately 17,845 people have lost their homes, and 80 transitional camps - concentrated in Caracas, Miranda, and La Guaira - are now operating at 73 per cent capacity. Coordination of Urban Search and Rescue operations has formally transferred from international teams to Venezuela’s Civil Protection, though several international teams remain deployed to support recovery efforts. A seven-day national mourning period began on 1 July. Priority needs remain concentrated in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security, particularly among displaced families and those in areas closest to the epicentre. The humanitarian response continues to scale up across sectors, with health, protection, and psychosocial support services reaching several hundred affected people through consultations, counselling, and case management in transitional camps.

chunks.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #1: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 06 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
chunks.text: In response to the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, AMDA has dispatched its emergency relief team to reach out to people in affected areas. The team comprises four members, including AMDA President Dr. Takushi Sato, one nurse, and two physicians from AMDA Peru. At around 6:00 p.m. on 24 June local time, two powerful earthquakes measuring magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 struck northwestern Venezuela in succession. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA), the earthquakes had claimed 2,295 lives, injured 11,267 people, and affected more than 26,000 people (as of 1 July).

chunks.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #1: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 06 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
chunks.text: At around 6:00 p.m. on 24 June local time, two powerful earthquakes measuring magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 struck northwestern Venezuela in succession. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA), the earthquakes had claimed 2,295 lives, injured 11,267 people, and affected more than 26,000 people (as of 1 July). As of now, an advance team of two physicians from AMDA Peru and a Japanese nurse from the U.S. has already arrived in Venezuela since 5 July. Upon arrival, the team held a meeting with local counterparts in Caracas to coordinate relief efforts. Meanwhile, AMDA President Dr. Takushi Sato departed from Okayama, Japan, on 6 July to join the mission.

chunks.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #1: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 06 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
chunks.text: Upon arrival, the team held a meeting with local counterparts in Caracas to coordinate relief efforts. Meanwhile, AMDA President Dr. Takushi Sato departed from Okayama, Japan, on 6 July to join the mission. He is expected to arrive at Arturo Michelena International Airport in the city of Valencia the next day, where he will join AMDA’s local partners. Prior to the personnel deployment, an AMDA coordinator paid a courtesy visit to the Embassy of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in Tokyo to report on the project implementation. During his visit, Venezuelan Ambassador to Japan His Excellency Seiko Luis Ishikawa Kobayashi expressed his full support for AMDA's medical relief activities.

chunks.title: Todas las ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español responden a las necesidades de la población en Venezuela tras los terremotos
chunks.text: Las 8 ONG del Comité de Emergencia, Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision, se han volcado en la respuesta a los terremotos que sufrió Venezuela el pasado 24 de junio que dejan, hasta el momento según las últimas cifras oficiales, 235 personas fallecidas y 4.300 heridas. Ante una primera evaluación y análisis de la situación, y una vez garantizada la seguridad e integridad de sus equipos, el objetivo principal de estas organizaciones es atender a la población más vulnerable, junto con las organizaciones locales, que tienen presencia y arraigo en Venezuela para poder prestarles apoyo, de manera coordinada con los actores humanitarios y estructuras de coordinación que ya existen en el país. El objetivo fundamental de las organizaciones es dar soporte a personas enfermas, niños, niñas y mujeres, cubriendo sus necesidades más inmediatas en las áreas de trabajo en las que suelen trabajar como alimentación e higiene, refugio y atención sanitaria y psicológica. La afectación de los seísmos se concentra en la franja centro-norte del país —incluyendo Caracas, Valencia y estados cercanos—, una de las zonas más densamente pobladas de Venezuela.

La afectación de los seísmos se concentra en la franja centro-norte del país —incluyendo Caracas, Valencia y estados cercanos—, una de las zonas más densamente pobladas de Venezuela. Las autoridades han confirmado daños estructurales y colapsos parciales de edificios en distintas zonas de Caracas y en el estado Aragua, así como afectaciones en infraestructuras clave como hospitales. Respuesta a las necesidades humanitarias urgentes Las principales necesidades identificadas en estos momentos incluyen: Alojamiento seguro para familias cuyas viviendas han quedado dañadas o inhabitables. Acceso a agua potable, saneamiento e higiene y materiales de primera necesidad como mantas o ropa.

Empresas y medios de comunicación también se solidarizan con las víctimas Los grupos y empresas que son parte del Comité de Emergencia están volcados y colaborando ya en la recaudación de fondos, activando sus planes de llamamiento a la ayuda. En estas primeras horas ya se han unido a la respuesta Allianz Partners, Atresmedia, Atrevia, CaixaBank, Correos España, Editorial Santillana, Exterior Plus, Forética, Fundación Quirónsalud, Iberdrola, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, PayPal, Prisa, Televisión Canaria, Televisión de Galicia, TuMedio, RTVE, Tragsa, Unidad Editorial, Vivir Ediciones, Vocento y Worldcoo, cediendo sus espacios en medios de comunicación, publicidad, digital, programas de televisión y radio y soportes publicitarios para difundir el llamamiento que desde el Comité de Emergencia Español se está realizando. chunks.title: Families displaced by Venezuela earthquakes at risk of infection amid water and sanitation shortages
chunks.text: **CARACAS, 7 July 2026** **–** Hundreds of people displaced by Venezuela’s devastating earthquakes are sharing extremely limited toilets in informal camps, while others are risking returning to damaged homes to use bathrooms despite fears the buildings could collapse, Save the Children said. Thousands of people sheltering in tents for the past 12 days are without regular access to safe drinking water, running water and toilets, putting them at risk of skin infections, diarrhea and gastrointestinal illnesses, with children particularly vulnerable. Women and girls are having to manage their periods without privacy, clean water and sanitary products. In some informal camps, there are only one or two pre-existing toilets, some of which were damaged by the earthquake, shared among hundreds of displaced people.

chunks.text: Women and girls are having to manage their periods without privacy, clean water and sanitary products. In some informal camps, there are only one or two pre-existing toilets, some of which were damaged by the earthquake, shared among hundreds of displaced people. Many people are instead defecating and urinating outdoors, including in places where children play. Ongoing thundershowers and high daytime temperatures risk exacerbating the spread of infections. **Gabriela\*, 31, is a doctor working with Paluz,** a Save the Children local partner running mobile health clinics for people affected by the earthquake. **Gabriela\* said:** *“People are defecating out in the open, whether it's in the woods, behind rubble, or right in the sea, which means that the water that they are bathing in is contaminated. This can cause skin diseases and eye irritations.”* **Isabel\*, 44, from Caracas** was displaced with her husband and three children and now lives in a tent in front of the building in which the family used to live. **Her oldest child, David\*,9,** was already suffering from a kidney problem.

The earthquake also damaged waste management systems and water pipelines. chunks.title: Séismes au Venezuela : l'IFRC déploie un hôpital de campagne d'urgence et soutient la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne dans la distribution de kits de secours humanitaires. | IFRC
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: **Caracas / Panama / Genève, le 6 juillet 2026** – La Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) poursuit l'intensification de sa réponse aux récents séismes au Venezuela et renforce son soutien à la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne afin de fournir une assistance humanitaire aux populations touchées par cette catastrophe sans précédent. Au cours du week-end (5 juillet), l'IFRC a déployé un hôpital de campagne d'urgence à La Guaira, en partenariat avec la Croix-Rouge espagnole, qui a également mobilisé des médecins et d'autres professionnels de santé. Cet hôpital de campagne est en mesure de fournir des soins de santé primaires à 30 000 personnes et sera pleinement opérationnel dans les prochains jours. Il pourra également assurer des services de santé maternelle et infantile, des campagnes de vaccination, la surveillance épidémiologique et nutritionnelle, ainsi qu'un soutien en santé mentale et psychosocial.

chunks.title: Séismes au Venezuela : l'IFRC déploie un hôpital de campagne d'urgence et soutient la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne dans la distribution de kits de secours humanitaires. | IFRC
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: Cet hôpital de campagne est en mesure de fournir des soins de santé primaires à 30 000 personnes et sera pleinement opérationnel dans les prochains jours. Il pourra également assurer des services de santé maternelle et infantile, des campagnes de vaccination, la surveillance épidémiologique et nutritionnelle, ainsi qu'un soutien en santé mentale et psychosocial. Il dispose en outre d'une capacité d'accueil pouvant aller jusqu'à 20 patients en observation pendant la nuit. Des cliniques de santé mobiles commenceront également à être déployées afin d'atteindre les populations affectées et de garantir l'accès aux soins dans les communautés que nous accompagnons. Cet hôpital de campagne d'urgence viendra renforcer celui déjà exploité par la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne depuis le début de la crise.

chunks.title: Séismes au Venezuela : l'IFRC déploie un hôpital de campagne d'urgence et soutient la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne dans la distribution de kits de secours humanitaires. | IFRC
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: Des cliniques de santé mobiles commenceront également à être déployées afin d'atteindre les populations affectées et de garantir l'accès aux soins dans les communautés que nous accompagnons. Cet hôpital de campagne d'urgence viendra renforcer celui déjà exploité par la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne depuis le début de la crise. Ce dernier a déjà pris en charge des centaines de blessés traumatiques dans les jours qui ont suivi les deux séismes et concentre désormais de plus en plus ses activités sur les soins de santé primaires et le soutien psychosocial aux personnes affectées. En complément de ces services de santé, la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne, avec le soutien de l'IFRC, distribue des articles de secours dans les zones touchées, notamment dans la paroisse de San Martín à Caracas, où des familles dont les habitations ont été endommagées par les séismes sont hébergées dans une école. Les articles distribués comprennent des kits d'hygiène, des kits de nettoyage, des kits de couchage, des filtres à eau et des jerrycans.

chunks.title: Séismes au Venezuela : l'IFRC déploie un hôpital de campagne d'urgence et soutient la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne dans la distribution de kits de secours humanitaires. | IFRC
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: En complément de ces services de santé, la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne, avec le soutien de l'IFRC, distribue des articles de secours dans les zones touchées, notamment dans la paroisse de San Martín à Caracas, où des familles dont les habitations ont été endommagées par les séismes sont hébergées dans une école. Les articles distribués comprennent des kits d'hygiène, des kits de nettoyage, des kits de couchage, des filtres à eau et des jerrycans. Cette distribution fait partie des 36 tonnes d'aide humanitaire acheminées au Venezuela depuis les plateformes logistiques humanitaires de l'IFRC au Panama et en Argentine. L'intensification des services de santé et de la distribution de l'aide intervient alors que les opérations de recherche et de sauvetage ralentissent progressivement. À mesure que la crise évolue, les besoins sanitaires des communautés touchées évoluent également. Dans les premiers jours suivant les séismes, les interventions étaient principalement axées sur les soins d'urgence.

chunks.title: Séismes au Venezuela : l'IFRC déploie un hôpital de campagne d'urgence et soutient la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne dans la distribution de kits de secours humanitaires. | IFRC
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
chunks.text: L'intensification des services de santé et de la distribution de l'aide intervient alors que les opérations de recherche et de sauvetage ralentissent progressivement. À mesure que la crise évolue, les besoins sanitaires des communautés touchées évoluent également. Dans les premiers jours suivant les séismes, les interventions étaient principalement axées sur les soins d'urgence. Les évaluations actuelles identifient désormais le soutien en santé mentale et psychosocial, les soins de santé primaires et maternels, les activités de prévention, ainsi que l'accès à l'eau potable et à l'assainissement comme des priorités essentielles pour cette nouvelle phase de la réponse humanitaire. L'IFRC appelle la communauté internationale, les donateurs et les partenaires à soutenir son [appel d'urgence]( afin que les communautés touchées au Venezuela puissent bénéficier de toute l'assistance vitale dont elles ont un besoin urgent. Les porte-parole de l'IFRC sont disponibles pour des entretiens depuis Caracas et peuvent faciliter la couverture médiatique des opérations menées à Caracas et à La Guaira, notamment sur la situation humanitaire, les efforts de secours, les besoins humanitaires et la nécessité de maintenir un soutien international dans les semaines à venir. **Au Venezuela:** Paolo Cravero, +41 79 894 8396 **A Panama:** Susana Arroyo Barrantes, +507 6999-3199 **A Genève:** Scott Craig, +41 76 370 3575

chunks.text: L'IFRC appelle la communauté internationale, les donateurs et les partenaires à soutenir son [appel d'urgence]( afin que les communautés touchées au Venezuela puissent bénéficier de toute l'assistance vitale dont elles ont un besoin urgent. Les porte-parole de l'IFRC sont disponibles pour des entretiens depuis Caracas et peuvent faciliter la couverture médiatique des opérations menées à Caracas et à La Guaira, notamment sur la situation humanitaire, les efforts de secours, les besoins humanitaires et la nécessité de maintenir un soutien international dans les semaines à venir. **Au Venezuela:** Paolo Cravero, +41 79 894 8396 **A Panama:** Susana Arroyo Barrantes, +507 6999-3199 **A Genève:** Scott Craig, +41 76 370 3575

chunks.title: Public health emergency looms in Venezuela as health system struggles to meet heightened needs following twin earthquakes | The IRC
chunks.text: Caracas, Venezuela, July 7, 2026 — A public health emergency is unfolding in Venezuela as already overstretched health systems struggle to meet heightened need following twin earthquakes, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) is warning. An IRC-led assessment in the affected areas found that 20 health facilities are facing severe shortages of vital medical supplies. The assessment also found that there are only 1,038 healthcare workers serving a total population of over 1.7 million people–about one healthcare worker for every 1700 people. Venezuela's health system was already short of equipment, medications, and reliable power before the earthquakes, leaving little capacity to both provide emergency first aid to the over 16,000 injured and meet the ongoing needs of vulnerable communities. **IRC’s Emergency Response Lead for the Venezuela Earthquakes, Rafael Velasquez Garcia, said:** *“The second phase of this crisis is just beginning.

chunks.text: The assessment also found that there are only 1,038 healthcare workers serving a total population of over 1.7 million people–about one healthcare worker for every 1700 people. Venezuela's health system was already short of equipment, medications, and reliable power before the earthquakes, leaving little capacity to both provide emergency first aid to the over 16,000 injured and meet the ongoing needs of vulnerable communities. **IRC’s Emergency Response Lead for the Venezuela Earthquakes, Rafael Velasquez Garcia, said:** *“The second phase of this crisis is just beginning. What started as a devastating natural disaster is quickly ballooning into a public health emergency. Rising displacement, failing health infrastructure, and waterborne and respiratory diseases threaten to push thousands of more people into humanitarian need when the capacity to respond is at its lowest. Even with sustained international support it will take many months for health systems to recover.”* Air quality in rubble zones has severely deteriorated due to concrete dust and unrecovered remains.

chunks.text: Rising displacement, failing health infrastructure, and waterborne and respiratory diseases threaten to push thousands of more people into humanitarian need when the capacity to respond is at its lowest. Even with sustained international support it will take many months for health systems to recover.”* Air quality in rubble zones has severely deteriorated due to concrete dust and unrecovered remains. Combined with disrupted water and sanitation systems, the IRC is deeply concerned about the high risk of the rapid spread of waterborne and airborne diseases–a risk that will only intensify as the initial rescue phase winds down and international attention wanes. Thirty-eight hospitals were damaged by the earthquakes. The main referral hospital in La Guaira, the hardest hit city, exceeded capacity within one day, and resources continue to run dangerously low even as aid arrives.

chunks.text: Thirty-eight hospitals were damaged by the earthquakes. The main referral hospital in La Guaira, the hardest hit city, exceeded capacity within one day, and resources continue to run dangerously low even as aid arrives. As hospitals focus on treating survivors, mobile health teams have reported a surge in people seeking non-emergency health and prenatal care. Even those who weren’t directly affected by the earthquakes are now being impacted as medical care becomes increasingly difficult to access. As search and rescue teams begin to wind down, the crisis is not subsiding, it is just becoming less visible.

chunks.text: Even those who weren’t directly affected by the earthquakes are now being impacted as medical care becomes increasingly difficult to access. As search and rescue teams begin to wind down, the crisis is not subsiding, it is just becoming less visible. Teams report families moving between parks throughout the day, making it difficult to locate patients and continue their care. Families who have lost their homes are relocating to urban centers, where they’ll be harder to reach, but their needs will remain just as urgent. The IRC is prioritizing health services both in stationary centers and mobile units to meet people where they are, focusing on displaced people, the elderly, those with mobility issues, and children who may not be able to get themselves to health facilities.

The IRC is prioritizing health services both in stationary centers and mobile units to meet people where they are, focusing on displaced people, the elderly, those with mobility issues, and children who may not be able to get themselves to health facilities. In addition, the IRC is supporting the reactivation of the Bacteriology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine (IMT) of the Central University of Venezuela to help mitigate the rise in respiratory and water-borne diseases as well as procuring and distributing hundreds of standard hygiene kits and water purification kits.

chunks.text: **Situation Report No. 13** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **06 July 2026** **Time: 8:00 pm** **Highlights** Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,000 aftershocks.** At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state. Official toll: **3,535 people dead and 16,740 injured.** A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.** Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams remain deployed in the affected areas, in coordination with OCHA, more than one week after the earthquakes. **The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.** **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1.048 aftershocks.** More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **3,535 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued s**ince the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately **17,854** people lost their homes.

Impact on infrastructure  Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.  An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) indicates that direct damage to housing and infrastructure amounts to approximately US$37 billion.
